paper_a_title: Backdoored Retrievers for Prompt Injection Attacks on Retrieval Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
paper_b_title: Defense Against Prompt Injection Attack by Leveraging Attack Techniques
gold_rationale: Paper A is an offensive study that develops corpus poisoning and a novel backdoor attack on the dense retriever during fine-tuning, with the goal of maximizing Attack Success Rate (ASR) for goals like malicious link injection and denial of service. Paper B is a defensive study that inverts training-free prompt injection attack methods to build a defense that operates at the prompt/generation level, with the goal of minimizing ASR against existing attacks. The action_policy is opposite (attack vs. defense), the intervention_point differs (retriever fine-tuning vs. inference-time prompt manipulation), the failure_type differs (retrieval-stage poisoning susceptibility vs. generator inability to ignore injected instructions), and although both report ASR, the optimization direction is inverted, so the metric_target is not commensurable. Evidence_assumption also diverges: Paper A presumes attacker control over corpus or training data, Paper B presumes a deployed LLM facing standard injection attempts in retrieved content.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both papers to either (a) attack the same RAG configuration under a shared threat model and report ASR in the same direction, or (b) evaluate Paper B's defense against Paper A's specific retriever-poisoning/backdoor attacks on a shared benchmark, with matched LLMs, retrievers, corpora, and injection payloads, so that lower ASR for the defended system can be directly contrasted with the undefended ASR achieved by the attack.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper is trying to make a number go up because that number represents an adversary winning, while the other paper is trying to make essentially the same number go down because the same outcome means the system was compromised. They also touch different parts of the retrieval-augmented pipeline and operate under different threat scenarios. Putting their headline numbers next to each other on a single leaderboard would lead a practitioner to draw conclusions about relative strength that the underlying studies do not support.

paper_a_title: ADMIT: Few-shot Knowledge Poisoning Attacks on RAG-based Fact Checking
paper_b_title: Hidden-in-Plain-Text: A Benchmark for Social-Web Indirect Prompt Injection in RAG
gold_rationale: Paper A proposes a novel offensive technique (ADMIT) and reports a single headline number — 86% attack success rate at a 0.93×10^-6 poisoning ratio — in a fact-checking setting where credible evidence dominates the pool. Paper B is a benchmark/harness paper (OpenRAG-Soc) targeting indirect prompt injection and retrieval poisoning on social-web content, reporting a basket of measures (attack-time-of-response, rank shifts in sparse/dense retrievers, utility, latency) alongside deployable defenses (HTML/Markdown sanitization, Unicode normalization, attribution-gating). The failure_type differs (semantic veracity flip vs. web-native IPI carriers); the evidence_assumption differs (cross-domain fact-checking corpora vs. social-web UGC); the metric_target differs (single ASR vs. multi-axis benchmark scores); and the action_policy differs (introduce one attack method vs. release a benchmark and harness with mitigations). These cannot be placed on a shared leaderboard meaningfully.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both works would need to (i) attack the same threat model on the same corpus (e.g., either both run on OpenRAG-Soc's social-web carriers or both on RAG-fact-checking corpora), (ii) share an identical ASR definition with the same poisoning budget and retriever/LLM stack, and (iii) play the same role — either both as attack methods evaluated under a common harness, or ADMIT plugged into OpenRAG-Soc as one of several attackers and reported with the benchmark's full metric panel including defenses. Without at least a shared corpus, shared retriever/LLM, and a shared ASR definition under matched poisoning budgets, the headline numbers are not on the same scale.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper delivers a single offensive technique with one headline success-rate number on fact-checking corpora; the other delivers a reproducible test suite for social-web content that reports a panel of scores covering both attackers and defenders. The target tasks, corpora, and reporting styles do not line up, and the deliverables play different roles in a practitioner's workflow. Listing the 86% number next to OpenRAG-Soc scores in one ranked table would lead a practitioner to draw conclusions the two works do not jointly support.

paper_a_title: ProGRank: Probe-Gradient Reranking to Defend Dense-Retriever RAG from Corpus Poisoning
paper_b_title: On the Vulnerability of Applying Retrieval-Augmented Generation within Knowledge-Intensive Application Domains
gold_rationale: Both papers address corpus poisoning of dense-retriever RAG and propose retriever-side defenses, so there is genuine topical overlap. However, the coordinates diverge meaningfully. Paper A treats a broad family of poisoning threats (retrieval-optimized, joint, trigger-based, misleading-evidence) across three general datasets and three retrievers, with a reranking mechanism scored on defense strength and a robustness–utility tradeoff in both retrieval and end-to-end settings. Paper B is framed around universal poisoning in knowledge-intensive medical Q&A, characterizes a specific embedding-deviation pattern, and reports detection rates from a detection-based defense. The threat scope, evaluation suites, defense mechanism (rerank vs detect/filter), and headline metric (defense/utility tradeoff vs detection rate) are only partially commensurable.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation protocol with (1) the same corpora, retrievers, and poisoning families spanning both general and medical domains; (2) aligned threat models clarifying universal vs targeted, query-conditioned vs query-agnostic poisoning; (3) common metrics that both methods can report, e.g., post-defense top-K poisoning rate and end-to-end attack success, plus precision/recall of any flagging step, with clean-query utility held fixed; and (4) matched compute/latency budgets so reranking and detection pipelines are scored under comparable cost constraints.
independent_rubric_rationale: Both works propose defenses for poisoned passages in RAG, so a reader could reasonably put them side by side. But the headline numbers describe different things: one is a reranking score reported with a utility tradeoff across general benchmarks and several attack styles, while the other is a detector tuned to a particular embedding pattern in medical Q&A. Treating the two reported figures as comparable entries on a single leaderboard would give a partially misleading picture of which approach is stronger, because the test conditions and scoring conventions do not line up cleanly.

paper_a_title: Defending against Indirect Prompt Injection by Instruction Detection
paper_b_title: A Few Words Can Distort Graphs: Knowledge Poisoning Attacks on Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Paper A is a defense-side contribution: it proposes InstructDetector, which uses hidden-state and gradient features from intermediate LLM layers to detect indirect prompt injection in standard RAG, reporting detection accuracy (99.60% in-domain, 96.90% OOD) and reduced attack success rate (0.03%) on BIPIA. Paper B is an attack-side contribution targeting Graph-based RAG via knowledge poisoning of source text before graph construction, reporting attacker success (TKPA 93.1%; UKPA collapses QA accuracy from 95% to 50% with <0.05% text edited). The threat models differ (instruction injection vs. corpus knowledge poisoning), the system under study differs (vanilla RAG vs. GraphRAG), the stage of operation differs (post-retrieval detection vs. pre-construction corpus manipulation), the benchmarks and metric semantics differ (defender detection accuracy vs. attacker success rate), and the role differs (defender vs. attacker). None of the five coordinates align.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both works would need to address the same role (e.g., both defenses or both attacks), the same RAG architecture (standard RAG or GraphRAG), the same threat model (e.g., both IPI or both knowledge poisoning), shared benchmarks/datasets, and a common metric defined identically (e.g., post-defense attack success rate on the same attacker, or attack success rate against the same defended pipeline). At minimum, Paper A would need to be evaluated against knowledge poisoning of GraphRAG, or Paper B's attacks would need to be tested against InstructDetector on the same benchmark.
independent_rubric_rationale: A practitioner reading the two headline numbers side by side (≈99.6% versus ≈93.1%) on one leaderboard would draw entirely wrong conclusions, because the numbers describe opposite roles in different pipelines: one summarizes how well a defender catches injected text in a standard retrieval pipeline, while the other summarizes how often an attacker succeeds against a graph-structured retrieval pipeline using corpus rewriting. They are not measuring the same phenomenon on the same system, so ranking them together would mislead deployment decisions.

paper_a_title: Decide Then Retrieve: A Training-Free Framework with Uncertainty-Guided Triggering and Dual-Path Retrieval
paper_b_title: Know Or Not: a library for evaluating out-of-knowledge base robustness
gold_rationale: Paper A proposes a training-free RAG method (DTR) that uses generation uncertainty to gate retrieval and a dual-path retriever, targeting EM/F1 improvements on five open-domain QA benchmarks against RAG baselines. Paper B presents an evaluation library (knowornot) and the PolicyBench benchmark for measuring out-of-knowledge-base (OOKB) robustness — essentially whether models appropriately abstain when context is missing — and does not propose a new RAG method. The two works diverge across all five coordinates: the failure mode addressed (noisy/unnecessary retrieval and sparse-query handling vs. hallucination on OOKB queries / failure to abstain), the evidence assumption (open-domain corpora with answerable queries vs. domain-specific KBs with potentially unanswerable queries), the locus of change (modifying the RAG pipeline vs. building an evaluation tool), the headline metric (EM/F1 vs. abstention/OOKB robustness), and the deliverable policy (a method to deploy vs. a benchmark/library to measure).
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both papers to report on a shared task with a shared metric — for example, running DTR through the knowornot/PolicyBench OOKB-robustness pipeline and reporting abstention behavior, or evaluating knowornot-instrumented systems on the same open-domain QA benchmarks (NQ, TriviaQA, etc.) with EM/F1. It would also require matched LLM generators, retrievers, and KB construction so that the contribution of method vs. evaluation harness is separable. Without such overlap, any leaderboard placement conflates a system-improvement claim with an evaluation-tool claim.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works are doing different jobs: one builds a smarter RAG pipeline aimed at boosting exact-match and F1 on standard open-domain QA, while the other releases a library plus a government-policy benchmark for probing whether systems appropriately decline to answer when the knowledge base lacks the needed information. Their headline numbers live in different units, on different datasets, with different definitions of success (better answers vs. better refusals). Dropping them side by side on one leaderboard would lead a practitioner to draw conclusions about relative quality that the underlying studies do not support.

paper_a_title: Over-Searching in Search-Augmented Large Language Models
paper_b_title: QuCo-RAG: Quantifying Uncertainty from the Pre-training Corpus for Dynamic Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Paper A studies over-searching (unnecessary tool invocation harming cost and abstention on unanswerable queries) and contributes a diagnostic benchmark (OverSearchQA) plus a cost-aware metric (Tokens Per Correctness), with mitigations applied at the query and retrieval levels. Paper B targets the opposite-leaning failure mode—hallucinations from poorly-calibrated internal-signal triggers in dynamic RAG—and proposes a new retrieval-triggering method (QuCo-RAG) grounded in pre-training corpus statistics, evaluated by EM gains on multi-hop QA. The two assume different sources of unreliability (search-tool overuse vs. model-internal confidence miscalibration), intervene at different decision points, and report incommensurate primary metrics (TPC and abstention vs. EM). Therefore they cannot be placed on a common leaderboard or directly ranked.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation setting where both systems are run on the same benchmarks (covering both answerable and unanswerable queries, and ideally multi-hop QA), using a common cost-quality metric such as TPC alongside EM/abstention, with matched LLM backbones, identical retrieval corpora, and reporting of both retrieval-trigger frequency and downstream answer correctness. Without that joint protocol—and clarity on whether the goal is reducing unnecessary retrievals or improving triggered-retrieval quality—the two contributions remain complementary rather than rankable.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works pursue opposite-facing goals in retrieval-augmented generation: one diagnoses and discourages excessive tool use (highlighting cost and abstention on unanswerable inputs), while the other proposes a corpus-statistics trigger to improve answer correctness on multi-hop QA. They report on different benchmarks with different headline numbers (a cost-per-correctness ratio and abstention behavior versus exact-match gains), so a practitioner reading them side-by-side on one leaderboard would draw faulty conclusions about which system is 'better' for their use case.

paper_a_title: When to Trust: A Causality-Aware Calibration Framework for Accurate Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation.
paper_b_title: GRACE: Reinforcement Learning for Grounded Response and Abstention under Contextual Evidence
gold_rationale: Paper A has no text snippet available, only a title indicating a causality-aware calibration framework specifically for Knowledge Graph RAG. Paper B's snippet describes an RL-trained system (GRACE) for general textual retrieval with grounded answering plus explicit abstention, trained via a multi-stage gated reward and evaluated on two unspecified RAG benchmarks. From the visible information, the evidence_assumption diverges (structured KG triples vs. heterogeneous textual retrievers), the intervention_point diverges (calibration/trust scoring vs. RL fine-tuning of the generator), and the metric_target likely diverges (KG-RAG accuracy vs. joint accuracy/abstention balance). However, without Paper A's snippet, the actual benchmarks, baselines, and reported numbers cannot be verified, so a definitive valid/invalid call is not warranted. Conservatively underspecified.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers would need to (1) operate on the same evidence modality (either KG or text) or report a shared evaluation that abstracts across both; (2) report on at least one overlapping benchmark with identical splits and metrics; (3) use a comparable definition of 'correct' that handles abstention consistently (e.g., a unified accuracy/abstention-aware score); and (4) be evaluated under matched retriever quality and base-LLM choices so the two interventions act on comparable upstream pipelines.
independent_rubric_rationale: Because Paper A has no excerpt provided, its benchmarks, scoring protocol, and headline numbers are unknown. The title suggests it is scoped to knowledge-graph retrieval and trust calibration, whereas Paper B's visible abstract scopes to textual passages with grounding plus explicit 'I don't know' responses scored on a joint correctness/refusal balance. These look like different evaluation regimes, but without Paper A's reported setup and numbers it is not possible to confirm whether any shared leaderboard entry actually exists, so a confident judgment about practitioner-level confusion is not supportable from the supplied material.

paper_a_title: Reliable Decision‑Making via Calibration‑Oriented Retrieval‑Augmented Generation
paper_b_title: Sufficient Context: A New Lens on Retrieval Augmented Generation Systems
gold_rationale: Paper A has no text snippet available, only a title indicating a calibration-oriented approach to RAG for reliable decision-making. Paper B clearly proposes a 'sufficient context' classifier and a selective generation/abstention method, evaluated on selective accuracy (correct answers among responses) for Gemini, GPT, and Gemma. Without Paper A's methodology, datasets, baselines, and reported numbers, the five coordinates cannot be filled in for A with any confidence. From titles alone, the two works appear to address related reliability concerns in RAG via plausibly different mechanisms (calibration of confidence vs. context-sufficiency-guided abstention), but a coordinate-by-coordinate comparison is not possible from the supplied material.
what_valid_comparison_requires: At minimum: (1) Paper A's text or abstract to identify its failure mode (miscalibration vs. hallucination vs. retrieval error), (2) the evaluation datasets and retrievers used by both papers, (3) the target metric definitions (e.g., expected calibration error vs. selective accuracy vs. abstention rate), (4) the base LLMs and baselines so any reported improvements are over comparable starting points, and (5) whether both methods are training-free or require fine-tuning. Only then could the calibration-based and sufficient-context-based approaches be aligned for a fair side-by-side ranking.
independent_rubric_rationale: With no content available for Paper A, it is not possible to determine whether their headline numbers were produced on comparable datasets, models, and scoring conventions as Paper B's selective-generation results, so a single leaderboard placement cannot be safely judged either way.

paper_a_title: PrismRAG: Boosting RAG Factuality with Distractor Resilience and Strategized Reasoning
paper_b_title: The Curse of Helpfulness: Inverse Scaling Law in Robustness to Distractor Instructions via DistractionIF
gold_rationale: Although both papers share the umbrella term 'distractor' in RAG/reference-grounded settings, they target fundamentally different failure modes. Paper A (PrismRAG) addresses semi-relevant distractor passages that confuse a model during factual QA, and intervenes via supervised fine-tuning with synthetic distractor-aware QA pairs plus reasoning training, measured as factuality (+5.4% on 12 open-book QA benchmarks). Paper B (DistractionIF) addresses instruction-like semantic noise embedded in reference text (editorial comments, UI residues) that the model wrongly interprets as commands, intervenes via GRPO reinforcement learning, and measures robustness to distractor instructions (+15.5%) on its own benchmark. The headline percentages are computed on disjoint benchmarks evaluating different phenomena, so a direct ranking is not defensible.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation that fixes (a) the type of distractor (semi-relevant content distractors vs instruction-like noise distractors), (b) the same evaluation benchmark and scoring protocol (factuality vs strict-data-following robustness), and (c) comparable base models and budgets. Either both methods would need to be run on PrismRAG's 12-benchmark factuality suite, or both on DistractionIF's instruction-robustness suite (ideally both), with the same backbone LLMs and training compute. Without such a common axis, the +5.4% and +15.5% numbers are not commensurable.
independent_rubric_rationale: Despite shared 'distractor' vocabulary, the two works tackle conceptually distinct problems: one concerns whether noisy retrieved passages degrade answer correctness in question answering, while the other concerns whether command-like fragments inside reference text hijack the model into following them instead of the user. Their headline numbers come from entirely different test suites measuring different behaviors on potentially different base models, so juxtaposing them on a single leaderboard would suggest a head-to-head competition that simply does not exist and could lead a practitioner to pick the wrong technique for their actual problem.

paper_a_title: Parallel Key-Value Cache Fusion for Position Invariant RAG
paper_b_title: Beyond RAG vs. Long-Context: Learning Distraction-Aware Retrieval for Efficient Knowledge Grounding
gold_rationale: Paper A (KV Fusion) targets positional bias ('Lost in the Middle') in decoder-only generators by altering KV-cache prefill so that order of retrieved passages does not affect output; its headline metrics are position invariance and accuracy on NQ/TriviaQA/POPQA under shuffled passage order. Paper B (LDAR) targets distractor interference and the RAG-vs-long-context trade-off by training an adaptive retriever that selects a variable number of passages; its headline metric is the performance/token-usage Pareto curve over six knowledge-intensive benchmarks across multiple LLM backbones (including GPT-4o). The pipeline stage being modified differs (generator-side cache fusion vs. retriever-side selection policy), the headline failure mode differs (order sensitivity vs. distractor amplification under large contexts), and the reported quantities are not on a common axis. Datasets overlap only loosely, and neither paper's numbers are reported under conditions that the other's framework controls for.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation suite with overlapping LLM backbones and identical retriever/candidate pool, reporting (a) accuracy under shuffled vs. canonical passage order at matched k and token budgets, and (b) accuracy vs. token-usage Pareto curves. Ideally one would also run a combined system (LDAR retriever feeding into a KV-Fusion generator) to disentangle retriever-side and generator-side contributions, and report variance across at least the union of NQ/TriviaQA/POPQA and the six LDAR benchmarks under one prompting protocol.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems modify different parts of the RAG pipeline and report headline numbers on largely different benchmarks with different LLM backbones, different passage-count regimes, and different evaluation emphases (robustness to context ordering versus a performance-vs-token-cost curve). Dropping their top-line scores into a single leaderboard would lead a practitioner to infer a head-to-head ranking that the underlying experiments do not actually support, and could obscure the fact that the two approaches are largely complementary rather than substitutable.

paper_a_title: Entropy-Based Decoding for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models
paper_b_title: RAFT: Adapting Language Model to Domain Specific RAG
gold_rationale: The two papers occupy fundamentally different positions in the RAG pipeline. Paper A targets the distractibility failure with a training-free, inference-time entropy-based ensemble plus contrastive decoding policy, assuming a frozen LLM and retrieved passages at test time, and is benchmarked on open-domain QA. Paper B targets a related but distinct failure (poor domain-specific grounding and distractor handling) via a supervised fine-tuning recipe with CoT and verbatim citation, assuming access to in-domain training data, and is benchmarked on PubMed, HotpotQA, and Gorilla. The intervention points (decoding vs training), evidence assumptions (frozen general LLM vs domain-tuned LLM), action policies, and target benchmarks differ substantially, so reported numbers are not on a common axis.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation suite (same datasets, retriever, base model, and top-k context), matched compute/data budgets that account for RAFT's fine-tuning cost vs the decoding method's zero training cost, and a clearly stated common failure target (e.g., distractor robustness on the same QA benchmark). Ideally one would also report both methods, and a combined RAFT+entropy-decoding variant, under identical conditions before ranking them.
independent_rubric_rationale: One work is a plug-in decoding trick that needs no extra training and is shown on open-domain QA, while the other is a domain-specific fine-tuning recipe evaluated on specialized corpora like PubMed and Gorilla. Dropping their headline numbers into a single leaderboard would hide the differences in training cost, required data, base model state, and benchmark scope, and a practitioner picking the higher number would likely be choosing for the wrong reasons.

paper_a_title: Can Small Language Models Use What They Retrieve? An Empirical Study of Retrieval Utilization Across Model Scale
paper_b_title: END: Early Noise Dropping for Efficient and Effective Context Denoising
gold_rationale: Paper A is a diagnostic empirical study of whether sub-7B models can utilize retrieved passages, using an oracle-retrieval design to isolate utilization from retrieval quality; it proposes no new technique and concludes that RAG at this scale is net-negative. Paper B proposes END, a context-denoising method that uses early-layer probes to discard noisy chunks, reporting performance and efficiency gains on multiple datasets. The two diverge on nearly every coordinate: A's failure_type is small-model utilization breakdown vs. B's general noise-distraction; A has no intervention while B introduces a denoising algorithm; A's metric_target is the magnitude of the utilization bottleneck while B's is task accuracy plus compute savings; A's action_policy discourages deploying RAG at small scale while B's prescribes adopting END. Only evidence_assumption (both treat irrelevant/oracle context as a key lever) overlaps loosely.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head would need either (a) both papers reporting on the same tasks/datasets at overlapping model scales under matched retrieval conditions, or (b) END being evaluated specifically on the sub-7B utilization regime Paper A characterizes, so one could test whether END closes the bottleneck Paper A documents. As written, Paper A produces no method-level number that belongs on the same leaderboard as Paper B's reported improvements.
independent_rubric_rationale: Paper A is a diagnostic empirical study showing that small models (≤7B) cannot reliably use retrieved passages even when those passages contain the answer, and it proposes no new technique. Paper B introduces a denoising algorithm (END) and reports accuracy and efficiency gains, evaluated on different setups and likely on larger models. Placing the two main numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would mislead a practitioner because the papers answer different questions, operate at different scales, and one is a characterization of model limitations while the other is a system-level improvement.

paper_a_title: {MIRAGE}: A Metric-Intensive Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Evaluation
paper_b_title: RAGAs: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Snippets are unavailable, so judgment relies on titles and known scope. MIRAGE positions itself as a metric-intensive benchmark, i.e., a curated dataset plus a battery of scoring protocols for RAG systems. RAGAs positions itself as an automated, largely reference-free framework (typically LLM-judge based) for scoring RAG outputs along faithfulness/relevance/etc. These occupy different layers of the evaluation stack: one supplies the testbed, the other supplies the scorer. They are complementary, not substitutable, so any direct ranking would conflate distinct contributions. The break is primarily at the intervention_point (benchmark artifact vs. scoring methodology), the metric_target (benchmark numbers on RAG systems vs. correlation/agreement of an automatic judge with human ratings), and the action_policy (use this benchmark to grade your RAG pipeline vs. use this judge to grade RAG outputs anywhere).
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) both works evaluated as automatic judges on a common meta-evaluation set with matched correlation statistics against the same human references, or (b) both works evaluated as benchmarks using identical RAG systems, retrieval corpora, prompts, and metric implementations. At minimum, a shared protocol specifying dataset, models under test, and metric definitions is needed before any leaderboard placement.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works play different roles in the RAG evaluation pipeline: one supplies a scored test suite for grading RAG systems, while the other supplies an automatic scorer that can grade arbitrary RAG outputs. Putting their headline numbers side by side on one leaderboard would imply they are competing solutions to the same problem, which would steer a practitioner toward a false either-or choice. Confidence is tempered because no snippets were provided, but the titles make the role mismatch reasonably clear.

paper_a_title: ReEval: Automatic Hallucination Evaluation for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models via Transferable Adversarial Attacks
paper_b_title: Redefining Retrieval Evaluation in the Era of LLMs
gold_rationale: Paper A (ReEval) addresses hallucination/faithfulness failures in RAG generation via transferable adversarial attacks, producing hallucination-rate style measurements under perturbed evidence. Paper B (UDCG) addresses misalignment between classical IR scoring and downstream RAG accuracy, proposing a new retrieval-side scoring scheme whose target is correlation with end-to-end answer accuracy. The failure being diagnosed (generation hallucination vs. evaluation-metric misalignment), the locus of change (adversarial evaluation harness vs. redefined retrieval scoring), the headline number (hallucination/robustness rate vs. correlation with QA accuracy), and the recommended practice (probe LLMs adversarially vs. replace nDCG/MAP/MRR with UDCG) all differ. They share only the broad RAG-evaluation umbrella.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head comparison would require both papers to target the same evaluation construct (e.g., both predicting end-to-end RAG answer correctness, or both quantifying hallucination), share datasets and LLM generators, and report a common headline number on the same scale (e.g., correlation with answer accuracy, or hallucination rate under matched adversarial conditions). Without such alignment, any joint ranking conflates distinct objectives.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works pursue different goals within RAG evaluation. The first builds transferable adversarial probes to expose when generated answers contradict the supplied evidence, reporting how often models are fooled. The second redefines how retrieval quality scores should be computed so they better predict downstream answer correctness, reporting correlation with end-to-end accuracy. Their headline numbers live on different scales, use different datasets and pipelines, and answer different practitioner questions, so a single leaderboard entry placing them side by side would conflate unrelated research directions and likely mislead a reader about which approach is 'better'.

paper_a_title: MTRAG-UN: A Benchmark for Open Challenges in Multi-Turn RAG Conversations
paper_b_title: RAGLAB: A Modular and Research-Oriented Unified Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Paper A (MTRAG-UN) is a benchmark contribution targeting specific failure modes in multi-turn RAG (unanswerable, underspecified, nonstandalone questions, unclear responses), with the intervention at the evaluation-data level and metrics measuring retrieval/generation quality on challenging conversation turns. Paper B (RAGLAB) is a modular software framework for RAG research, with the intervention at the tooling/infrastructure level and the implicit metric being reproducibility and fair comparison across RAG methods. The action policy of Paper A is 'release a benchmark to test models', while Paper B's is 'release a framework to implement/compare methods'. These are categorically different artifacts and cannot be ranked on any single leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both works to deliver the same kind of artifact evaluated on the same axis - e.g., both being benchmarks with overlapping task distributions and shared scoring, or both being frameworks evaluated on the same engineering criteria. Alternatively, one could run RAGLAB's pipelines on MTRAG-UN and report scores, but that is a downstream use, not a head-to-head comparison of the two papers' headline contributions.
independent_rubric_rationale: Paper A delivers an evaluation dataset designed to stress-test multi-turn RAG systems on hard conversational cases, while Paper B delivers a software toolkit for building and studying RAG pipelines. These are different kinds of research outputs - one is test material, the other is engineering infrastructure - so placing their headline numbers side by side on a single ranking would give a practitioner a false impression that they are alternative approaches to the same problem.

paper_a_title: Generating Leakage-Free Benchmarks for Robust RAG Evaluation
paper_b_title: Judge as A Judge: Improving the Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation through the Judge-Consistency of Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Paper A (SeedRG) targets benchmark contamination/knowledge leakage as the failure mode, assumes that valid RAG evaluation requires questions outside parametric memory, intervenes at the dataset-construction stage via reasoning-graph extraction plus type-constrained entity substitution, optimizes for leakage reduction (~78%) while preserving reasoning difficulty, and recommends using regenerated benchmarks. Paper B (Judge-as-a-Judge) targets evaluator unreliability of LLM judges as the failure mode, assumes judge-consistency is a reasonable proxy for evaluation quality, intervenes at the judging/scoring layer, optimizes for judge-consistency, and recommends a consistency-based judging procedure. All five coordinates diverge: the two works fix orthogonal bottlenecks in the RAG evaluation pipeline (data quality vs. evaluator quality) and report numbers on incompatible quantities. Even though both nominally aim at 'better RAG evaluation,' their headline results do not occupy the same axis and cannot be ranked head-to-head. Paper B's snippet is unavailable, which limits certainty, but the title is sufficiently specific to ground the divergence.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head comparison would require both papers to (1) address the same bottleneck in RAG evaluation (either benchmark construction or judge scoring, not one each), (2) report results on a shared dataset and a shared evaluation protocol, and (3) optimize a common scoring quantity (e.g., both reporting leakage rates on the same seed benchmarks, or both reporting judge-human agreement on the same response set). Without that, only a complementary/stacked evaluation makes sense: apply SeedRG to build the test set, then apply Judge-Consistency to score outputs, and report separate diagnostic numbers for each layer rather than a single ranking.
independent_rubric_rationale: These two works approach RAG evaluation from very different angles. SeedRG rewrites benchmark questions so they can no longer be solved from a model's memorized knowledge, while Judge-as-a-Judge tries to make the LLM scorer itself more trustworthy by checking that its verdicts are self-consistent. Their headline numbers describe entirely different things — one is about how much memorization-shortcutting was removed from the test set, the other is about how stable or agreeable the scoring procedure is. Dropping both onto a single leaderboard and reading off 'who wins' would let a practitioner think one work supersedes the other, when in reality they fix complementary weaknesses in the evaluation pipeline.

paper_a_title: Whose Facts Win? LLM Source Preferences under Knowledge Conflicts
paper_b_title: Rethinking All Evidence: Enhancing Trustworthy Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Conflict-Driven Summarization
gold_rationale: Paper A is a diagnostic study of LLM source-credibility preferences under inter-context conflicts using synthetic, attribute-controlled sources (government, newspaper, person, social media). Its targeted problem is repetition-induced flipping of source preferences, and its proposed remedy is a fine-tuning procedure measured by source-preference scores, repetition-bias reduction (79.2%), and preference retention (72.5%). Paper B addresses a broader notion of knowledge conflict (parametric vs. contextual, plus noisy retrieval) and proposes CARE-RAG, a multi-stage pipeline with parameter-aware and context-aware evidence plus a distilled 3B summarizer, evaluated by QA accuracy on revised QA benchmarks. The conflict construct, the evidence pool (synthetic credibility metadata vs. real retrieved passages with QA Repair), the locus of change (model fine-tuning vs. pipeline orchestration with distilled summarizer), the headline numbers (preference/bias percentages vs. QA accuracy), and the deployment goal (bias-mitigation analysis vs. end-task RAG system) all differ. The two contributions cannot be ranked against each other.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared task with shared metrics on shared data: e.g., both methods evaluated on the same conflict-laden QA benchmark with the same accuracy/faithfulness scoring, or both evaluated on the same controlled source-credibility probe with the same preference scoring. Common baselines, matched LLM backbones, and a consistent definition of 'conflict' (inter-context source disagreement vs. parametric-vs-context disagreement) would also be needed before any leaderboard ranking would be meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two headline numbers describe fundamentally different things. Paper A's main result is a percentage describing how much a credibility-related bias is reduced (and how much of the original source ordering is preserved) when LLMs read synthetic, attribute-controlled snippets. Paper B's main result is question-answering accuracy on revised real-world QA benchmarks using a multi-stage pipeline with a distilled summarizer. A practitioner placing these side by side on one leaderboard would be seriously misled, since the inputs, the phenomenon being scored, and the units of the numbers do not line up at all.

paper_a_title: Context-DPO: Aligning Language Models for Context-Faithfulness
paper_b_title: FaithfulRAG: Fact-Level Conflict Modeling for Context-Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Both papers target the same failure_type (LLMs ignoring or contradicting retrieved context when it conflicts with parametric knowledge in RAG) and share a similar evidence_assumption (a retrieved passage that may conflict with internal knowledge). However, they diverge sharply on intervention_point: Paper A modifies model parameters via DPO alignment (training-time), while Paper B keeps weights frozen and adds an inference-time self-thinking pipeline that surfaces fact-level conflicts. Their action_policy differs accordingly (preference-optimized weight update vs. multi-step reasoning over conflicting facts). Paper A also reports headline numbers on its own ConFiQA benchmark with knowledge-conflict scenarios, whereas Paper B's main results appear to use different established RAG/QA benchmarks, so the metric_target is not aligned either.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on the same base models and the same benchmark suite (including at minimum ConFiQA-style counterfactual-context tasks and FaithfulRAG's chosen QA sets), report context-faithfulness under matched knowledge-conflict conditions, and disclose training cost, inference overhead, and applicability to closed-weight models. Ideally also test the two as complements (Context-DPO checkpoint + FaithfulRAG decoding) to separate gains from each stage.
independent_rubric_rationale: Both works tackle the same underlying problem of keeping a language model loyal to a retrieved passage when it disagrees with what the model already 'knows,' but one of them rewrites model weights through preference tuning while the other leaves the model untouched and inserts a reasoning step at generation time. They report their headline numbers on different test suites and have very different compute and deployment trade-offs, so dropping both onto a single leaderboard row would give a practitioner an incomplete and somewhat skewed picture of which is actually stronger for their setting.

paper_a_title: Position: Retrieval-augmented systems can be dangerous medical communicators
paper_b_title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
gold_rationale: Paper A is a position paper arguing that retrieval-augmented systems can mislead in patient-facing medical communication, addressing a safety/pragmatic failure mode with argumentative or case-illustrative evidence, targeting system design and deployment policy in healthcare, and recommending caution and redesign. Paper B is an empirical study showing that LLMs underweight information in the middle of long input contexts, evidenced by controlled multi-document QA and key-value retrieval experiments, targeting positional utilization measured by task accuracy, and motivating prompt/context engineering or modeling fixes. The failure types, evidence regimes, intervention loci, metric targets, and recommended actions diverge across all five coordinates, so the two headline claims do not sit on the same leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head would require both papers to study the same phenomenon (e.g., both measuring positional bias in medical RAG, or both quantifying safety of long-context QA) on shared benchmarks with overlapping metrics, comparable evidence types (both empirical with effect sizes, or both normative arguments), and parallel recommended interventions that could be ranked against each other.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works ask different questions about different systems for different audiences: one warns about patient-safety risks when retrieval-based assistants speak to medical users, while the other documents a positional pattern in how language models attend to long inputs on general question-answering tasks. Putting their headline takeaways onto a single leaderboard would invite a practitioner to read one as 'better' or 'stronger' than the other when they are not addressing the same problem, the same evaluation setup, or the same downstream concern, so a side-by-side ranking would seriously mislead.

paper_a_title: KnowPO: Knowledge-aware Preference Optimization for Controllable Knowledge Selection in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
paper_b_title: Why So Gullible? Enhancing the Robustness of Retrieval-Augmented Models against Counterfactual Noise
gold_rationale: Paper A (KnowPO) targets conflict between the model's parametric knowledge and the retrieved context, training via knowledge-aware preference optimization on a custom-constructed conflict dataset and reporting a ~37% relative gain on its own benchmarks. Paper B (Discern-and-Answer) targets conflict among the retrieved documents themselves (counterfactual noise within the relevant set), using either a fine-tuned discriminator or GPT-3.5 prompting, evaluated on ODQA with the MACNOISE dataset. The notion of 'conflict,' the data construction, base models, and evaluation suites all differ, and the desired model behavior also differs (Paper A: adhere to retrieved context while filtering noise; Paper B: discriminate which of several relevant-looking documents to trust). Each of the five coordinates diverges in non-trivial ways.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation that defines a single conflict taxonomy (parametric-vs-context and intra-context counterfactuals), uses the same base LLM(s) and identical retrieval corpus, runs both KnowPO training and the Discern-and-Answer discriminator/prompting pipelines, and reports the same metrics (e.g., EM/F1 on overlapping conflict and clean subsets such as NQ/TriviaQA with MACNOISE-style perturbations). Comparable baselines and matched compute budgets, plus a held-out OOD slice, would be needed before placing the two on one leaderboard.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works define 'conflict' differently (model knowledge versus retrieved text in one; disagreements among retrieved passages in the other), use different training data, base models, and benchmark suites, and the headline numbers were obtained under non-overlapping experimental conditions. A practitioner reading a single leaderboard row for each would likely draw the wrong conclusion about which approach is stronger or even about what problem each one actually solves.

paper_a_title: Hierarchical Planning for Complex Tasks with Knowledge Graph-RAG and Symbolic Verification
paper_b_title: RAG4GFM: Bridging Knowledge Gaps in Graph Foundation Models through Graph Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Based solely on titles (no snippets provided), Paper A targets hierarchical planning for complex tasks, combining knowledge-graph retrieval with symbolic verification to repair planning errors. Paper B targets knowledge gaps inside graph foundation models, using graph-structured retrieval to augment GFM predictions. The failure modes (plan correctness vs. GFM knowledge coverage), evidence sources (KG for plan grounding/verification vs. graph subgraphs for GFM context), intervention points (planner loop vs. GFM inference), likely metric families (task/plan success vs. node/graph-level prediction quality), and the resulting policies (verify-and-replan vs. retrieve-and-condition) all diverge. They sit in different problem regimes.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Shared task formulation (either both on planning benchmarks or both on graph-learning benchmarks), overlapping datasets and evaluation protocols, a common notion of correctness or quality, and comparable baselines. Alternatively, a meta-analysis framing where both are positioned as 'graph-aware RAG' on a defined common test bed with matched compute and retrieval budgets.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works address quite different problems — one produces and checks plans for complex tasks, the other enriches graph foundation models with retrieved subgraph context. Their headline numbers come from different benchmark families and mean different things. Putting them on one leaderboard would lead a practitioner to read a ranking that does not exist and to pick the wrong system for whichever real use case they have in mind.

paper_a_title: Entity-Focused Dense Passage Retrieval for Outside-Knowledge Visual Question Answering
paper_b_title: Quebec Automobile Insurance Question-Answering With Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: judgment based on titles and venues only. Paper A targets outside-knowledge Visual Question Answering, requiring image understanding combined with knowledge retrieval over an open-domain corpus, almost certainly evaluated on benchmarks like OK-VQA with VQA-style accuracy. Paper B targets a narrow, text-only, French-language legal/insurance domain (Quebec automobile insurance) using a RAG pipeline, with domain-specific QA evaluation. The failure_type differs (knowledge-intensive multimodal QA vs domain-specialized legal QA), the evidence_assumption differs (image+text corpus vs curated legal text), the metric_target differs (different datasets, languages, and likely scoring), and the action_policy differs (short factoid answers to visual questions vs longer generated legal/insurance answers). Only the intervention_point (retrieval-augmented QA architecture) is loosely shared, and even there the specific component being modified is different (entity-focused dense retriever vs full RAG stack).
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both systems would need to be evaluated on the same task formulation, the same input modality, the same corpus and language, and the same benchmark with identical metrics. At minimum, one would need a shared QA benchmark (e.g., both run on the same legal RAG benchmark or both on OK-VQA) and matched answer evaluation protocols. Without that, any leaderboard placement is meaningless.
independent_rubric_rationale: assessment: the two systems address very different problems — one answers questions about images using broad world knowledge, while the other answers narrow French-language questions about Quebec auto insurance from a specialized text corpus. They use different inputs, different languages, different evaluation datasets, and different answer styles, so placing their headline numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would give a practitioner a false impression that one system is 'better' than the other when in reality they solve unrelated tasks.

paper_a_title: Think-on-Graph 2.0: Deep and Faithful Large Language Model Reasoning with Knowledge-guided Retrieval Augmented Generation
paper_b_title: ReFIR: Grounding Large Restoration Models with Retrieval Augmentation
gold_rationale: Based on titles (no snippets available), Paper A (Think-on-Graph 2.0) addresses LLM reasoning shortcomings on knowledge-intensive text tasks by injecting structured knowledge-graph evidence into an iterative reasoning loop, with text-QA-style targets. Paper B (ReFIR) addresses hallucination/ungrounded outputs in large image restoration models by retrieving reference images and conditioning the restoration pipeline on them, with image-quality targets (e.g., PSNR/SSIM/perceptual scores). Every coordinate diverges: the deficiency being fixed (text reasoning faithfulness vs. visual restoration fidelity), the evidence source (KG triples vs. retrieved images), where retrieval is plugged in (LLM chain-of-thought vs. restoration network), the evaluation space (QA benchmarks vs. image quality benchmarks), and the produced output (text answer vs. restored image). The only shared label is the umbrella term 'retrieval augmentation.'
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers would need to target the same task and modality (e.g., both on knowledge-grounded text QA, or both on retrieval-augmented image restoration), share at least one common benchmark, report on the same evaluation scores, and produce comparable outputs. Absent that, only a high-level methodological discussion of RAG strategies — not a head-to-head ranking — is defensible.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works tackle very different problems in different modalities: one improves text reasoning over knowledge graphs and is scored on question-answering benchmarks, while the other improves image restoration quality using retrieved reference images and is scored on image-quality benchmarks. Inputs, outputs, and scoring scales do not overlap, so placing their headline numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would give a practitioner a false sense that one method is 'better' than the other when they solve unrelated problems.

paper_a_title: TRACE: Grounding Time Series in Context for Multimodal Embedding and Retrieval
paper_b_title: Unified Generative and Discriminative Training for Multi-modal Large Language Models
gold_rationale: No text snippets are supplied, so reasoning rests on titles alone. Paper A (TRACE) appears to target multimodal embedding and retrieval grounded in time-series context, implying retrieval-style evaluation over a time-series-plus-text corpus. Paper B addresses a unified generative+discriminative training recipe for general multimodal LLMs, implying vision-language benchmarks (VQA, captioning, image-text matching, etc.). The intervention_point differs (an embedding/retrieval model vs. an LLM training objective), the metric_target differs (retrieval scores over time-series corpora vs. mixed generative and discriminative scores over vision-language tasks), and the evidence_assumption differs (that strong time-series-text alignment improves retrieval, vs. that joint training objectives improve general MLLM quality). Direct ranking on a single leaderboard would conflate distinct problems.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared task formulation evaluated under a matched protocol: the same benchmark suite, the same input modalities, the same query/target definitions, and the same scoring procedure. Concretely, both systems would need head-to-head numbers on at least one common retrieval or multimodal understanding benchmark where each method is naturally applicable, with comparable model scale and training data disclosed. Absent that, only narrow sub-claims (e.g., both improve a particular cross-modal alignment score on a common dataset) could be ranked.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works look like they tackle different problem areas: one is about retrieving and embedding time-series content alongside text in a multimodal corpus, while the other is about a training recipe for general multimodal large language models on vision-language tasks. Their headline numbers would almost certainly come from different benchmark suites, different input types, and different task definitions, so placing them on a single leaderboard would likely lead a practitioner to draw conclusions the underlying experiments do not support.

paper_a_title: Chunk-Distilled Language Modeling
paper_b_title: Context Tuning for Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: No text snippets are provided for either paper; only titles are available. From titles alone, Paper A ('Chunk-Distilled Language Modeling') appears to focus on distilling chunk-level knowledge into a language model, likely modifying training or decoding. Paper B ('Context Tuning for Retrieval Augmented Generation') appears to adapt or optimize context selection for a RAG pipeline. While both touch language modeling and possibly retrieval, I cannot verify the targeted problem, the datasets or evidence base, the pipeline stage being modified, the evaluation metric(s), or the recommended deployment policy for either paper. Without this information any judgment of direct comparability would be speculation, so the only defensible verdict is underspecified.
what_valid_comparison_requires: At minimum, abstracts or method/results snippets establishing: (1) that both papers tackle the same problem framing (e.g., both improve factual QA accuracy under retrieval), (2) overlapping or convertible evaluation benchmarks and metrics, (3) compatible base models or fair-comparison controls, (4) clarity on whether the modification is at training time vs. inference time, and (5) similar deployment regimes (e.g., both assume access to an external corpus). Without snippets, none of these can be confirmed.
independent_rubric_rationale: Because no abstracts, methods, datasets, or results are supplied for either paper, there is no basis to judge whether placing their headline numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would mislead a practitioner. The titles hint at overlapping territory (language modeling with chunk-level knowledge vs. context optimization for retrieval-augmented generation), but overlap in topic does not establish overlap in benchmark, base model, or reported quantity. A responsible reader cannot decide from titles alone.

paper_a_title: Cooperative Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Question Answering: Mutual Information Exchange and Ranking by Contrasting Layers
paper_b_title: Separate the Wheat from the Chaff: Winnowing Down Divergent Views in Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Paper A has no text snippet provided; only the title is available. The title hints at a cooperative RAG approach combining mutual information exchange between modules with a contrasting-layers reranking signal, while Paper B (WinnowRAG) is a two-stage clustering plus critic-LLM filtering framework. Without Paper A's actual problem framing, datasets, retrievers, base LLMs, and reported numbers, none of the five coordinates can be reliably populated for Paper A, so no defensible alignment with Paper B can be established. Both clearly target noisy retrieval in open-domain QA, but that thematic overlap is not sufficient to declare the comparison valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Paper A's text or at least its experimental section is needed: the specific QA benchmarks (e.g., NQ, TriviaQA, HotpotQA, PopQA), the retriever (BM25, Contriever, DPR, etc.), the candidate pool size k, the base generator LLM(s), the evaluation metric definitions (EM vs. F1 vs. accuracy vs. recall@k), and whether the contribution is at the reranking stage or the generation stage. Only if Paper B is re-run, or compared on, the same benchmark-retriever-generator-metric configuration that Paper A reports would a side-by-side ranking be defensible; otherwise the two systems would need a shared third-party reproduction.
independent_rubric_rationale: With one paper reduced to a title and the other described only at the abstract level, there is no way to know whether the two reported headline numbers come from overlapping benchmarks, comparable retrieval pools, similar backbone models, or matching scoring conventions. A leaderboard-style juxtaposition might or might not mislead a practitioner, and the available material is simply not enough to decide either way.

paper_a_title: RankRAG: Unifying Context Ranking with Retrieval-Augmented Generation in LLMs
paper_b_title: xRAG: Extreme Context Compression for Retrieval-augmented Generation with One Token
gold_rationale: Based on titles alone (no snippets available), the two papers target orthogonal weaknesses in RAG. RankRAG addresses context-relevance failure by teaching the LLM to rank retrieved passages before generation, optimizing primarily for answer quality with full-length context. xRAG addresses computational/length burden by compressing retrieved context into a single embedding token via a projection, optimizing primarily for efficiency while attempting to preserve quality. Their intervention points (re-ranking vs. compression projector), action policies (rank-then-generate vs. embed-then-generate), and headline metric targets (quality on QA leaderboards vs. quality-at-1-token efficiency) differ. A single leaderboard cell would obscure the efficiency/quality trade-off that is central to xRAG and irrelevant to RankRAG. Confidence is held to 3 because no snippets were provided to confirm the benchmark overlap and exact evaluation setup.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Shared evaluation benchmark (e.g., NQ, TriviaQA, HotpotQA) reported with the same retriever, the same base LLM (or at least matched parameter count and training data), and joint reporting of both answer-quality scores and context-length/compute cost so the quality-vs-efficiency trade-off is visible. Ideally each method would also be tested under the other's regime (RankRAG with compressed context; xRAG with reranked candidates) to isolate the contribution.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems chase different goals. One reorders retrieved passages so the model sees the most relevant text at full length, aiming to lift answer accuracy. The other squeezes the retrieved text into a single dense vector to slash compute and token count. If a practitioner saw only their headline numbers in one table, they would miss the efficiency-versus-quality trade-off and could easily pick the wrong tool for their deployment budget.

paper_a_title: SEER: Self-Aligned Evidence Extraction for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper_b_title: Neuro-RIT: Neuron-Guided Instruction Tuning for Robust Retrieval-Augmented Language Model
gold_rationale: Both papers target the same broad failure_type — RAG performance degradation under noisy or irrelevant retrieved contexts — and both likely report QA benchmark accuracy as the metric_target. However, the intervention_point and action_policy differ substantially: SEER (Paper A) operates upstream by extracting and self-aligning evidence from retrieved passages before generation, whereas Neuro-RIT (Paper B) operates inside the generator LLM via neuron-level attribution and a two-stage instruction-tuning regime that selectively deactivates noise-responsive neurons. Their evidence_assumptions also diverge: SEER assumes a useful evidence span can be isolated from a passage, while Neuro-RIT assumes noise-vs-signal processing is sufficiently neuron-sparse to be disentangled. Comparison is therefore only partial — the goals overlap, but the mechanisms are at different layers of the pipeline and could in principle be complementary. The missing Paper A snippet, the implausible 2026 date and arXiv ID for Paper B, and the absence of shared benchmark/base-model details further weaken any direct head-to-head ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both systems would need to be evaluated on the same QA benchmarks (e.g., NQ, TriviaQA, HotpotQA, PopQA) with the same base generator LLM, identical retriever and top-k retrieved contexts, matched noise injection protocols (e.g., same ratio of irrelevant or counterfactual passages), and the same answer-evaluation procedure (EM/F1). Ideally, an ablation showing whether SEER-style evidence extraction and Neuro-RIT-style neuron-guided tuning are substitutes or stack additively would be needed before placing them on one leaderboard.
independent_rubric_rationale: Both papers aim to make retrieval-augmented generation more robust to noisy retrieved passages, but they operate at very different stages of the pipeline. SEER refines the retrieved evidence itself before it reaches the generator, while Neuro-RIT leaves retrieval alone and instead reshapes the generator model's internal neuron behavior through targeted tuning. If their headline numbers were placed side by side on one leaderboard, a practitioner could easily read them as direct alternatives and pick a 'winner,' when in reality the two techniques address different parts of the system and might even be combined. Without the SEER text snippet and without confirmation that the benchmarks, base LLMs, retrievers, and noise conditions line up, a clean ranking is not warranted, so the comparison is partly misleading rather than outright safe.

paper_a_title: Towards Secure Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Comprehensive Review of Threats, Defenses and Benchmarks
paper_b_title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
gold_rationale: Paper A is a survey of RAG security, cataloguing threats (data poisoning, adversarial, membership inference), defenses (encryption, federated isolation, differential privacy, sanitization), and security benchmarks. Paper B is the original Lewis et al. empirical paper introducing the RAG architecture and evaluating it on knowledge-intensive NLP tasks (open-domain QA, fact verification, generation). The failure_type differs (security/confidentiality compromise vs. knowledge gaps and hallucination on QA). The evidence_assumption differs (literature synthesis across many works vs. controlled benchmark experiments). The intervention_point differs (pipeline-wide defensive add-ons vs. a parametric+non-parametric generation architecture). The metric_target differs (security/robustness properties vs. exact-match/accuracy/generation quality). The action_policy differs (hardening recommendations vs. adopting a new generation framework). No headline number from either paper maps onto the other.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers would need to report a common quantitative claim on overlapping benchmarks with comparable evaluation protocols, e.g., both reporting defense effectiveness on the same poisoning benchmark, or both reporting QA accuracy on Natural Questions under matched retrieval conditions. Here, the survey provides no original numerical result and the topical scope (security vs. task accuracy) is disjoint, so no leaderboard placement is meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works pursue different goals on different scales. One is a 2026 literature synthesis of attacks and defenses for RAG systems, summarizing what others have published about safety properties. The other is the 2020 empirical paper that introduced the RAG model and reported accuracy and generation quality on standard knowledge-intensive NLP benchmarks. Putting their headline results side by side on a single leaderboard would mislead a practitioner because the two are not measuring the same thing, were produced by different study types (review vs. primary experiments), and have non-overlapping evaluation regimes.

paper_a_title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Comprehensive Survey of Architectures, Enhancements, and Robustness Frontiers
paper_b_title: LLM-Oriented Information Retrieval: A Denoising-First Perspective
gold_rationale: Both items are non-empirical synthesis works in the RAG / LLM-IR space, so they share topical territory. However, Paper A is a comprehensive survey that taxonomizes the entire RAG landscape (retriever-centric, generator-centric, hybrid, robustness-oriented) and reports comparative QA performance trends, while Paper B is a focused perspective paper arguing that denoising is THE primary bottleneck and proposing a specific four-stage framing (inaccessible → undiscoverable → misaligned → unverifiable). The papers diagnose different sets of problems, optimize against different quality targets (broad pipeline trade-offs vs. signal-to-noise / evidence density / verifiability), and recommend different organizing principles for the field. Neither presents head-to-head empirical numbers that could populate a single leaderboard row.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A defensible comparison would require either (a) restricting the contrast to the explicit overlap area, namely how each work characterizes noise/robustness in retrieval for LLMs, while bracketing Paper A's broader architectural taxonomy and Paper B's denoising-first thesis; or (b) extracting a shared sub-claim (e.g., the role of context filtering or verification) and judging both against the same set of cited primary studies. Treating them as interchangeable 'RAG survey' entries without flagging the scope asymmetry (comprehensive map vs. focused paradigm argument) and the differing organizing lenses would not be sound.
independent_rubric_rationale: A reader who saw both side by side on one list would correctly perceive them as related synthesis pieces about LLM-coupled retrieval, and on the overlap (noise, robustness, verification in RAG pipelines) the two largely agree in direction. The risk is that one is a broad cartography of the whole field with comparative QA discussion, while the other is a focused thesis advocating a single organizing principle with its own four-stage lens; a flat ranking would hide that the two are doing different jobs and at different breadths, which could partly mislead a practitioner choosing between them as a reference.

paper_a_title: Towards Trustworthy Retrieval Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
paper_b_title: Trustworthiness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems: A Survey
gold_rationale: Both works are surveys of trustworthy RAG and share substantial topical overlap (fairness, privacy, accountability appear in both taxonomies). However, their primary deliverables diverge: Paper A is a literature-roadmap survey organized around six perspectives (reliability, privacy, safety, fairness, explainability, accountability) without an accompanying empirical benchmark in the visible snippet, while Paper B contributes both a taxonomy across six different-but-overlapping dimensions (factuality, robustness, fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy) AND a new evaluation benchmark (TRC Bench) with empirical results on multiple LLMs. The dimensional vocabularies do not align one-to-one (e.g., Paper A's 'reliability' overlaps but is not identical to Paper B's 'factuality' + 'robustness'; Paper A's 'explainability' partially aligns with Paper B's 'transparency'). Some side-by-side comparison of taxonomic coverage is reasonable, but ranking them as competing artifacts conflates a conceptual roadmap with a taxonomy-plus-benchmark contribution.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head comparison would require (1) explicit mapping between the two taxonomies' dimensions, (2) restricting the comparison to a shared contribution type (e.g., taxonomy coverage and citation breadth only, excluding Paper B's benchmark results), (3) disclosure that Paper A does not include an empirical benchmark so its 'results' are organizational/analytical rather than measured, and (4) separate evaluation of benchmark utility for Paper B against other RAG trust benchmarks rather than against Paper A.
independent_rubric_rationale: Both works address the same broad subject and overlap in several pillar categories, so a practitioner skimming a combined leaderboard would correctly see them as adjacent contributions. However, one provides a conceptual organizing roadmap while the other delivers a structured taxonomy plus a fresh empirical benchmark with model-level numbers, and the two category vocabularies do not line up cleanly. Treating them as interchangeable entries on one ranked list would obscure these differences and could mislead a reader about what each work actually delivers, though not catastrophically since the topical scope is genuinely similar.

paper_a_title: Securing Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Taxonomy of Attacks, Defenses, and Future Directions
paper_b_title: RAPID: Long-Context Inference with Retrieval-Augmented Speculative Decoding
gold_rationale: Paper A is a survey/taxonomy paper that organizes the literature on RAG security (attacks, defenses, evaluation) using a SLOT framework along four axes. Paper B, judging from its title, is an empirical methods paper proposing a specific algorithm (RAPID) that combines retrieval augmentation with speculative decoding to improve long-context inference. They address fundamentally different problem classes (adversarial security vs. inference efficiency/quality), use different evidence types (literature synthesis vs. empirical benchmarks), operate at different points in the pipeline (cross-cutting threat model vs. decoding-time algorithm), target different outcome measures (security/CIA properties vs. latency/quality on long-context tasks), and deliver different outputs (conceptual taxonomy vs. runnable method). None of the five coordinates align.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both papers to address the same problem class with commensurable outcomes, e.g., two RAG security taxonomies/defenses on shared adversarial benchmarks, or two long-context inference acceleration methods on shared latency/accuracy benchmarks. At minimum, the papers would need to share a target problem, evaluation regime, and reportable headline number on the same axis.
independent_rubric_rationale: Placing a broad survey that maps the landscape of adversarial threats against retrieval-augmented systems next to a concrete long-context decoding algorithm on a single leaderboard would seriously mislead a practitioner. The two works answer different questions for different audiences (a security architect looking for threat coverage vs. an inference engineer looking to speed up long-context generation), and any apparent ranking between them would reflect category confusion rather than relative quality.

paper_a_title: Trust or Abstain? A Self-Aware RAG Approach
paper_b_title: PoisonedRAG: Knowledge Corruption Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Paper A (SABER) addresses naturally arising knowledge conflicts between parametric and retrieved contextual knowledge, proposing an inference-time self-aware belief estimator that drives a 4-cell trust/abstain decision, evaluated on end-to-end accuracy, conflict-specific faithfulness, and risk-coverage curves. Paper B (PoisonedRAG) is an offensive work that injects adversarially crafted malicious texts into the knowledge database and reports attack success rate (~90% with 5 injected texts). The failure_type differs (organic PK/CK disagreement vs. deliberate corpus poisoning), the evidence_assumption differs (standard retrieval corpora vs. attacker-controlled injected passages), the intervention_point differs (defender at inference time vs. attacker at the database), the metric_target differs (accuracy/faithfulness/risk-coverage vs. attack success rate), and the action_policy differs (trust-or-abstain answering vs. generating optimized malicious texts). All five coordinates break, so the works are not on the same axis of evaluation.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A meaningful comparison would require either (a) evaluating SABER's abstention/decision policy on a PoisonedRAG-style adversarial corpus using a shared metric such as attack success rate or robust accuracy under injection, or (b) framing PoisonedRAG as a stress-test environment and reporting both papers on the same defender-side leaderboard with matched LLM backbones, retriever, knowledge base, query set, attack budget, and a common scoring metric (e.g., robust accuracy with abstention credit). Without that shared adversarial setup and common metric, the two papers cannot be ranked against each other.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper proposes a defender-side technique that improves answering reliability and abstention on naturally conflicting evidence, while the other proposes an attacker that injects crafted passages into the corpus and reports how often it fools the system. Placing their headline numbers (accuracy/faithfulness vs. attack success rate) side by side on one leaderboard would lead a practitioner to draw conclusions that the underlying experiments simply do not support, because the two works are operating on opposite sides of the system and measuring different outcomes on different inputs.

paper_a_title: Magic Mushroom: A Customizable Benchmark for Fine-grained Analysis of Retrieval Noise Erosion in RAG Systems

gold_rationale: Paper A targets answer-quality degradation caused by heterogeneous retrieval noise, intervening at the generator/denoiser level and reporting QA correctness across configurable noise mixtures. what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head would need both papers to (i) address the same failure mode (either both answer correctness under noise, or both uncertainty calibration), (ii) operate at the same RAG pipeline stage (e.g., both as post-hoc calibrators or both as generation-time denoisers), (iii) report a shared headline metric on overlapping datasets and noise/retrieval conditions, and (iv) compare techniques with the same downstream use case (e.g., both producing a final answer, or both producing an abstain/confidence signal). independent_rubric_rationale: The first paper reports how often RAG outputs remain correct when supporting passages are deliberately corrupted with surface-relevant but misleading content. The second paper reports how well confidence scores attached to RAG outputs track whether those outputs are right or wrong, judged through a set of behavioral principles and correlation numbers. Putting these two headline results side by side on a single leaderboard would lead a practitioner to treat them as competing approaches to the same goal, when in fact one is about generated-answer quality under noisy contexts and the other is about confidence calibration of RAG responses, so direct ranking would seriously mislead.

paper_a_title: Toward Robust RALMs: Revealing the Impact of Imperfect Retrieval on Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
paper_b_title: RoseRAG: Robust Retrieval-augmented Generation with Small-scale LLMs via Margin-aware Preference Optimization

Putting their headline numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would suggest a head-to-head winner that does not exist: the quantities reported are not the same kind of thing, the document conditions are constructed differently, and the model scopes (general RALMs vs. small LLMs specifically) do not line up, so a practitioner reading the combined ranking would draw conclusions the evidence does not support.

paper_a_title: Hierarchical Planning for Complex Tasks with Knowledge Graph-RAG and Symbolic Verification
paper_b_title: Supportiveness-based Knowledge Rewriting for Retrieval-augmented Language Modeling

A practitioner seeing their headline numbers side-by-side on one leaderboard would have no basis to infer which approach is 'better,' because the tasks, inputs, and success criteria do not line up.

paper_a_title: Overcoming the Retrieval Barrier: Indirect Prompt Injection in the Wild for LLM Systems
paper_b_title: GRACE: Reinforcement Learning for Grounded Response and Abstention under Contextual Evidence
gold_rationale: Paper A is an offensive security study that constructs an indirect prompt injection attack against RAG/agentic pipelines, with the failure of interest being adversarial hijacking of LLM behavior via poisoned corpora, evidence assumed to be attacker-controlled, intervention at the attacker's trigger-fragment construction stage, metric of interest being retrieval rate and attack success (e.g., ~100% retrieval, >80% SSH key exfiltration), and an offensive action policy (demonstrating vulnerability). Their headline numbers (retrieval/exfiltration success against adversaries vs. answer correctness and refusal quality on HotpotQA-style data) live in different units on different evaluation setups. Placing them in a single leaderboard would suggest a 'winner' where no shared yardstick exists, and a practitioner would likely draw wrong conclusions about which system is more useful for any concrete deployment decision.

paper_a_title: DRAGged into Conflicts: Detecting and Addressing Conflicting Sources in Search-Augmented LLMs
paper_b_title: Rescuing the Unpoisoned: Efficient Defense against Knowledge Corruption Attacks on RAG Systems

Putting their headline numbers on one leaderboard would mix two very different problems with incompatible success criteria and threat scenarios, so a practitioner would likely draw the wrong conclusion about which approach is 'better.'

paper_a_title: TrustRAG: Enhancing Robustness and Trustworthiness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
