gold_rationale: The two papers diverge on essentially every coordinate. Paper A (TrustRAG) addresses an adversarial failure mode — corpus poisoning attacks where malicious documents are deliberately injected into the retrieval corpus (PoisonedRAG-style threat model) — and intervenes by filtering retrieved documents through cluster analysis plus LLM self-assessment, with primary metrics around attack resistance and robustness under adversarial evidence. Paper B (SUGAR) addresses a benign efficiency/noise failure mode — that always-on retrieval is wasteful and that noisy but non-adversarial retrieved content can distract the model — and intervenes upstream of retrieval by using semantic-entropy-based confidence to decide whether to retrieve at all and whether to do single- vs multi-step retrieval, with metrics around QA accuracy and inference efficiency on standard (non-poisoned) QA benchmarks. Without that joint protocol — or at minimum a clear declaration that the two systems target distinct sub-problems and are not in competition — they cannot be ranked head-to-head.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems solve different problems within RAG: one defends against deliberately poisoned documents in the corpus, the other decides when retrieval is even worth doing and how deep it should go, evaluated on ordinary question-answering. Their reported numbers come from different benchmarks, different threat conditions, and different success criteria, so a practitioner who saw the headline scores placed on one shared ranking would likely draw the wrong conclusion about which approach is stronger or more appropriate for their deployment.

paper_a_title: Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth: Revealing the Behavior of Large Language Models in Knowledge Conflicts
paper_b_title: GraphRAG under Fire
gold_rationale: Paper A is a controlled behavioral study of how LLMs reconcile parametric memory with conflicting external context, using synthetic counter-memory and measuring receptiveness / confirmation bias on general tool-augmented LLMs. Paper B is an adversarial security study that crafts poisoned text exploiting shared graph relations in GraphRAG, reporting attack success rate and amount of poisoning text needed. The two works target different failure modes (naturally-arising knowledge conflict vs. deliberate poisoning), make different evidence-source assumptions (curated conflicting passages vs. injected malicious documents into a graph index), report incompatible primary outcomes (receptiveness/bias proportions vs. attack success rate / poison budget), and serve different goals (diagnostic understanding vs. offense plus preliminary defense). They also evaluate different system stacks (generic RAG/LLMs vs. GraphRAG variants).
what_valid_comparison_requires: Shared system under test (e.g., both on GraphRAG or both on standard RAG), a common threat or stress model (e.g., both either naturally conflicting evidence or both adversarial poisoning), aligned outcome measures on the same datasets (e.g., both reporting answer correctness under conflicting/poisoned context with identical query sets), and matched scope of contribution (diagnostic vs. proposed attack/defense). Without harmonizing at least the metric and the threat model, leaderboard-style ranking is not meaningful.

Putting these two headline numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would suggest they measure the same phenomenon on the same system, which they do not, so a practitioner trying to choose a deployment setup or assess robustness would draw incorrect conclusions about both the threat profile and the model's reliability.

paper_a_title: Adaptive Contrastive Decoding in Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Handling Noisy Contexts
paper_b_title: Know Or Not: a library for evaluating out-of-knowledge base robustness
gold_rationale: Paper A targets distraction by noisy-but-in-scope retrieved passages and proposes a decoding-time adjustment (adaptive contrastive decoding) measured by open-domain QA correctness. Paper B targets a different error mode entirely: hallucination when queries are out-of-knowledge-base, and contributes an evaluation library plus a PolicyBench benchmark whose primary measurement concerns appropriate abstention rather than answer accuracy. The error mode being addressed, the locus of contribution (model decoding vs. evaluation tooling), the success criterion (correct answer vs. correct refusal), and the operational policy (generate-with-modified-weights vs. provide a benchmarking pipeline) all diverge.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require either (a) running ACD through the knowornot/PolicyBench pipeline and reporting OOKB abstention metrics alongside answer-quality metrics on a shared dataset that contains both noisy-in-scope and out-of-scope queries, or (b) restricting comparison to a shared QA dataset where both works report identical metrics (e.g., EM/F1 on the same noisy-RAG benchmark) with matched LLM backbones and retrievers. Without harmonized datasets, error taxonomies (noisy-but-relevant vs. OOKB), and outcome definitions (correctness vs. calibrated abstention), placing them in the same ranking is not meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper delivers a decoding-time technique scored by answer correctness on open-domain QA with noisy retrieved passages; the other delivers an evaluation library and a policy-domain benchmark whose headline outcome concerns whether models appropriately decline to answer when the knowledge base does not cover the query. A practitioner skimming a single leaderboard row for each would conflate two different problem settings and two different definitions of success, and could pick the wrong tool for their deployment need.

paper_a_title: Generating Leakage-Free Benchmarks for Robust RAG Evaluation

gold_rationale: Paper A (SeedRG) targets the failure mode of knowledge leakage and benchmark aging in RAG evaluation; its intervention point is the dataset construction pipeline, its metric targets are leakage reduction, preserved reasoning difficulty, and discriminative power across RAG systems, and its action policy delivers a semi-synthetic benchmark generator. Paper B (Superposition Prompting) addresses the failure mode of slow or suboptimal RAG inference; its intervention point is the prompt construction at inference time, its metric targets are answer quality and latency/throughput, and its action policy delivers a new prompting/decoding technique. The two works produce different artifact types (an evaluation benchmark vs. an inference method), rest on different evidentiary assumptions, and report results on different quantities. Treating their headline results as comparable on one leaderboard would mix an evaluation-tooling contribution with a RAG-method contribution, which the breaking-coordinate analysis flags as invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both works to be of the same artifact class evaluated on overlapping benchmarks with shared metrics. For example, one could run Superposition Prompting (Paper B) as one of the RAG systems benchmarked under SeedRG (Paper A) alongside HippoRAG, GraphRAG, OGRAG, and SemanticRAG, and then compare answer accuracy on the leakage-filtered evaluation set. Alternatively, both would need to propose competing benchmark-generation pipelines or both propose competing RAG inference methods evaluated on a common, leakage-controlled test bed with matched retrievers, base LLMs, and metrics (accuracy, EM/F1, latency).
independent_rubric_rationale: These two works pursue different goals and deliver different kinds of artifacts. The first builds new test sets designed to expose true differences between retrieval-augmented systems by removing overlap with model pretraining content. The second proposes a prompting and decoding scheme meant to make retrieval-augmented generation both faster and more accurate at inference time. Placing their headline numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would suggest they compete on the same task, when in reality one delivers an evaluation resource and the other delivers a runtime technique. A practitioner trying to pick a winner between them would draw incorrect conclusions about what either one provides.

paper_a_title: RAG-SR: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Neural Symbolic Regression
paper_b_title: HippoRAG: Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Although both papers share the 'RAG' label, they target fundamentally different problem settings. Paper A addresses neural symbolic regression, where the failure mode is poor discovery of mathematical expressions fitting numerical data; its intervention augments a symbolic regression pipeline with retrieved expression fragments, and its metrics are regression-quality measures (e.g., R^2, MSE) on SR benchmarks. Paper B addresses long-term memory and multi-hop reasoning in LLMs; its intervention modifies the indexing/retrieval architecture using a hippocampus-inspired graph, and its metrics are QA accuracy on multi-hop text benchmarks (e.g., MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA). The evidence bases, downstream use cases, and evaluation suites do not overlap, so all five coordinates diverge.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head comparison would require the two systems to be evaluated on a shared task with a shared metric on a shared benchmark — for example, both being tested on either symbolic regression problems or multi-hop QA. Alternatively, comparison could be framed at a meta level (e.g., 'retrieval-augmentation as a paradigm across domains'), but that is a qualitative discussion rather than a direct ranking. As stated, no common axis of measurement exists.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works tackle entirely different problem domains: one discovers closed-form mathematical formulas from numerical datasets, the other improves how language models recall and reason over text-based knowledge corpora. They report scores on disjoint benchmarks aimed at disjoint user communities (scientific ML practitioners vs. knowledge-intensive NLP practitioners). Placing their headline numbers side-by-side on one leaderboard would give a practitioner no usable signal for choosing between them, and could easily suggest a false equivalence simply because both names contain 'RAG'.

paper_a_title: Safeguarding RAG Pipelines with GMTP: A Gradient-based Masked Token Probability Method for Poisoned Document Detection

Paper B (Editable Memory Graphs) addresses lack of personalization in agent responses, assumes a benign per-user history corpus, intervenes by structuring memory as an editable graph used during retrieval, and is evaluated on personalization/task quality rather than robustness. All five coordinates diverge, so any head-to-head ranking would be category-confused.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both systems would need to be evaluated on the same task with the same threat or use-case model (e.g., either both on poisoned-RAG benchmarks with detection and downstream QA metrics, or both on personalization benchmarks with the same user-memory setup), using a shared retriever/generator backbone and shared corpora, so that the reported numbers reflect performance on the same underlying problem.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works tackle fundamentally different RAG problems — one is a security defense against adversarially injected documents, the other is a personalization system built on user-editable memory graphs — and they report numbers on entirely different benchmarks and evaluation goals. Placing their headline results side by side on a single leaderboard would suggest a comparability that does not exist and would likely lead a practitioner to draw unwarranted conclusions about which system is 'better.'

paper_a_title: Seeing through the Conflict: Transparent Knowledge Conflict Handling in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper_b_title: Cordon-MAS: Defending RAG against Knowledge Poisoning via Information-Flow Control
gold_rationale: Paper A (TCR) targets benign knowledge conflicts between parametric memory and noisy retrieved context, treating the failure_type as hallucination/over-trust on non-adversarial snippets; its evidence_assumption is that retrieved passages may be inconsistent but not maliciously crafted. Its intervention_point is signal injection through dual contrastive encoders plus a soft-prompt, and its metric_target is conflict-detection F1, knowledge-gap recovery (+21.4 pp), and misleading-context overrides (-29.3 pp) across seven benchmarks; the action_policy is a plug-and-play 0.3%-parameter add-on. independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems are solving different problems on different datasets with different headline numbers: one reports gains on conflict-detection F1 and override reduction across seven QA-style benchmarks against non-adversarial noisy context, while the other reports a 92.4% relative drop in adversarial poisoning success across five BEIR datasets. Putting these side by side on a single leaderboard would let a reader infer that one approach 'outperforms' the other when in fact they have not been evaluated under the same conditions or against the same threat, so a practitioner choosing between them based on the reported numbers would draw an unsupported conclusion.

paper_a_title: Robust Fine-tuning for Retrieval Augmented Generation against Retrieval Defects.

what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head comparison would require both systems to operate on the same modality and task (e.g., both text QA with retrieval, or both image restoration with retrieval), be evaluated on a shared benchmark with the same metrics, and share an evidence type and integration point so that any performance delta reflects method design rather than task or modality differences.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works live in different modalities and solve different end-user problems—one produces text answers grounded in structured knowledge, the other produces restored images grounded in similar reference pictures. They share no common benchmark, no common output type, and no common quality scale. Placing their headline numbers side by side on a single ranking would give a practitioner a false sense that one method is 'better' when the two are not solving the same problem at all.

paper_a_title: RankRAG: Unifying Context Ranking with Retrieval-Augmented Generation in LLMs
paper_b_title: xRAG: Extreme Context Compression for Retrieval-augmented Generation with One Token
gold_rationale: Without text snippets, judgment relies on title-level signals. RankRAG appears to address retrieval relevance by unifying ranking with generation (intervention at the ranking stage, targeting answer quality on QA benchmarks). xRAG addresses context-length efficiency by compressing retrieved passages to a single token embedding (intervention at the context-encoding stage, targeting compute/latency-quality tradeoffs). paper_a_title: SEER: Self-Aligned Evidence Extraction for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

The evidence_assumption also differs: SEER assumes retrieved passages contain extractable supporting spans that can be isolated; Neuro-RIT assumes neurons can be disentangled by relevance and that parameter updates can confer robustness. Paper A's snippet is unavailable, which further limits a confident judgment, and Paper B carries a future-dated 2026 preprint label that should be treated cautiously.

independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems sit at different points in the retrieval-augmented pipeline — one cleans up what is fed to the model, the other reshapes the model itself — so putting their headline numbers side by side on one leaderboard could lead a reader to treat them as substitutes when they are largely complementary and were probably tuned under different generator backbones, retrievers, and noise settings. They share enough goal-level framing (robust QA under noisy retrieval) that some comparison is meaningful, but a practitioner picking one purely on a single ranked score could easily draw the wrong conclusion about which technique is 'better.'

paper_a_title: Towards Secure Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Comprehensive Review of Threats, Defenses and Benchmarks

gold_rationale: Paper A is a survey of RAG security threats, defenses, and benchmarks, while Paper B is the original Lewis et al. paper proposing the RAG architecture for knowledge-intensive NLP tasks. They diverge on every coordinate: A is concerned with security/privacy weaknesses (poisoning, adversarial, membership inference), while B is concerned with closing knowledge gaps in parametric LMs; A relies on literature synthesis as its evidentiary basis, while B reports empirical QA experiments; A reviews input/output defense modules, while B proposes a retriever+generator architecture; A targets security evaluation standards, while B targets task accuracy on open-domain QA; A produces a design taxonomy and recommendations, while B introduces a trainable model. The two works are simply not the same kind of artifact.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A meaningful side-by-side ranking would require either two empirical RAG systems evaluated on overlapping benchmarks with shared scoring, or two surveys of the same scope (e.g., two RAG security reviews) compared on coverage. A survey covering security cannot be ranked against a foundational method paper proposing the RAG architecture; the comparison would need both to share a problem definition, an evaluation protocol, and a common result type.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works play entirely different roles in the RAG literature. One is a broad review consolidating the landscape of security threats and defensive designs around RAG pipelines; the other is the foundational research paper that introduces RAG itself and reports question-answering results. Placing their headline outcomes together on one leaderboard would conflate a literature synthesis with a model proposal, and would suggest a head-to-head comparability that does not exist in topic, scope, or evaluation setup. A practitioner reading such a ranking would draw incorrect conclusions about what either paper actually delivers.

paper_a_title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Comprehensive Survey of Architectures, Enhancements, and Robustness Frontiers
paper_b_title: LLM-Oriented Information Retrieval: A Denoising-First Perspective

However, one offers a wide-angle reference map of the whole landscape with comparative tables, while the other is a viewpoint essay pushing a particular reframing of priorities around signal-to-noise. However, they use different category schemes with only partial overlap, and one of them adds an empirical leaderboard of model performance while the other stays purely descriptive. Placing their headline contributions side-by-side on a single ranking would give a practitioner a partly distorted view of what each work actually delivers.

paper_a_title: Securing Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Taxonomy of Attacks, Defenses, and Future Directions
paper_b_title: RAPID: Long-Context Inference with Retrieval-Augmented Speculative Decoding

They would also need compatible evaluation protocols and headline numbers reported on overlapping benchmarks.

Their headline results live in entirely different evaluation worlds — defense success rates and threat coverage on one side, decoding speed and long-context quality on the other — so a practitioner who saw them ranked together on a single leaderboard would draw badly wrong conclusions about what either paper actually delivers.

paper_a_title: Trust or Abstain? A Self-Aware RAG Approach
paper_b_title: PoisonedRAG: Knowledge Corruption Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Paper A (SABER) targets benign knowledge-conflict failures where parametric and retrieved context may disagree or both be unreliable, and proposes an inference-time belief estimator that drives a trust/abstain decision, reporting end-to-end accuracy, faithfulness, and risk-coverage curves. Paper B (PoisonedRAG) targets an adversarial threat model in which an attacker injects malicious passages into the knowledge store, and reports attack success rate from the attacker's perspective (with brief defense evaluation). The failure modes (naturally arising conflict vs. crafted poisoning), the evidence model (independent unreliable sources vs. adversary-controlled corpus), the locus of change (defender-side decision module vs. attacker-side corpus manipulation), the headline numbers (accuracy/faithfulness/coverage vs. ASR), and the operative policies (trust-PK/trust-CK/trust-either/abstain vs. inject malicious texts) all diverge. None of the five coordinates aligns, so the two main results cannot be put on a shared leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation in which both systems play the same role on the same task: e.g., evaluate SABER as a defender against PoisonedRAG attacks, reporting matched quantities such as accuracy under attack, attack success rate, and abstention/coverage on the same datasets, retrievers, LLM backbones, and poisoning budgets. Alternatively, restrict to a common non-adversarial benchmark where PoisonedRAG's components (or a defense baseline derived from it) are scored on the same conflict-QA accuracy and faithfulness used by SABER.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works tackle different problems with different roles: one helps a model decide what to trust when retrieved passages and the model's own internal knowledge disagree under ordinary conditions, while the other studies how an adversary can corrupt the retrieval store to steer the model toward a chosen wrong answer. Their headline numbers describe opposite sides of the system (defender quality vs. attacker effectiveness) and live on incompatible scales over different datasets and threat models, so a practitioner shown both numbers in a single ranking would draw incorrect conclusions about which system is 'better' or what either result implies for deployment.

paper_a_title: Magic Mushroom: A Customizable Benchmark for Fine-grained Analysis of Retrieval Noise Erosion in RAG Systems
paper_b_title: Why Uncertainty Estimation Methods Fall Short in RAG: An Axiomatic Analysis
gold_rationale: Paper A diagnoses generation-quality degradation caused by heterogeneous retrieval noise, using a benchmark with four noise categories and evaluating answer correctness of generators and denoising pipelines. Paper B diagnoses miscalibration of uncertainty estimation methods in RAG, using an axiomatic framework of five constraints and proposing a calibration function whose target is correlation between uncertainty scores and correctness. The failure modes (noise-induced answer errors vs. unreliable confidence scores), the evidentiary setups (curated noisy contexts vs. axiom-based perturbations), the intervention points (denoising/robust generation vs. uncertainty calibration), the headline metrics (QA correctness under noise distributions vs. axiom satisfaction and uncertainty-correctness correlation), and the practitioner takeaways (choose noise-robust pipelines vs. choose better-calibrated UE) all diverge. None of the five coordinates align.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head would require both papers to target the same construct on the same evaluation setup—e.g., both reporting uncertainty-correctness correlation under matched retrieval-noise distributions on the same QA datasets and base LLMs, with comparable axiom or robustness diagnostics. Alternatively, Paper B's calibration could be applied on top of Paper A's noisy contexts and judged by Paper A's QA correctness curves, or Paper A's denoising baselines could be scored on Paper B's axioms. Without such a shared protocol, only narrative complementarity, not ranking, is supportable.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works target fundamentally different questions about RAG: one studies how answer quality degrades as retrieved passages become surface-plausible but misleading, while the other studies whether confidence scores attached to RAG outputs faithfully track output correctness. Their headline numbers live on incompatible scales (answer correctness across noise mixes versus correlation of confidence with correctness and satisfaction of formal principles), use different datasets and protocols, and recommend different remedies. A practitioner scanning a single leaderboard with both entries would likely conflate noise-robustness gains with calibration gains and pick the wrong tool for their problem.

paper_a_title: Toward Robust RALMs: Revealing the Impact of Imperfect Retrieval on Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
paper_b_title: RoseRAG: Robust Retrieval-augmented Generation with Small-scale LLMs via Margin-aware Preference Optimization
gold_rationale: Paper A is a diagnostic/benchmark contribution: it characterizes three problematic retrieval scenarios (unanswerable, adversarial, conflicting), proposes a new attack generator (GenADV) and a new robustness metric (RAD), and reports how existing RALMs degrade. Paper B is a model-training contribution: it proposes RoseRAG, a margin-aware preference optimization pipeline (multi-turn prompting, rejection sampling, contrastive preference selection) to make small-scale LLMs more robust on three open-domain QA benchmarks, reporting EM/F1 against SOTA baselines. They differ on what they perturb (diverse scenario taxonomy with custom adversarial generation vs. generic noisy/retrieved-document setting), where they act (no model change, evaluation only vs. preference-based fine-tuning of SLMs), what they measure (RAD plus scenario-detection behavior vs. EM/F1 on HotpotQA-style tasks), and what they ultimately deliver (diagnostic framework vs. trained robust model). Only the broad framing of 'imperfect retrieval' is shared.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) running RoseRAG and an equivalent baseline through Paper A's scenario suite using the same backbone models and reporting RAD plus unanswerable/conflict detection behavior, or (b) running Paper A's evaluated RALMs through Paper B's three QA benchmarks under matched retrievers, k, and EM/F1 protocol. Without aligning model scale, retrieval pipeline, perturbation distribution, and the reported metric, the two headline numbers refer to different quantities.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper delivers a diagnostic study with a custom robustness score on hand-crafted problematic document sets, while the other delivers a trained small-model system reporting standard exact-match and F1 on open-domain QA. Putting their headline numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would suggest the two systems were solving the same task under the same conditions, when in fact the benchmarks, the backbones, the document perturbations, and the scoring quantities are all different, so a practitioner choosing between them based on such a table would draw conclusions that the underlying experiments do not support.

paper_a_title: Hierarchical Planning for Complex Tasks with Knowledge Graph-RAG and Symbolic Verification
paper_b_title: Supportiveness-based Knowledge Rewriting for Retrieval-augmented Language Modeling
gold_rationale: These papers address fundamentally different problems. Paper A (per title, as no snippet is available) targets hierarchical planning of complex tasks using structured knowledge graphs and symbolic verification, presumably evaluated on planning benchmarks with success-rate-style outcomes. Paper B targets noise/irrelevance in retrieved unstructured text for RAG-based QA, intervening via a DPO-trained rewriter aligned to a 'supportiveness' signal, evaluated on six knowledge-intensive QA tasks across four LLMs. The failure modes (planning errors vs. unhelpful retrieved passages), evidence form (KG triples vs. retrieved documents), pipeline stage of intervention (plan generation/verification vs. retrieved-content rewriting), evaluation metrics, and operational policy all diverge. Even though both invoke 'retrieval-augmented' framings, there is no shared task or metric on which their headline results could be placed on the same axis.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both systems would need to be evaluated on the same task set (e.g., the same knowledge-intensive QA suite OR the same planning benchmark), with the same backbone LLM(s), the same retrieval corpus and retriever, and the same metric definitions. Alternatively, one could compare them only after re-instantiating each method on a common downstream benchmark where both are applicable (e.g., running SKR-style rewriting in front of a planning task, or running KG-RAG + symbolic verification on the QA benchmarks used by SKR), holding the LLM and retrieval substrate fixed.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works solve different problems on different benchmarks with different scoring conventions. One is about producing verified multi-step plans grounded in structured graphs; the other is about reshaping retrieved passages so a downstream language model answers questions better. If a practitioner saw their headline numbers in one ranked table, they would likely infer a head-to-head ordering that does not exist, because the systems are not competing on the same task, the same data, or the same scoring scale.

paper_a_title: Overcoming the Retrieval Barrier: Indirect Prompt Injection in the Wild for LLM Systems
paper_b_title: GRACE: Reinforcement Learning for Grounded Response and Abstention under Contextual Evidence
gold_rationale: Paper A is an offensive security study: it constructs adversarial trigger fragments to guarantee retrieval of poisoned content, reporting near-100% retrieval and ~80% SSH-key exfiltration success under a malicious-corpus threat model. Paper B is a defensive RL training framework that teaches a generator to ground answers in retrieved evidence or explicitly abstain, evaluated on QA accuracy/abstention balance over benign corpora. The failure mode (adversarial poisoning vs. ungrounded/hallucinated generation), the evidence regime (attacker-controlled vs. naturally retrieved), the pipeline stage being modified (retrieval-side attack construction vs. training-time policy on the LLM), the headline numbers (attack/retrieval success vs. answer accuracy and rejection balance), and the goal direction (break the system vs. make the system reliable) all differ. There is no shared benchmark, no shared outcome variable, and no common operating point that would let one rank these two works against each other.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head would require evaluating both methods on the same task with the same dataset and a shared outcome, e.g., (i) running GRACE-style grounded/abstaining generation against poisoned corpora produced by the IPI attack and reporting attack success or refusal rate under that adversarial setting, or (ii) measuring whether the IPI attack still succeeds when the downstream model is GRACE-trained vs. a vanilla RAG generator. Without such a shared adversarial-robustness or grounded-QA benchmark, the two single-number results have no common axis.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works study essentially different problems that only share the broad RAG context. One reports how often a crafted poisoned document can be pulled into the context and steer the model toward an attacker's goal; the other reports how often a trained model gives an evidence-supported answer or correctly says 'I don't know' under benign retrieval. Their headline percentages live on different scales, are computed on different benchmarks, and point in opposite directions (one wants the number high because it means a successful exploit, the other wants the number high because it means trustworthy QA). A practitioner who saw them side by side on a single leaderboard would draw conclusions that neither paper actually supports.

paper_a_title: DRAGged into Conflicts: Detecting and Addressing Conflicting Sources in Search-Augmented LLMs
paper_b_title: Rescuing the Unpoisoned: Efficient Defense against Knowledge Corruption Attacks on RAG Systems
gold_rationale: Paper A addresses naturally-occurring knowledge conflicts in retrieved sources (freshness differences, debatable topics, opinions) and proposes a taxonomy plus a benchmark (CONFLICTS) evaluating response quality and appropriateness when LLMs encounter such legitimate discrepancies, primarily via prompting strategies that ask the model to reason about conflict type. Paper B addresses adversarial knowledge corruption (data poisoning) and proposes RAGDEFENDER, a post-retrieval filter using lightweight ML to remove malicious passages, evaluated via attack success rate (ASR) against baselines like RobustRAG and Discern-and-Answer. The threat models (benign disagreement vs. malicious injection), interventions (generation-time prompting vs. retrieval-time filtering), and metrics (response appropriateness vs. ASR reduction) are essentially disjoint, so all five coordinates diverge.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation in which both systems are tested on the same data containing both types of source disagreement (natural conflicts and adversarially injected content), under a unified metric (e.g., joint accuracy on benign-conflict cases AND ASR on poisoned cases), with the same retrieval pipeline and base LLM, so trade-offs between handling legitimate disagreement and filtering malicious content can be measured.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works target entirely different problems in retrieval-augmented systems: one studies how models should respond when honest sources legitimately disagree (e.g., outdated vs current facts, debatable opinions), while the other studies how to strip out maliciously planted passages designed to subvert answers. They use incompatible evaluation setups and scoring conventions, so dropping their headline numbers side-by-side on a single leaderboard would lead a practitioner to draw conclusions about whichever method 'wins' that have no real bearing on the scenario they actually care about.

paper_a_title: RoseRAG: Robust Retrieval-augmented Generation with Small-scale LLMs via Margin-aware Preference Optimization
paper_b_title: Faithfulness-Aware Uncertainty Quantification for Fact-Checking the Output of Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Paper A (RoseRAG) addresses generation quality of small-scale LLMs under noisy retrieval, intervening at training time via margin-aware preference optimization, and reports answer correctness (EM/F1) on open-domain QA. Paper B (FRANQ) addresses post-hoc hallucination detection in RAG outputs by applying uncertainty quantification conditioned on faithfulness to retrieved context, and reports detection performance on a long-form QA dataset annotated for factuality and faithfulness. The two papers target fundamentally different problems (improving generation vs. flagging unreliable spans), operate at different stages of the pipeline (training vs. inference-time detection), and use non-overlapping evaluation metrics. Their outputs are not interchangeable on any shared leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head comparison would require both systems to be evaluated on the same task with shared inputs and a shared scoring protocol — e.g., either (1) using FRANQ's detector as a filter/abstention layer on top of RoseRAG outputs and measuring end-task QA accuracy (or selective QA with risk-coverage curves) on the same benchmarks, or (2) producing per-statement confidence/correctness scores from both systems on a common hallucination-detection benchmark with AUROC/PRR. Without a shared dataset, shared output type, and shared scoring function, the reported numbers are not commensurable.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems do different jobs: one tries to produce better short answers from a small model when retrieved passages are noisy, while the other tries to flag which parts of a long generated answer are likely to be factually wrong. They report different kinds of scores on different kinds of benchmarks, so placing their headline numbers side-by-side on a single leaderboard would lead a practitioner to think one beats the other when in fact they solve unrelated problems.

paper_a_title: Redefining Retrieval Evaluation in the Era of LLMs

gold_rationale: Paper A targets the misalignment of classical IR ranking metrics (nDCG, MAP, MRR) with LLM-as-consumer behavior in RAG, proposing UDCG, a utility/distraction-aware metric evaluated by correlation with end-to-end RAG answer accuracy across five datasets and six LLMs. Paper B (title only: 'Chunk-Distilled Language Modeling') concerns a language modeling technique involving chunk-level distillation; this is a generative modeling contribution rather than a retrieval evaluation metric. The two works differ on essentially every coordinate: the problem being solved (retrieval-evaluation misalignment vs. LM modeling/efficiency), where the change is made (offline IR scoring vs. LM training/inference), the quantity being optimized (rank-quality/accuracy correlation vs. likely perplexity or generation quality), and the deliverable (a scoring metric vs. a modeling method). what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers would need to address the same task family (e.g., both proposing RAG components evaluated on the same QA benchmarks with the same LLM readers), use comparable evaluation targets (e.g., end-to-end answer accuracy or the same retrieval-quality correlation), and produce artifacts of the same type (either two metrics evaluated by correlation with downstream accuracy, or two retrieval/LM components evaluated on accuracy). A direct comparison would also require shared datasets, shared LLM backbones, and consistent reporting (e.g., the same accuracy/EM/F1 figures), none of which appear shared here.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works live in different research categories: one delivers a new scoring tool for judging retrieved passages in RAG and is validated by how well its scores track downstream answer correctness, while the other contributes a chunk-based language modeling approach whose headline numbers would naturally be generation-quality scores. Putting their headline numbers side by side on one leaderboard would suggest a head-to-head contest that does not actually exist, and a practitioner trying to choose between them for a real system would be drawing a conclusion the underlying evidence cannot support.

paper_a_title: TrustRAG: Enhancing Robustness and Trustworthiness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation

gold_rationale: Paper A (TrustRAG) targets adversarial corpus poisoning attacks, assuming an attacker has injected malicious documents into the retrieval corpus; its intervention is a two-stage post-retrieval filter (cluster filtering + LLM self-assessment) and its primary metrics are attack resistance and accuracy under attack. Paper B (SUGAR) targets a non-adversarial efficiency/distraction problem in standard QA: it estimates semantic uncertainty to decide whether to retrieve at all, and if so whether single- or multi-step. The intervention point is pre-retrieval (gating), the threat model is benign-noisy rather than malicious, and the headline metrics are QA accuracy and inference efficiency under clean conditions. All five coordinates diverge, so the works are not on the same task.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation setting would need (a) a common threat/operating regime (either both evaluated under PoisonedRAG-style corpus poisoning or both under clean adaptive-retrieval benchmarks like Natural Questions / 2WikiMQA / Self-RAG suite), (b) a common metric pairing (e.g., end-task QA accuracy plus retrieval/inference cost, or attack success rate plus clean accuracy), (c) ablations where each method is applied at the other's decision point (SUGAR run under poisoning; TrustRAG measured for unnecessary-retrieval savings), and (d) matched retriever, corpus, and base LLM. Without these, the systems optimize different objectives and cannot be ranked head-to-head.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems solve essentially different problems and would look incommensurable on one leaderboard: one is a defensive filter designed for settings where an adversary has planted poisoned documents in the corpus, while the other is an uncertainty-gated retrieval selector aimed at skipping unnecessary lookups on ordinary QA. paper_a_title: Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth: Revealing the Behavior of Large Language Models in Knowledge Conflicts

Intervention point: Paper A probes the generation/integration stage of general LLMs; Paper B targets the indexing and retrieval pipeline of GraphRAG specifically. Metric target: Paper A reports receptivity rates and confirmation bias indicators; Paper B reports attack success rate and poisoning-text efficiency. Paper B designs an adversarial poisoning technique against GraphRAG and reports success rates of compromising queries. They concern different systems, different threat models, and different outcome quantities. A practitioner seeing them on the same leaderboard would likely conflate benign integration behavior with adversarial robustness and draw incorrect conclusions about either system.

paper_a_title: Adaptive Contrastive Decoding in Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Handling Noisy Contexts
paper_b_title: Know Or Not: a library for evaluating out-of-knowledge base robustness
gold_rationale: Paper A proposes a decoding-time technique (Adaptive Contrastive Decoding) aimed at producing correct answers even when retrieved passages are noisy but the query is in-scope; it is evaluated on open-domain QA correctness. Paper B contributes an evaluation library and benchmark (knowornot / PolicyBench) for measuring whether LLMs abstain when queries fall outside the knowledge base. The targeted problem (noisy in-scope context vs. out-of-knowledge-base queries), the contribution type (decoding method vs. evaluation tooling), the success criterion (answer correctness vs. correct abstention), and the desired model behavior (answer better vs. refuse appropriately) all differ. There is no shared benchmark or shared scoring rule under which their headline numbers would mean the same thing.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation setting in which both systems are scored on the same task with the same metric — for example, running ACD inside the knowornot/PolicyBench pipeline and reporting OOKB abstention rates plus in-context answer correctness, or running the knowornot evaluation on Paper A's noisy-context open-domain QA setup. independent_rubric_rationale: The two works address different problems with different success criteria: one is a technique for getting better answers when retrieved passages contain distractors, while the other is a framework for checking whether a model refuses to answer when the knowledge base does not cover the query. Placing their headline numbers side by side on one leaderboard would suggest a head-to-head winner where none exists, and a practitioner could easily pick the wrong tool for their deployment need.

paper_a_title: Generating Leakage-Free Benchmarks for Robust RAG Evaluation

gold_rationale: Paper A is an evaluation-infrastructure contribution: it identifies knowledge leakage in existing RAG benchmarks and proposes SeedRG, a semi-synthetic pipeline that produces leakage-free test instances and then uses those instances to compare existing RAG systems. Its failure_type concerns contaminated/aged benchmarks, its evidence_assumption is that prior benchmarks overlap with parametric memory, its intervention_point is benchmark construction, its metric_target is leakage rate and discriminability across RAG systems, and its action_policy advises evaluators to adopt cleaner benchmarks. Paper B (Superposition Prompting), based on its title, is a method paper proposing a prompting/inference technique to improve quality and reduce latency of RAG itself. Its failure_type is suboptimal accuracy/speed of standard RAG prompting, its evidence_assumption is that existing prompting strategies leave headroom on standard benchmarks, its intervention_point is the prompting/decoding pipeline, its metric_target is QA accuracy and latency, and its action_policy is to adopt the new prompting method. The two works therefore differ on every coordinate of the frame and cannot be ranked against each other.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require either (a) running Superposition Prompting as one of the RAG systems benchmarked on SeedRG's leakage-free evaluation, so both works are scored on the same task and metric, or (b) framing both as contributions to a shared objective (e.g., end-to-end RAG QA accuracy on a fixed, uncontaminated benchmark) and reporting matched numbers. Absent such alignment, the two papers address different problem layers (evaluation methodology vs. inference-time method) and any direct leaderboard comparison would be a category error.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two papers target different layers of the RAG stack: one builds a cleaner testbed and uses it to re-rank existing systems, while the other proposes a new prompting/inference technique to make RAG itself better and faster. Placing their headline numbers side by side on one leaderboard would suggest they are competing solutions to the same problem, which they are not, and a practitioner trying to pick a 'winner' would be led toward an incoherent choice.

They use disjoint benchmarks and report numbers on incommensurable scales. Putting their headline results side by side on a single leaderboard would suggest a head-to-head relationship that does not exist and would push a practitioner toward unwarranted conclusions about which approach is 'better' when the two systems are simply doing different jobs.

paper_a_title: Safeguarding RAG Pipelines with GMTP: A Gradient-based Masked Token Probability Method for Poisoned Document Detection
paper_b_title: Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs

Absent a shared task definition and overlapping evaluation protocol, any ranking would conflate different objectives.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems pursue different goals within RAG: one is a security defense against adversarially injected documents in a public knowledge base, while the other constructs personalized user-memory graphs to support tailored agent responses. They are evaluated on different datasets, with different success criteria, and address users who have different needs (a developer hardening a pipeline versus a developer personalizing an assistant). Placing their headline numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would suggest a comparison that does not exist, and a practitioner choosing between them based on such a table would likely draw the wrong conclusion about which tool fits their use case.

paper_a_title: Seeing through the Conflict: Transparent Knowledge Conflict Handling in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper_b_title: Cordon-MAS: Defending RAG against Knowledge Poisoning via Information-Flow Control
gold_rationale: The two papers address fundamentally different problem regimes within RAG. Paper A (TCR) targets benign knowledge conflicts between parametric memory and noisy/contradictory retrieved context, assuming evidence is non-adversarial; its intervention is a plug-in signal-injection module (dual contrastive encoders + soft prompts) evaluated by conflict-detection F1, knowledge-gap recovery, and misleading-context override rates across seven QA benchmarks. Paper B (Cordon-MAS) targets adversarially optimized poisoning (Confundo-style) under the explicit assumption that detection alone fails due to a monitoring-control gap; its intervention is an architectural multi-agent decomposition enforcing information-flow control, evaluated by attack success rate reduction on five BEIR datasets under attack. Threat model, evaluation distribution, evaluation metric, and the locus of intervention all differ, so a direct comparison or ranking is not coherent.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) both systems evaluated on the same threat model—e.g., running TCR under Confundo-style poisoning on the same BEIR setup and reporting attack success rate, or running Cordon-MAS on TCR's seven conflict/QA benchmarks reporting conflict-detection F1 and knowledge-gap recovery—or (b) a shared benchmark that jointly covers natural conflicts and adversarial poisoning with a common set of metrics (e.g., faithfulness, ASR, and conflict F1 on the same inputs and base LLM). Without overlapping datasets, base models, and metrics, no ranking is meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works tackle different threat regimes in RAG: one handles naturally occurring contradictions between a model's internal memory and retrieved passages, while the other defends specifically against deliberately crafted poisoned documents. Their reported headline numbers (conflict-detection F1 and override-reduction percentages on seven QA benchmarks versus attack-success-rate reduction on five BEIR sets under attack) describe entirely different phenomena on different data. A practitioner who saw them on one leaderboard would likely draw wrong conclusions about which system is stronger, since neither has been shown to work in the other's setting.

paper_a_title: PR-Attack: Coordinated Prompt-RAG Attacks on Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Large Language Models via Bilevel Optimization
paper_b_title: Retrieval Augmented Generation or Long-Context LLMs? A Comprehensive Study and Hybrid Approach
gold_rationale: Paper A studies adversarial security of RAG systems, formulating a bilevel optimization to produce poisoned documents plus backdoor prompt triggers, and reports attack success rate / stealth under an adversary-controlled threat model. Paper B is a benign QA study comparing retrieval-augmented generation against long-context LLMs and proposing a hybrid routing strategy, reported with standard QA quality metrics. paper_a_title: Unified Generative and Discriminative Training for Multi-modal Large Language Models
paper_b_title: Accelerating Inference of Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Sparse Context Selection
gold_rationale: Paper A targets a training-time failure mode in multi-modal LLMs (the perceived split between generative and discriminative objectives) and intervenes by unifying the two training paradigms; its evidence base is multi-modal understanding/generation benchmarks and its metric target is task quality on those benchmarks. Paper B targets an inference-time efficiency failure in retrieval-augmented generation (latency and compute cost from long retrieved contexts) and intervenes via sparse context selection at inference; its evidence base is RAG/QA workloads and its primary metric target is the speed-quality trade-off. The two works diverge on every coordinate of the frame, and there is no shared baseline, task, or metric to anchor a direct comparison. Even without snippets, the titles and problem framings make this divergence clear.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Comparability would require the two papers to share at least (i) the same task family or workload, (ii) the same primary outcome measure (e.g., both reporting accuracy on an overlapping benchmark, or both reporting latency-quality Pareto curves on the same RAG pipeline), (iii) compatible stages of the model lifecycle (both at training or both at inference), and (iv) a common baseline system. None of these alignments are present here, so any 'A vs. B' ranking would be category error rather than evaluation.
independent_rubric_rationale: Putting these two results on a single leaderboard would seriously confuse a practitioner. One paper concerns how to train a multi-modal language model so it can do both understanding and generation well; the other concerns how to make retrieval-augmented question answering run faster by trimming retrieved context. They live in different problem areas, optimize for different goals (quality on multi-modal tasks versus inference speed on text QA), and their recommendations operate at different stages of the model lifecycle. There is no shared yardstick by which one could be declared better than the other.

paper_a_title: CPA-RAG: Covert Poisoning Attacks on Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Large Language Models
paper_b_title: Divide-Then-Align: Honest Alignment based on the Knowledge Boundary of RAG
gold_rationale: All five coordinates diverge. Paper A studies a security failure_type (adversarial corpus poisoning) under an adversary-controlled evidence_assumption, with the intervention_point being malicious document injection into the retrieval corpus; its metric_target is Attack Success Rate and the action_policy is generating covert adversarial passages. Paper B studies an honesty/hallucination failure_type under a benign-but-noisy evidence_assumption, with the intervention_point being post-training DPO alignment; its metric_target is the accuracy/abstention balance and the action_policy is teaching the model to emit 'I don't know' when outside the knowledge boundary. The two works do not share an evaluation surface and are not on a common scale.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A direct comparison would require (i) a shared task and dataset, (ii) a common evaluation surface (e.g., both reporting ASR under poisoning, or both reporting accuracy/abstention under noisy retrieval), (iii) a matched threat or noise model, and (iv) compatible system roles — either both attacking RAG, both defending RAG, or one paper proposed as a defense explicitly tested against the other's attack on identical corpora, retrievers, and LLMs.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two headline numbers describe fundamentally different phenomena: one reports how often crafted malicious passages flip a RAG system's answer to an adversary-chosen target, while the other reports how well a tuned model balances correct responses with appropriate 'I don't know' replies on standard QA benchmarks. Placing these scores side by side on a single leaderboard would suggest a shared yardstick that does not exist, and a practitioner could easily draw unwarranted conclusions about which system is 'better' for RAG.

paper_a_title: Cutting Off the Head Ends the Conflict: A Mechanism for Interpreting and Mitigating Knowledge Conflicts in Language Models
paper_b_title: A Few Words Can Distort Graphs: Knowledge Poisoning Attacks on Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Paper A addresses organic knowledge conflicts between parametric memory and benign retrieved context in standard RAG/QA, with a defensive mechanistic intervention (pruning memory/context attention heads via PH3) measured by controllability gains (↑44.0% memory use, ↑38.5% context use) and open-domain QA improvement. Paper B addresses adversarial knowledge poisoning of Graph-based RAG, where a few-word edits to source text corrupt LLM-extracted knowledge graphs, measured by attack success rate (93.1% TKPA) and QA collapse (95%→50% UKPA). The systems (vanilla RAG vs GraphRAG), threat model (no adversary vs adversary), intervention locus (model internals vs corpus text), goal direction (mitigate vs attack), and headline metrics are entirely different. None of the five coordinates align.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers would need to share (1) the same system architecture (either both standard RAG or both GraphRAG), (2) a common threat/usage model (e.g., both evaluating robustness to adversarial corpus poisoning or both evaluating handling of organic context-memory conflict), (3) a shared metric computed on the same task and dataset (e.g., end-to-end QA accuracy under identical conditions), and (4) the same role (both proposing defenses or both proposing attacks). At minimum, one would need PH3 evaluated as a defense on GraphRAG under TKPA/UKPA, or the poisoning attacks evaluated against a knowledge-conflict mitigation baseline on the same QA suite.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works target fundamentally different problems on different system types. Paper A modifies model internals to steer a standard retrieval-augmented model toward either its own stored knowledge or the supplied passage when the two disagree organically, reporting steering rates. Paper B instead corrupts the input corpus of a graph-structured retrieval pipeline so that an attacker drives the answer, reporting attack success and accuracy degradation. One is a defensive controllability story; the other is an offensive vulnerability story on a different pipeline. A practitioner reading their headline numbers on a single leaderboard would draw badly wrong conclusions about which approach is 'better,' since the numbers measure unrelated things on unrelated setups.

paper_a_title: FiD-Light: Efficient and Effective Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
paper_b_title: SURE-RAG: Sufficiency and Uncertainty-Aware Evidence Verification for Selective Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: The two papers address fundamentally different problems within the RAG umbrella. Paper A (FiD-Light) targets efficiency/latency of generation in an FiD architecture and reports answer-quality plus efficiency metrics under an always-answer policy. Paper B (SURE-RAG) targets evidence sufficiency verification with a three-way SUPPORTED/REFUTED/INSUFFICIENT decision and selective abstention, evaluated by Macro-F1 and risk-at-coverage on HotpotQA-RAG v3 and HaluBench. The failure modes (slow/expensive generation vs. unjustified answers), the evidence treatment (passages consumed by a decoder vs. set-level sufficiency aggregation over a pair verifier), the intervention point (decoder architecture vs. post-retrieval verification layer), the headline metrics (efficiency + QA quality vs. sufficiency Macro-F1 / selective risk), and the answering policy (always answer vs. answer-or-abstain) all diverge. Without a shared task, benchmark, or scoring rule, no leaderboard-style ranking is meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared task definition (e.g., open-domain QA with or without abstention), the same benchmark and split, a common evaluation protocol covering both quality and either efficiency or selective-prediction outcomes, and matched retrieval/reader stacks so that one system's contribution can be isolated against the other under identical inputs and scoring.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems are solving different jobs on different datasets with different scoring rules: one is about making retrieval-augmented generation faster while keeping answer quality, the other is about deciding whether retrieved passages actually justify an answer and abstaining when they do not. Putting their headline numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would suggest a head-to-head winner where none exists, so a practitioner would likely draw the wrong conclusion about which approach is 'better'.

paper_a_title: The LiveRAG Challenge at SIGIR 2025
paper_b_title: Multi-Hop Paragraph Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
gold_rationale: Based on titles and venues alone (no snippets supplied), Paper A is an overview/report of a 2025 SIGIR shared-task challenge on live retrieval-augmented generation, which typically aggregates heterogeneous submissions evaluated under organizer-defined protocols on a fixed live corpus. Paper B is a 2019 ACL methods paper proposing a specific multi-hop paragraph retriever evaluated on standard open-domain QA benchmarks (e.g., HotpotQA). The failure_type differs (broad live-RAG ecosystem reporting vs. insufficiency of single-hop retrieval); evidence_assumption differs (live/streaming or fixed challenge corpus vs. static Wikipedia paragraph index); intervention_point differs (system-level submissions to a challenge vs. component-level retriever); metric_target differs (challenge leaderboard metrics, likely faithfulness/relevance composites vs. retrieval recall and downstream QA EM/F1); action_policy differs (running a competition with constrained inference vs. a published trained retriever). All five coordinates plausibly diverge, so a direct comparison or ranking would not be meaningful. Confidence is capped at 3 because the snippets are missing and the exact challenge metrics and evaluation rules are not in front of me.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both papers to report a comparable headline number on a shared task with the same corpus, the same retrieval candidate pool, the same QA or generation evaluation protocol, and matched compute/inference constraints. At minimum one would need Paper B's retriever (or its successor) to be entered into the LiveRAG evaluation harness on the same dataset and scoring rubric, with controlled generator and prompting, so that any ranking reflects the retrieval contribution rather than differences in tasks, eras, corpora, or end-to-end system design.
independent_rubric_rationale: These two works sit in different roles in the literature: one is a 2025 community competition report summarizing many heterogeneous submissions under organizer-defined rules, and the other is a 2019 research paper introducing a particular open-domain question answering retriever evaluated on its own benchmark. Putting their headline numbers next to each other on a single leaderboard would conflate a venue-level event summary with a single technical contribution and span six years of changing datasets, baselines, and evaluation conventions, so a practitioner reading such a leaderboard would likely draw conclusions that the underlying evidence does not support.

paper_a_title: Backdoored Retrievers for Prompt Injection Attacks on Retrieval Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
paper_b_title: Defense Against Prompt Injection Attack by Leveraging Attack Techniques
gold_rationale: Paper A is an offensive paper proposing a backdoored dense retriever and corpus poisoning to inject attacker-chosen instructions into RAG prompts; its headline number (ASR) is something the authors want to maximize. Paper B is a defensive paper that inverts training-free prompt injection techniques to suppress injected instructions at the LLM stage; its headline number is reduction of injection success against existing defenses. The two works sit on opposite sides of the attack/defense ledger, target different stages of the RAG pipeline (retriever training vs. generator prompting), assume different adversary capabilities (corpus/fine-tune access vs. an already-injected context), and optimize ASR in opposite directions. There is no shared task setup, dataset, threat model, or success criterion that would make their headline numbers commensurate.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation would need (1) a single fixed threat model (e.g., indirect prompt injection via retrieved documents), (2) the same RAG stack, corpus, and query set, (3) Paper B's defense actually instantiated against Paper A's backdoored-retriever and corpus-poisoning attacks (not just against the prior attacks B was tested on), and (4) a common, identically-defined ASR (or injection-success) metric reported with and without the defense, plus utility on clean queries. Only then could one place an 'attack strength' number and a 'defense strength' number into a coherent table.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two papers answer opposite questions on different parts of the RAG pipeline using numbers that move in opposite desirable directions, and they never share a benchmark or threat setup. A practitioner who saw their headline scores side by side on one leaderboard would likely treat them as competing systems on the same task, when in fact a high score in one paper and a high score in the other describe entirely different phenomena and cannot be traded off against each other.

paper_a_title: ADMIT: Few-shot Knowledge Poisoning Attacks on RAG-based Fact Checking
paper_b_title: Hidden-in-Plain-Text: A Benchmark for Social-Web Indirect Prompt Injection in RAG
gold_rationale: Paper A (ADMIT) is an offensive contribution proposing a semantic, few-shot poisoning attack against RAG-based fact-checking pipelines, reporting an ~86% Attack Success Rate at a 0.93x10^-6 poisoning ratio across 4 retrievers/11 LLMs/4 benchmarks. Paper B (OpenRAG-Soc/Hidden-in-Plain-Text) is a benchmark/harness contribution focused on web-native indirect prompt injection carriers (HTML/Markdown/Unicode) on social-web content, evaluating retriever rank shifts, utility/latency, and deployable mitigations (sanitization, normalization, attribution-gating). The five coordinates diverge across the board: the threat surface differs (semantic content poisoning vs. format/carrier-based IPI), the corpus and evidence regime differ (credible fact-checking pools vs. social-web text), the role differs (new attack vs. benchmark + defenses), and the reported numbers (ASR on factuality flips vs. multi-axis benchmark scores including rank shift, utility, latency) are not on the same scale. There is no shared task, dataset, or score that would make their headline results comparable.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared threat model (e.g., both indirect-injection or both knowledge-poisoning), a common corpus and retriever/LLM stack, an aligned evaluation protocol with identical primary scores (e.g., ASR on the same target task at matched poisoning budgets), and a comparable role (either both attacks or both defenses tested on the same benchmark). Ideally Paper A's attack would be run inside Paper B's harness, or both works would report against a common third-party benchmark with the same generator and retriever configurations.
independent_rubric_rationale: Paper A introduces an offensive technique targeted at fact-checking pipelines and reports a single high success-rate number under a very low injection budget, while Paper B delivers a benchmark and testbed for web-native injection carriers with multiple defenses, reporting things like rank shifts, utility, and latency. The two works tackle different problem framings (semantic content manipulation versus HTML/Unicode/Markdown trickery on social-web text), play different roles (proposing an attack versus standardizing an evaluation suite with mitigations), and produce headline numbers that live on entirely different scales. A practitioner skimming a single leaderboard row for each would draw an apples-to-oranges conclusion about which work is stronger or more relevant.

paper_a_title: ProGRank: Probe-Gradient Reranking to Defend Dense-Retriever RAG from Corpus Poisoning
paper_b_title: On the Vulnerability of Applying Retrieval-Augmented Generation within Knowledge-Intensive Application Domains
gold_rationale: Both papers address corpus poisoning of dense-retriever RAG and propose retriever-side defenses, but the five-coordinate frame diverges materially. Paper A defines a broad corpus-poisoning threat covering retrieval-optimized, joint, trigger-based, and misleading-evidence attack families on three general-purpose QA datasets with three retriever backbones, and pursues a post-hoc reranking remedy using probe gradients. Paper B narrows the threat to universal poisoning aimed at injecting targeted information (e.g., PII) in medical QA across 225 setup combinations, and proposes a detection-based filter exploiting embedding-deviation patterns. The intervention mechanism (reranking vs. detection/filtering), the headline metric (defence success / robustness-utility trade-off and end-to-end ASR vs. detection rate), and the evidence base (general-domain breadth vs. medical-domain depth) differ substantially. Placing the two headline numbers on one leaderboard would not give an apples-to-apples comparison.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require: (1) a shared attack taxonomy and threat model (or restriction to the intersection, e.g., universal poisoning on the same corpora); (2) the same retrieval corpora, retriever backbones, query distributions, and poison-injection budgets; (3) re-implementation of both defenses inside the same pipeline, scored on a common metric set covering both pre-generation detection/rerank effectiveness and downstream end-to-end task quality, plus utility loss on clean queries; (4) consistent budget for adaptive/evasive attackers; and (5) reporting of confidence intervals or seeds so that ranked differences are interpretable.
independent_rubric_rationale: If the two headline numbers were placed side-by-side on a single leaderboard, a practitioner would likely draw the wrong conclusions. The first study reports broad-domain robustness and end-to-end downstream quality against several poisoning families on general QA corpora, while the second reports detection rates for a narrower, universal-poisoning threat largely scoped to medical QA with a different evaluation suite. The reported scores live on different axes and reflect different problem framings, so any ranking would conflate scope, defender strategy, and scoring conventions rather than reveal which approach is actually stronger in a shared deployment.

paper_a_title: Defending against Indirect Prompt Injection by Instruction Detection
paper_b_title: A Few Words Can Distort Graphs: Knowledge Poisoning Attacks on Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Paper A is a defense paper proposing InstructDetector, which classifies retrieved documents using LLM hidden states/gradients to detect Indirect Prompt Injection in standard text-chunk RAG (reports detection accuracy 99.60%/96.90% and ASR reduction to 0.03% on BIPIA). Paper B is an offense paper proposing TKPA and UKPA, which perturb source text before graph construction to corrupt the LLM-extracted knowledge graph in GraphRAG (reports 93.1% targeted attack success and QA accuracy collapse from 95% to 50%). Every coordinate diverges: the threat model is hidden-instruction injection at retrieval time vs. semantic poisoning of source narratives at graph-build time; the system under study is text RAG vs. GraphRAG; the policy is detection/filtering vs. adversarial generation; the headline numbers are defense effectiveness vs. attack effectiveness, so higher numbers mean opposite things.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers would need to occupy the same role (e.g., both attacks or both defenses) on the same RAG variant (text RAG or GraphRAG), use a shared benchmark and threat model, and report a common metric oriented the same way (e.g., post-defense ASR under matched attacks, or attack success under matched defenses). Pairing a defense ASR-reduction number with an attack ASR number on one leaderboard is category-mismatched.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two headline numbers describe opposite roles in different pipelines: one reports how well a detector keeps a standard RAG system safe, while the other reports how easily a graph-built RAG system can be subverted by editing a tiny fraction of source text. Putting them side by side on a single leaderboard would invite a practitioner to read one as 'safer' than the other, when the systems, threat models, and direction of the score are not aligned.

paper_a_title: Decide Then Retrieve: A Training-Free Framework with Uncertainty-Guided Triggering and Dual-Path Retrieval
paper_b_title: Know Or Not: a library for evaluating out-of-knowledge base robustness
gold_rationale: Paper A proposes a training-free RAG method (DTR) with uncertainty-guided retrieval triggering and dual-path retrieval, evaluated on five open-domain QA benchmarks using EM/F1 against standard RAG baselines. Paper B is an evaluation library (knowornot) plus a benchmark (PolicyBench) for measuring out-of-knowledge-base robustness, i.e., whether LLMs appropriately abstain when context is missing. The two works target distinct failure modes (noisy/sparse-query retrieval vs. unsafe answering on OOKB queries), operate at incompatible points in the pipeline (a new RAG technique vs. a measurement framework), report incompatible metrics on incompatible datasets, and rest on different evidence assumptions (knowledge base is relevant and helpful vs. queries may fall outside the KB). They cannot be ranked on a shared leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both systems would need to be evaluated on a common task with shared datasets and metrics. For example, Paper A's DTR could be run on PolicyBench using OOKB robustness/abstention metrics, or Paper B's evaluation methodology could be applied to a setting where Paper A's open-domain QA benchmarks include OOKB-style queries with measurable abstention. Without this overlap in benchmark, scoring criterion, and system-under-test scope (method vs. evaluation library), no direct comparison is meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper presents a new retrieval-augmented generation technique scored with exact-match and F1 on open-domain question answering, while the other delivers an evaluation toolkit and a policy-domain benchmark focused on whether models appropriately decline to respond when relevant context is absent. Putting their headline numbers side-by-side on a single leaderboard would conflate accuracy on standard QA with abstention behavior on out-of-scope queries, leading a practitioner to draw entirely wrong conclusions about which approach is 'better.'

paper_a_title: Over-Searching in Search-Augmented Large Language Models
paper_b_title: QuCo-RAG: Quantifying Uncertainty from the Pre-training Corpus for Dynamic Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Paper A is a diagnostic/benchmark study of over-searching: it characterizes when search-augmented LLMs invoke retrieval unnecessarily (including on unanswerable queries), introduces Tokens Per Correctness (TPC) as a cost-efficiency metric, releases OverSearchQA, and stresses abstention behavior. Paper B is a method paper for dynamic RAG that triggers retrieval based on pre-training corpus statistics (entity frequency and co-occurrence via Infini-gram), reporting EM gains of 5–12 points on multi-hop QA with OLMo-2, Llama-3, Qwen2.5, GPT-4.1/5. The two operate on different problems (suppress unnecessary searches and improve abstention vs. trigger retrieval to reduce hallucination), use disjoint benchmarks (OverSearchQA vs. multi-hop/biomedical QA), and report different headline numbers (TPC and abstention vs. EM). Their action policies (abstain/search vs. retrieve/not retrieve based on corpus signal) and intervention designs (analysis + lightweight mitigation vs. novel trigger method) diverge. The evidence_assumption axis is partially shared (both touch retrieval-time signals) but used to different ends.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A direct comparison would need (1) a shared evaluation suite that mixes answerable and unanswerable queries, (2) joint reporting of both a cost-efficiency score (e.g., TPC or search-call rate) and an accuracy/EM score, (3) the same backbone models and retriever, and (4) a unified policy space (when-to-retrieve and when-to-abstain) so each system's trigger logic is evaluated on identical inputs. Without these, TPC/abstention numbers from A and EM-gain numbers from B cannot be placed on one axis.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works target different problems within retrieval-augmented LLMs. Paper A studies when systems call the search tool too often, including on questions that have no answer, and scores systems with a cost-per-correct-answer style score plus abstention behavior on its own benchmark. Paper B proposes a corpus-statistics trigger for dynamic retrieval and reports exact-match improvements on multi-hop and biomedical QA with a different model lineup. The benchmarks, headline numbers, and goals (cut wasteful searches and refuse unknowable questions vs. lift answer correctness on answerable multi-hop questions) do not align, so putting A's TPC/abstention results next to B's EM gains on one leaderboard would suggest the two are competing on the same task when they are not, leading a practitioner to draw unwarranted conclusions about which approach is 'better.'

paper_a_title: When to Trust: A Causality-Aware Calibration Framework for Accurate Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation.
paper_b_title: GRACE: Reinforcement Learning for Grounded Response and Abstention under Contextual Evidence
gold_rationale: Paper A's title positions it as a calibration framework for Knowledge Graph RAG using a causality-aware mechanism, presumably reweighting or calibrating trust signals over KG-sourced evidence. Paper B is a reinforcement learning framework over text retrieval with heterogeneous retrievers, training a multi-stage gated reward for evidence sufficiency, evidence extraction, and abstention. The evidence source (structured KG vs. unstructured text passages) differs, the intervention layer differs (calibration of trust scores vs. RL training of generation+abstention behavior), and the action policy differs (trust-gated answering vs. explicit 'I don't know' abstention with extracted evidence spans). Paper A's snippet is unavailable, so confidence is moderate, but the title alone is sufficient to identify these mismatches.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both systems should operate over the same evidence modality (either both KG-grounded or both text-grounded), share at least one common benchmark and split, and report a shared headline number defined identically (e.g., the same accuracy/abstention trade-off curve or the same calibration metric). Backbone LLM and retriever should be matched or ablated, and the abstention/trust decision should be evaluated under a common protocol.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems draw evidence from very different sources (structured knowledge graphs versus textual passages retrieved by heterogeneous retrievers) and adjust model behavior through very different machinery (calibrating a trust signal versus training the generator with staged rewards to abstain). Placing their headline numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would suggest a head-to-head ranking that the underlying setups, datasets, and reporting conventions do not support, and a practitioner would likely draw the wrong conclusion about which approach is stronger.

paper_a_title: Reliable Decision‑Making via Calibration‑Oriented Retrieval‑Augmented Generation
paper_b_title: Sufficient Context: A New Lens on Retrieval Augmented Generation Systems
gold_rationale: Paper A has no text snippet available, leaving its precise framing, method, datasets, and evaluation metrics unknown. From its title alone, Paper A appears to target calibration quality in RAG decision-making, while Paper B introduces a 'sufficient context' construct (with an autorater-based classifier) and uses it to drive selective generation/abstention, reporting accuracy-among-responses on QA benchmarks for Gemini/GPT/Gemma. The likely metric families (calibration error vs. accuracy-conditional-on-response and abstention rates) and the intervention loci (probability calibration vs. context-sufficiency-gated abstention) differ in kind, but without Paper A's snippet the overlap in benchmarks, models, and reported numbers cannot be confirmed. This makes the pair underspecified rather than confidently invalid.
