what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid direct comparison would require: (1) a shared evaluation suite (same QA datasets, same retrieval setup, same base LLMs); (2) a common headline metric reported by both papers (e.g., selective accuracy at matched coverage, or calibration error at matched accuracy), with the alternative method re-implemented under the other's protocol; (3) aligned abstention semantics so that 'not answering' is treated identically; and (4) confirmation from Paper A's actual content of its evidence assumptions, intervention stage, and target metric so the two systems are placed on the same axis rather than adjacent axes.
independent_rubric_rationale: With no excerpt from the first paper, it is not possible to confirm whether the headline numbers from the two works are produced on overlapping benchmarks, identical base models, and the same scoring convention. The titles hint at related but distinct goals (probability reliability versus reasoning about whether retrieved passages contain enough information), which suggests their main numbers may not sit on a shared scale, but this cannot be verified from the supplied material.

paper_a_title: PrismRAG: Boosting RAG Factuality with Distractor Resilience and Strategized Reasoning
paper_b_title: The Curse of Helpfulness: Inverse Scaling Law in Robustness to Distractor Instructions via DistractionIF
gold_rationale: Although both papers share the word 'distractor' and operate in the RAG/reference-grounded setting, they address fundamentally different phenomena. Paper A (PrismRAG) targets content-level distractors—semi-relevant passages mixed with gold evidence—and measures QA factuality across 12 open-book benchmarks, reporting a 5.4% average factuality gain via SFT on synthetic distractor-aware QA pairs plus reasoning scaffolds. Paper B (DistractionIF) targets a distinct failure mode: instruction-like fragments embedded in reference text (editorial notes, UI residue) that the model erroneously executes as commands; it measures instruction-following robustness on its own benchmark and reports a 15.5% gain via GRPO. The underlying error mode (factual hallucination from semantic noise vs. data/instruction boundary violation), the metric (factuality vs. instruction-following robustness), and the action policy the model is meant to enforce all diverge.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both systems would need to be evaluated on a common benchmark that either (a) isolates content-distractor robustness with a shared factuality metric, or (b) isolates instruction-distractor robustness with a shared instruction-following-under-noise metric. A unified evaluation suite separating 'noise that misleads about facts' from 'noise that hijacks the task' is needed, with both interventions applied to the same base models and scored under identical protocols.
independent_rubric_rationale: Placing the 5.4% number next to the 15.5% number on one leaderboard would mislead a practitioner because the two numbers describe different problems despite shared vocabulary. One quantifies how well a model produces correct answers when irrelevant passages are mixed into retrieved context; the other quantifies how well a model resists treating embedded textual fragments as commands. A reader could wrongly conclude that one approach dominates the other on a common challenge, when in reality each addresses a separate weakness measured on disjoint benchmarks.

paper_a_title: Parallel Key-Value Cache Fusion for Position Invariant RAG
paper_b_title: Beyond RAG vs. Long-Context: Learning Distraction-Aware Retrieval for Efficient Knowledge Grounding
gold_rationale: Paper A targets positional bias / 'Lost in the Middle' and intervenes inside the LLM via a parallel KV-cache fusion decoder, evaluating on NQ/TriviaQA/POPQA with emphasis on position invariance and robustness to irrelevant passages at a fixed passage set. Paper B targets the distraction-vs-coverage tradeoff between RAG and long-context, and intervenes at the retriever level (LDAR) to choose how many passages to forward, evaluating on six knowledge-intensive benchmarks across multiple LLMs with a cost-performance (token-usage vs accuracy) frame. The failure modes addressed, the pipeline stage changed, the headline metric (order-invariant QA accuracy vs Pareto efficiency at variable token budgets), and the resulting policy (consume all retrieved passages in parallel vs adaptively select a subset) all diverge.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared benchmark suite and shared base LLMs; matched retrieval budgets (same top-k or same token budget); a common evaluation protocol that scores both position robustness (e.g., shuffled-context variance) and cost-performance (accuracy at fixed token usage); and clarity about whether the two methods are being compared as drop-in replacements at the same pipeline stage or as composable components (LDAR could feed passages into a KV-Fusion reader, in which case they are complementary rather than competing).
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems sit at different stages of the retrieval-augmented pipeline and are graded on overlapping-but-different yardsticks. One asks whether the reader produces the same answer regardless of where the gold passage sits among a fixed bundle; the other asks how to pick a smaller, cleaner passage bundle so that quality stays high while token cost drops. Their reported headline numbers are not on the same axes (one reports order-robust accuracy on three QA sets, the other reports a cost-quality frontier across six benchmarks and several LLMs), so dropping them into a single leaderboard column would invite a reader to infer a winner that the evidence does not support.

paper_a_title: Entropy-Based Decoding for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models
paper_b_title: RAFT: Adapting Language Model to Domain Specific RAG
gold_rationale: Paper A proposes a training-free, inference-time decoding modification (entropy-based ensemble plus contrastive decoding) for general open-domain QA with retrieved passages. Paper B proposes a supervised fine-tuning recipe (RAFT) that teaches a model to ignore distractor documents in domain-specific RAG corpora (PubMed, HotpotQA, Gorilla). The interventions sit at fundamentally different stages of the pipeline (decoding vs. model weights via SFT), assume different evidence regimes (open-domain general retrieval vs. known specialized domain), and impose very different cost/data prerequisites. While both nominally address distractor robustness in RAG QA, their headline results are not produced under comparable conditions.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head would need (i) the same base LLM and retriever, (ii) overlapping evaluation benchmarks under the same retrieval setup and prompt format, (iii) matched evidence regime (either both in-domain with domain training data available, or both open-domain), (iv) reporting compute/data overhead so a training-free decoder is not silently credited against a fine-tuned model, and (v) at minimum an ablation showing RAFT under A's open-domain QA sets or A applied on top of/against a RAFT-tuned base.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems operate in different regimes: one is a plug-in decoder usable with any base model at no training cost on general open-domain QA, the other is a domain-tuned model that requires curated in-domain training data and updates weights. A practitioner glancing at a single leaderboard would likely conflate these and pick the higher number without realizing the prerequisites, deployment constraints, and target benchmarks differ substantially, leading to a poor choice for their actual setting.

paper_a_title: Can Small Language Models Use What They Retrieve? An Empirical Study of Retrieval Utilization Across Model Scale
paper_b_title: END: Early Noise Dropping for Efficient and Effective Context Denoising
gold_rationale: Paper A is a diagnostic empirical audit of context utilization across model scale (360M–8B), with no proposed method, using an oracle retrieval condition to isolate utilization from retrieval quality. Paper B proposes a new architectural method (END) that uses a linear prober on early LLM layers to drop noisy context chunks, primarily targeting general (often larger) LLMs in noisy long-context settings. The five coordinates diverge: (1) failure_type — A frames the problem as scale-specific utilization deficit; B frames it as generic noise distraction; (2) evidence_assumption — A includes an oracle clean-context regime to isolate behavior; B assumes mixed informative/noisy chunks; (3) intervention_point — A performs no model or pipeline modification; B inserts an early-layer chunk-dropping module; (4) metric_target — A reports extraction accuracy, parametric-knowledge retention, and error-mode breakdowns; B reports task accuracy and computational efficiency gains; (5) action_policy — A concludes RAG yields a net-negative trade-off at sub-7B scale; B recommends adopting END to improve performance and efficiency. The studies answer different questions on different model regimes.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both works to share a common evaluation: (a) the same model-size ladder (including sub-7B models that Paper A studies and any larger models END is tuned on), (b) overlapping retrieval/noise conditions (oracle clean passages plus noisy passages), (c) common outcome measures (e.g., accuracy on parametric-known vs. parametric-unknown questions, plus efficiency), and (d) a clear ablation showing whether END changes the utilization bottleneck Paper A identifies. Without such a shared protocol, a numeric or ranked comparison is not meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper is a diagnostic study concluding that small (≤7B) models largely cannot exploit retrieved passages, even when the answer is provably present. The other introduces an early-layer chunk-dropping technique for LLMs in noisy contexts and reports accuracy and efficiency gains, mostly outside the small-model regime. Putting these two headline numbers on a single leaderboard would let a practitioner read a pessimistic scale-limited diagnosis and an optimistic engineering result as if they spoke to the same question, and would obscure that the two are evaluated under different model sizes, different context regimes, and different reporting conventions.

paper_a_title: {MIRAGE}: A Metric-Intensive Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Evaluation
paper_b_title: RAGAs: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: judgment based on titles only since no text snippets were supplied. Both papers target RAG evaluation, so the broad problem framing and evidence_assumption (retrieved context grounds generation) appear aligned. However, MIRAGE presents itself as a benchmark dataset with intensive metrics, while RAGAs presents an automated evaluation framework/methodology. These are structurally different artifacts: one is a fixed test resource, the other is a procedure that could in principle be applied to many datasets including MIRAGE. Their intervention points (where they sit in the evaluation pipeline) differ, their metric_targets are defined at different layers (benchmark-supplied scores vs. framework-computed scores), and their action_policy (how a practitioner uses the output) differ. They are partially comparable as artifacts in the RAG evaluation ecosystem, but not directly rankable head-to-head without further specification.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) running RAGAs' automated scoring on MIRAGE's test set and comparing those scores to MIRAGE's native scoring scheme on a shared task and shared system outputs, or (b) restricting the comparison to a common dimension such as correlation with human judgment on a fixed RAG output set, with matched systems, matched questions, and matched ground-truth annotations. Access to each paper's specific evaluation dimensions, datasets used, and reported headline numbers would also be required.
independent_rubric_rationale: Placing these two side by side on one leaderboard would likely confuse a practitioner because one work delivers a fixed test resource with built-in scoring while the other delivers a reusable scoring pipeline that can be pointed at many resources. They occupy complementary slots in a RAG evaluation stack rather than competing for the same slot, so a single ranked comparison risks suggesting a head-to-head winner where none exists. Without the text snippets, certainty is limited, hence partly rather than seriously misleading.

paper_a_title: ReEval: Automatic Hallucination Evaluation for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models via Transferable Adversarial Attacks
paper_b_title: Redefining Retrieval Evaluation in the Era of LLMs
gold_rationale: Paper A (ReEval) targets hallucination in RAG generation, using transferable adversarial perturbations of retrieved evidence to elicit and measure hallucinated outputs. Paper B (UDCG) targets misalignment of classical IR ranking metrics (nDCG/MAP/MRR) with LLM consumption of retrieved passages, proposing a utility- and distraction-aware cumulative gain that correlates better with end-to-end answer accuracy. The failure mode being diagnosed differs (generation hallucination vs. retrieval-metric–LLM misalignment), the intervention point differs (perturb evidence to stress-test generator vs. redesign ranking metric for retriever evaluation), the headline metric differs (hallucination/robustness rates vs. correlation between ranking metric and answer accuracy), and the operational policy differs (produce adversarial test items vs. score rankings with a new gain function). Only the evidence_assumption partially overlaps in that both presume retrieved passages condition LLM output, but they exploit this assumption in incompatible ways.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared task and outcome would be needed, e.g., both methods evaluated as predictors of the same downstream RAG answer quality on the same datasets and LLMs, or both used to score the same retriever/generator pipeline on a common hallucination or accuracy benchmark with matched evidence sets and held-out splits. Without alignment on what is being measured and which stage of the pipeline is being scored, single-leaderboard placement is not meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two papers address substantively different questions about retrieval-augmented systems. One probes how easily a generator can be pushed into producing wrong content when its supporting passages are adversarially altered; the other proposes a new way to score ranked lists of passages so the score tracks downstream answer correctness. Their headline numbers live in different units and answer different practitioner questions, so juxtaposing them on a single leaderboard would suggest a head-to-head contest that does not exist and would likely cause a reader to draw conclusions neither paper supports.

paper_a_title: MTRAG-UN: A Benchmark for Open Challenges in Multi-Turn RAG Conversations
paper_b_title: RAGLAB: A Modular and Research-Oriented Unified Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Paper A (MTRAG-UN) is an evaluation benchmark of 666 multi-turn RAG tasks specifically probing unanswerable, underspecified, non-standalone questions and unclear responses. Paper B (RAGLAB) is a modular research-oriented framework/toolkit for building and experimenting with RAG systems. These artifacts occupy different layers of the RAG research stack: one is test data with diagnostic findings, the other is infrastructure for running experiments. They diverge on every coordinate of the frame - the kind of weakness being studied, what evidence is being produced, where in the pipeline the contribution sits, what is being measured, and how a downstream researcher would use the output. No shared numerical headline result exists between them.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both papers to be the same kind of artifact - either two benchmarks evaluated under comparable protocols on overlapping skill sets, or two frameworks/methods reporting numbers on a shared benchmark. Alternatively, a study could run systems implemented in RAGLAB against the MTRAG-UN benchmark, but that is a complementary integration, not a head-to-head ranking of the two papers themselves.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper delivers a curated test set of difficult multi-turn dialogue cases together with diagnostic findings about where retrieval and generation models struggle, while the other delivers a software library that researchers install and configure to run their own RAG experiments. Putting these two outputs on a single ranked list would mislead a practitioner because the artifacts answer different questions, produce different kinds of outputs, and have no shared quantity that could place one above the other.

paper_a_title: Generating Leakage-Free Benchmarks for Robust RAG Evaluation
paper_b_title: Judge as A Judge: Improving the Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation through the Judge-Consistency of Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Paper A (SeedRG) targets benchmark contamination — questions answerable from LLM parametric memory — and intervenes at the dataset construction stage by generating semi-synthetic, leakage-free instances via reasoning-graph-based entity replacement. Its headline metrics are knowledge-leakage reduction (≥78%), preservation of reasoning difficulty, and improved discrimination among RAG systems. Paper B (Judge as A Judge) instead targets unreliability of LLM-based judges of RAG outputs, intervening at the evaluator stage via a judge-consistency mechanism, and reports metrics about judging quality/consistency. The two works address distinct failure modes (data leakage vs. judge reliability), operate at distinct points in the evaluation pipeline (test set vs. scoring function), and report non-overlapping metrics, so a head-to-head ranking is not meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both methods to be evaluated on the same axis — e.g., both producing a final RAG-system score on a shared, fixed benchmark using a shared scoring protocol, so that one could ask whether SeedRG's benchmark or Judge-as-Judge's evaluator better differentiates RAG systems or better correlates with human judgments. Alternatively, the two could be combined (SeedRG benchmark + Judge-as-Judge scoring) and compared against each component alone. Without such shared anchors (common test set, common metric like correlation with human ratings or discrimination power across RAG variants), the reported numbers measure different quantities and cannot be ranked.
independent_rubric_rationale: The first paper rebuilds the test data so that RAG questions cannot be answered from a model's memorized knowledge, while the second paper rebuilds the scoring procedure by using consistency among language-model graders. These improve different stages of evaluating retrieval-augmented systems — what you test on versus how you score the answers — and their headline numbers measure entirely different things (leakage reduction and difficulty preservation vs. grader reliability/consistency). Placed side by side on one leaderboard, a practitioner would likely think one is 'better' than the other when in fact they solve disjoint problems and could even be used together.

paper_a_title: Whose Facts Win? LLM Source Preferences under Knowledge Conflicts
paper_b_title: Rethinking All Evidence: Enhancing Trustworthy Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Conflict-Driven Summarization
gold_rationale: Paper A is a diagnostic and debiasing study of source-credibility preferences under inter-context conflicts using synthetic sources, with primary numbers reported as source-preference scores and repetition-bias reduction percentages (e.g., up to 79.2% bias reduction while retaining 72.5% of preferences). Paper B is a pipeline (CARE-RAG) that combines parameter-aware evidence extraction, retrieved-evidence refinement, distilled conflict-driven summarization, and a QA Repair step, evaluated against RAG baselines on revised QA benchmarks with accuracy-style metrics. The targeted failure differs (source-credibility/repetition bias vs. internal/external knowledge conflict harming QA correctness), the evidence setup differs (synthetic source-annotated passages vs. real retrieval over QA corpora with internal model knowledge), the locus of change differs (fine-tuning the base LLM vs. an end-to-end multi-stage pipeline plus benchmark cleanup), the measurement differs (bias/preference metrics vs. QA accuracy), and the deployment story differs (preserve fair source treatment vs. produce trustworthy answers). None of the five coordinates align.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A meaningful comparison would require the two systems to be evaluated on the same task with the same metric, e.g., either (a) measuring CARE-RAG's source-preference and repetition-bias profile on Paper A's synthetic source benchmark, or (b) measuring Paper A's fine-tuned debiased model as a drop-in generator inside a RAG pipeline on Paper B's revised QA datasets with QA accuracy reported under matched retrievers and conflict conditions. The two should also share the same underlying base LLMs and the same definition of 'conflict' (inter-context source conflict vs. internal-vs-external conflict) before any ranking is attempted.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two headline numbers describe fundamentally different things: one reports how much a debiasing procedure shifts a model's tendency to favor certain kinds of source labels while preserving prior preference patterns, while the other reports answer-correctness gains for a multi-stage RAG pipeline on cleaned question-answering benchmarks. Placing 79.2% bias reduction next to QA accuracy gains on a single leaderboard would suggest the systems are solving the same problem and competing on the same yardstick, which they are not, so a practitioner choosing between them based on such a ranking would draw seriously wrong conclusions about which is 'better' for their use case.

paper_a_title: Context-DPO: Aligning Language Models for Context-Faithfulness
paper_b_title: FaithfulRAG: Fact-Level Conflict Modeling for Context-Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Both papers target the same problem (context-faithfulness under knowledge conflict in RAG) and share a similar failure_type framing. However, they diverge on three coordinates. Intervention_point: Paper A modifies model weights via DPO alignment training, while Paper B is a training-free inference-time framework using fact-level conflict identification plus self-thinking. Action_policy: preference optimization on faithful vs stubborn responses (A) versus a multi-step reasoning pipeline that explicitly reconciles parametric and retrieved facts (B). Evidence_assumption: Paper A evaluates primarily on its own ConFiQA synthetic conflict benchmark, whereas Paper B (from the snippet) refers to standard RAG benchmarks and SOTA baselines, so the evaluation suites likely do not align. Metric_target (faithfulness/accuracy under conflict) is broadly shared but operationalized differently. A side-by-side ranking is therefore only partially meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Run both methods on the same evaluation set (e.g., ConFiQA plus the conflict benchmarks used in Paper B such as ConflictQA-style suites) using the same backbone LLMs, the same faithfulness metric definitions, and report compute/training cost so that a fine-tuned alignment approach and a training-free inference framework are compared on equal footing. Ideally include baselines that both papers share (prompting baselines, CAD-style decoding) and report whether improvements hold both with and without gold retrieval.
independent_rubric_rationale: Both works pursue the same underlying goal of making language models stay loyal to retrieved passages when those passages contradict what the model already 'knows.' But the two solutions live in very different regimes: one retrains the model through preference learning on a purpose-built conflict dataset, while the other leaves the model untouched and adds a reasoning pipeline at generation time. Their headline numbers almost certainly come from different test collections and carry different deployment costs (GPU training vs extra inference passes). A practitioner glancing at a single combined leaderboard could be nudged toward the wrong choice without seeing these context differences spelled out.

paper_a_title: Position: Retrieval-augmented systems can be dangerous medical communicators
paper_b_title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
gold_rationale: Paper A is a position paper arguing that retrieval-augmented generation systems pose safety risks when deployed as medical communicators, while Paper B is an empirical characterization of positional bias in how LLMs use long contexts. They diverge on all five coordinates: failure_type (domain-specific patient-safety miscommunication vs. general positional underutilization of context), evidence_assumption (argumentation supported by case examples vs. controlled multi-document QA and key-value retrieval experiments), intervention_point (medical RAG pipeline and deployment posture vs. base model long-context handling and prompt construction), metric_target (qualitative safety/communication adequacy vs. quantitative accuracy as a function of gold-document position), and action_policy (call for caution, scoped use, and design changes for clinical RAG vs. recommendations like reranking, repositioning relevant content, or model-side long-context improvements). There is no shared benchmark or claim space on which a head-to-head ranking is meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both works would need to target the same problem (e.g., both evaluating medical-domain RAG accuracy, or both characterizing context utilization), report results on overlapping or convertible metrics, share an evidence regime (both empirical with comparable setups, or both normative position pieces), and propose interventions at the same level of the stack so that improvements or warnings can be weighed against one another. Here, one is a domain-scoped normative argument and the other a domain-general empirical study, so a leaderboard placement is not defined.
independent_rubric_rationale: Paper A is a normative position piece warning that retrieval-augmented systems can be unsafe when used to communicate medical information to patients, while Paper B is an empirical study describing how language models tend to underuse content placed in the middle of long input windows. The two works examine different phenomena in different domains, rely on different kinds of evidence (reasoned argument with illustrative examples vs. controlled experiments on QA and retrieval tasks), and report different kinds of outcomes (qualitative safety concerns vs. quantitative accuracy curves by document position). A practitioner shown both on a single leaderboard would be pushed toward unsupported conclusions about relative strength or priority, because the two results are not addressing the same question and cannot substitute for one another.

paper_a_title: KnowPO: Knowledge-aware Preference Optimization for Controllable Knowledge Selection in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
paper_b_title: Why So Gullible? Enhancing the Robustness of Retrieval-Augmented Models against Counterfactual Noise
gold_rationale: Paper A (KnowPO) targets conflicts between the LLM's parametric knowledge and external retrieved evidence, with an action policy of adhering to retrieved content while resisting noise, implemented via preference optimization (DPO-style) on a constructed conflict dataset. Paper B (Why So Gullible?) targets conflicts among retrieved documents themselves (counterfactual noise within the relevant set), with an action policy of discriminating which retrieved passages are trustworthy, implemented via a separately fine-tuned discriminator or GPT-3.5 prompting on its MACNOISE dataset. Although both sit under the 'knowledge conflict in RAG' umbrella, the failure modes are different (parametric-vs-context vs context-vs-context), the policies are different (trust-retrieval vs select-among-retrieval), and the training mechanisms operate at different points in the pipeline. Direct comparison on a single leaderboard would conflate distinct problem formulations.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared benchmark in which both inter-document conflicts (some retrieved passages are counterfactual) and parametric-vs-context conflicts are explicitly labeled, with a common evaluation protocol (same base LLM, same retrieval set, same answer-correctness scoring) and ideally a unified definition of the 'gold' behavior under each conflict subtype. Reporting both methods under each subtype, with matched data splits and OOD slices, would be needed before any single leaderboard number could be meaningfully compared.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two papers solve different sub-problems within retrieval-augmented QA: one teaches a generator to follow retrieved passages when its own memory disagrees, while the other teaches a separate selector to spot unreliable passages among the retrieved set. Their datasets, baselines, and notion of a 'correct' response diverge, so a practitioner reading their headline numbers side by side on one leaderboard would likely draw the wrong conclusion about which technique to deploy for any given scenario.

paper_a_title: Hierarchical Planning for Complex Tasks with Knowledge Graph-RAG and Symbolic Verification
paper_b_title: RAG4GFM: Bridging Knowledge Gaps in Graph Foundation Models through Graph Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Based on titles alone (no snippets available), Paper A targets hierarchical planning for complex multi-step tasks, combining KG-RAG with symbolic verification of generated plans. Paper B targets knowledge gaps in graph foundation models via graph-structured retrieval. The failure types differ (invalid/incomplete plans vs. missing graph-domain knowledge in GFMs), the intervention points differ (planner pipeline with verifier vs. GFM training/inference loop), the metric targets differ (plan validity / task completion vs. graph learning benchmarks such as node/link/graph-level tasks), and the action policies differ (emitting executable hierarchical plans vs. emitting graph predictions). The only shared trait is the broad evidence stance that graph-structured retrieval supplies useful context, which is too generic to support a head-to-head ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both systems would need to be evaluated on a shared benchmark with a shared task definition and identical scoring (e.g., both run on the same planning suite, or both run on the same GFM benchmark suite), with matched input/output formats and matched retrieval corpora. Absent that, any combined leaderboard would be conflating two different research problems.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works operate in different problem spaces: one produces executable multi-step plans that are checked symbolically, while the other strengthens general-purpose graph learning models with graph-based retrieval. Their reported scores would come from non-overlapping benchmarks and incompatible scoring schemes, so dropping them into a single ranking would push a practitioner toward conclusions the underlying numbers do not support.

paper_a_title: Entity-Focused Dense Passage Retrieval for Outside-Knowledge Visual Question Answering
paper_b_title: Quebec Automobile Insurance Question-Answering With Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: judgment based on titles and venues only (no snippets available). Paper A addresses outside-knowledge visual question answering (OK-VQA), a multimodal task requiring image understanding plus retrieval over a broad knowledge corpus (e.g., Wikipedia), with an entity-focused dense retriever as the proposed mechanism. Paper B addresses a text-only, domain-specific QA task over Quebec automobile insurance documents using a generic RAG pipeline, likely evaluated with generation-quality or factuality metrics in a legal-NLP setting. The two works differ on every coordinate: the diagnosed weakness (multimodal entity grounding vs. specialized-domain factual grounding), the evidence pool (broad encyclopedic corpus vs. narrow insurance corpus, plausibly bilingual), the modification locus (DPR encoder design vs. end-to-end RAG configuration), the evaluation surface (VQA accuracy/retrieval recall vs. QA/generation quality on legal text), and the deployment recommendation (OK-VQA system vs. legal-domain assistant). No shared benchmark, modality, or scoring protocol exists.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers would need to address the same task on a shared benchmark with identical inputs (same modality, same corpus, same question distribution) and a common scoring protocol. At minimum, they would need to overlap on either the OK-VQA setting or a domain-specific text-only QA setting with comparable retrievers and matched evaluation metrics. Alternatively, a meta-analysis would need a normalized improvement statistic (e.g., relative gain over a strong common baseline) computed under matched experimental conditions.
independent_rubric_rationale: one paper handles questions about images that need broad encyclopedic knowledge, while the other handles text-only questions about Quebec auto-insurance documents. They use different inputs, different corpora, likely different languages, and entirely different evaluation benchmarks. Placing their headline numbers on a single leaderboard would imply an apples-to-apples ranking that does not exist and would likely lead a practitioner to choose the wrong system for their use case.

paper_a_title: Think-on-Graph 2.0: Deep and Faithful Large Language Model Reasoning with Knowledge-guided Retrieval Augmented Generation
paper_b_title: ReFIR: Grounding Large Restoration Models with Retrieval Augmentation
gold_rationale: Paper A (Think-on-Graph 2.0) targets shallow or hallucinated reasoning in LLMs by combining knowledge-graph traversal with retrieval over textual corpora, evaluated on multi-hop QA-style reasoning benchmarks. Paper B (ReFIR) targets fidelity/grounding problems in large image restoration models by retrieving similar reference images to condition the restoration process, evaluated with image quality measures such as PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS. The failure modes (reasoning errors vs. hallucinated visual content), the evidence type (structured KG plus text vs. retrieved reference images), the targeted outputs (answers vs. restored pixels), and the control policy (graph-guided multi-step retrieval vs. single-shot image conditioning) all differ. No shared leaderboard or shared scoring scale exists in which their headline numbers would mean the same thing.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both works would need to share a common task family (e.g., both retrieval-augmented language reasoning, or both retrieval-augmented image restoration), the same modality, an overlapping benchmark suite scored with the same measures, and matched base-model and retrieval-corpus conditions. A meaningful comparison could only be drawn at a very abstract methodological level (e.g., 'retrieval augmentation helps grounding'), not at the level of reported headline results.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works live in different modalities and solve different tasks: one improves text-based reasoning by a language model over a knowledge graph, while the other improves image restoration quality by conditioning on retrieved reference images. Their reported numbers come from disjoint benchmark families measured on incompatible scales, so dropping them into a single ranked table would suggest a head-to-head winner where none exists and would mislead a practitioner about which approach is 'better'.

paper_a_title: TRACE: Grounding Time Series in Context for Multimodal Embedding and Retrieval
paper_b_title: Unified Generative and Discriminative Training for Multi-modal Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Based on titles alone (no snippets provided), the two papers target fundamentally different research problems. Paper A addresses time-series grounding for multimodal embedding and retrieval, which implies a retrieval-style evaluation regime with similarity/ranking metrics over time-series-and-text pairs. Paper B addresses unified generative and discriminative training for multimodal LLMs, which implies vision-language benchmarks spanning generation and classification/retrieval-style discrimination. The failure types being addressed (lack of time-series-aware retrieval representations vs. siloed training objectives in MLLMs), the model components being changed (a time-series-text embedding pipeline vs. an MLLM training recipe), and the evaluation targets (time-series retrieval scores vs. multimodal LLM benchmark suites) are all distinct, so a head-to-head numerical ranking is not meaningful. Confidence is moderated because text snippets were unavailable and the inference rests only on titles.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both systems would need to be evaluated on a shared benchmark with identical inputs (e.g., the same multimodal retrieval suite covering the same modality mix), identical evaluation protocol (same query/candidate construction, splits, and scoring), and overlapping target capabilities (both either doing time-series-grounded retrieval or both doing MLLM-style discriminative+generative tasks). At minimum, one paper would have to report results on a benchmark the other also reports, with matched modality coverage and matched metric definitions.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works appear to live in different research neighborhoods: one is about retrieving across time-series and text, the other is about training recipes for general multimodal large language models. Their headline numbers almost certainly come from different datasets, different scoring conventions, and different capability targets, so dropping them side by side in a single ranked table would give a reader a false sense that one system is 'better' than the other when in fact they are solving largely disjoint problems.

paper_a_title: Chunk-Distilled Language Modeling
paper_b_title: Context Tuning for Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: No text snippets were supplied for either paper, so only the titles are available. From titles alone, Paper A ('Chunk-Distilled Language Modeling') appears to target the failure_type of LM generation quality/efficiency via a training-time distillation intervention over retrieved chunks, while Paper B ('Context Tuning for Retrieval Augmented Generation') appears to target context selection/ordering for RAG as an inference- or retriever-side intervention. The intervention_point is plausibly different (model parameters/distillation vs. context construction for an external generator), and we have no information about the evidence_assumption (training corpora, retrieval index, domain), metric_target (perplexity vs. downstream QA accuracy/faithfulness vs. retrieval metrics), or action_policy (deploy distilled LM vs. apply a context-tuning module). Without snippets we cannot verify that any single coordinate aligns, so a direct comparison cannot be responsibly adjudicated as valid, partial, or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: At minimum: (1) shared evaluation tasks and datasets, (2) overlapping metric_target (e.g., both reporting QA accuracy or both reporting LM perplexity on the same benchmark), (3) comparable base models and retrieval corpora so the evidence_assumption matches, (4) clarity that the intervention_point is contrasted on equal footing (e.g., both evaluated end-to-end with the same generator), and (5) matched action_policy framing (training-time modification vs. inference-time context manipulation should be normalized or controlled). Snippets or abstracts confirming these would be needed before placing the two on one leaderboard.
independent_rubric_rationale: With only titles and no excerpts, a practitioner has no way to know whether the two systems were evaluated on the same tasks, datasets, base models, or scoring procedures. The titles hint at related but distinct research directions—one modifies how a language model is trained using retrieved text segments, the other modifies how surrounding context is prepared for a retrieval-augmented generator—so any side-by-side ranking would rest on guesses about the evaluation setups rather than verified common ground.

paper_a_title: Cooperative Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Question Answering: Mutual Information Exchange and Ranking by Contrasting Layers
paper_b_title: Separate the Wheat from the Chaff: Winnowing Down Divergent Views in Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Paper A provides only a title indicating a cooperative RAG approach using mutual information exchange and ranking by contrasting layers; no abstract or body text is available, so its datasets, retriever, base LLM, top-k, and reported scores are unknown. Paper B (WinnowRAG) is a model-agnostic multi-agent pipeline with query-aware clustering and a critic LLM that iteratively prunes noisy documents, with claims of effectiveness on 'various realistic datasets' but the snippet does not disclose which benchmarks, retrievers, or base LLMs. The two titles also suggest mechanisms at very different pipeline locations (intra-model layer contrasting versus multi-agent document filtering). Because Paper A's experimental coordinates are not observable, comparability cannot be verified along almost every dimension of the frame.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers must report on overlapping QA benchmarks (e.g., HotpotQA, NQ, TriviaQA, 2WikiMultihopQA), use the same retriever and corpus snapshot, the same generator LLM family and size, matched top-k retrieved documents, identical evaluation procedure (EM/F1 with same normalization), and disclosure of inference cost or document budget so that any quality gain is not confounded by additional compute. With Paper A's text missing, none of these can be confirmed.
independent_rubric_rationale: Because the first paper offers only a title and no body content, there is no way to confirm whether the datasets, retrievers, base models, top-k document budgets, or scoring procedures overlap with those used by the second paper. A practitioner placing the two headline numbers on a single leaderboard would have no basis for knowing whether the underlying experimental conditions actually line up.

paper_a_title: RankRAG: Unifying Context Ranking with Retrieval-Augmented Generation in LLMs
paper_b_title: xRAG: Extreme Context Compression for Retrieval-augmented Generation with One Token
gold_rationale: judgment based on titles only (no snippets provided). RankRAG targets the problem of irrelevant or poorly ordered retrieved contexts by unifying ranking with generation, intervening at the reranking stage to improve answer quality. xRAG targets the context-length/cost bottleneck by compressing retrieved passages into a single token embedding, intervening at the context-representation stage to enable efficient generation. The failure modes (relevance ordering vs. context size) and intervention points (reranker vs. compressor) differ, and primary metric targets diverge (quality-first vs. efficiency-quality trade-off). Even if both report QA accuracy on overlapping benchmarks, a single-axis comparison would conflate orthogonal objectives.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Shared QA benchmarks with matched base LLMs and retrievers; joint reporting of answer quality AND efficiency (input tokens, latency, FLOPs) so the quality-efficiency Pareto frontier is visible; explicit declaration of which problem each method is optimizing; and ideally a hybrid baseline where ranking and compression are combined to clarify whether the techniques are complementary or competing.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works pursue different goals inside a retrieval-augmented pipeline: one reorders which passages are surfaced to the model to boost answer quality, while the other shrinks passage representations down to a single embedding to slash compute. Placing their headline numbers on one shared scoreboard would hide that one prioritizes answer correctness given many candidate passages, while the other prioritizes throughput and cost with minimal context overhead. A practitioner skimming a single ranked list would likely pick the wrong tool for their deployment constraints.

paper_a_title: SEER: Self-Aligned Evidence Extraction for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper_b_title: Neuro-RIT: Neuron-Guided Instruction Tuning for Robust Retrieval-Augmented Language Model
gold_rationale: Both papers target robust retrieval-augmented generation, but they operate at substantively different pipeline locations. Paper A (SEER) appears, from its title, to operate on the evidence extraction stage via self-alignment, treating noisy retrieval as something to be filtered before generation. Paper B (Neuro-RIT) operates on the generator itself via neuron-level attribution and two-stage instruction tuning, treating noise robustness as a property to be learned inside the LLM. Their evidence_assumption also differs: SEER presumes that helpful evidence can be isolated from the retrieved set, while Neuro-RIT presumes the LLM must remain accurate even when noisy/irrelevant chunks are not removed. The shared metric_target (QA benchmarks) gives a surface-level basis for comparison, but the underlying experimental setups (base LLM, retriever, noise injection regime, training data) are very unlikely to align. Paper A's snippet is unavailable, which limits certainty.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared backbone LLM, identical retrieval pipeline (same retriever, top-k, corpus), matched QA benchmarks evaluated with the same metric definitions, a common noise/irrelevance protocol (so both methods see the same proportion and type of distractor passages), and either (a) reporting both methods composed in the same pipeline position with controlled ablations, or (b) clear separation that one is an extraction-stage module and the other a generator-stage module so they are not treated as substitutes. Reproducible code and matched training data budgets would also be needed.
independent_rubric_rationale: A practitioner glancing at a single leaderboard could be misled because the two systems modify different stages of the retrieval-augmented pipeline and likely rely on different backbones, retrievers, and noise protocols, so identical headline numbers would not imply equivalent capability. However, both aim at the same downstream goal of better question answering under imperfect retrieval, so a side-by-side reading is informative if the reader inspects the experimental setup carefully. The missing snippet for Paper A prevents a stronger verdict.

paper_a_title: Towards Secure Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Comprehensive Review of Threats, Defenses and Benchmarks
paper_b_title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
gold_rationale: Paper A is a survey/review paper cataloging security threats, defenses, and benchmarks for RAG systems (failure_type: security vulnerabilities like data poisoning, adversarial attacks, membership inference). Paper B is the original Lewis et al. RAG paper proposing the architecture and evaluating on knowledge-intensive NLP tasks (failure_type: parametric LMs lacking grounded knowledge). The evidence base differs fundamentally: Paper A synthesizes literature on attacks/defenses, while Paper B reports empirical QA/generation benchmarks. Intervention points differ (security hardening at input/output stages vs. introducing retrieval augmentation as a core architecture). Metric targets differ (attack success rates, leakage, defense efficacy vs. open-domain QA accuracy, fact verification, generation quality). Action policies differ (a taxonomy/survey for future security research vs. a concrete model proposal with empirical baselines). No shared axis of comparison exists.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both papers to address the same problem framing (e.g., both empirically evaluating RAG security defenses, or both proposing/evaluating RAG variants for knowledge-intensive tasks) on overlapping benchmarks with comparable metrics. Alternatively, two security-focused surveys, or two methodological RAG papers measured on the same QA datasets, could be ranked. Here, a survey on security and an original methodology paper on task performance share only the term 'RAG' in their titles.
independent_rubric_rationale: One document is a broad survey cataloging security risks, defensive techniques, and evaluation resources for RAG systems, while the other is the original research paper that introduced the RAG architecture and demonstrated it on open-domain question answering and related knowledge-intensive benchmarks. The two pieces serve incompatible purposes (literature synthesis versus a novel system with empirical numbers) and report results on entirely different dimensions (security posture versus task accuracy). A practitioner seeing them side by side on a single leaderboard would draw incorrect conclusions about what either contributes.

paper_a_title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Comprehensive Survey of Architectures, Enhancements, and Robustness Frontiers
paper_b_title: LLM-Oriented Information Retrieval: A Denoising-First Perspective
gold_rationale: Both papers are non-empirical works (Paper A is a comprehensive survey with taxonomic synthesis; Paper B is a perspective paper advocating a specific viewpoint) and neither presents a primary quantitative result that can be placed on a leaderboard. Their failure_type framing differs: Paper A enumerates multiple failure modes (retrieval noise, grounding fidelity, efficiency, robustness) while Paper B narrows to noise/verifiability as the dominant bottleneck. Intervention_point coverage overlaps (both span retrieval pipeline stages) but uses different organizing taxonomies (retriever/generator/hybrid/robustness vs. indexing/retrieval/context engineering/verification/agentic). Metric_target differs: A emphasizes retrieval precision, faithfulness, efficiency trade-offs; B emphasizes evidence density and signal-to-noise within context windows. Action_policy is fundamentally different: A consolidates the landscape neutrally, while B prescribes a denoising-first stance.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require either (a) both works presenting comparable empirical benchmarks under shared evaluation protocols on the same datasets, or (b) both works being framed at the same scope and contribution type (e.g., both comprehensive surveys with overlapping taxonomies, or both prescriptive perspectives on the same narrow problem). Additionally, comparable coverage windows, shared definitions of what counts as 'denoising' vs. 'robustness', and aligned target audiences would be needed before any side-by-side ranking would be meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: Placed side-by-side on a single comparison list, a practitioner would likely be misled because the two works occupy very different roles: one is a broad taxonomic overview of an entire field across many concerns, while the other is a viewpoint paper advocating that noise reduction is the central concern going forward. Neither offers head-to-head empirical numbers, their organizing frameworks differ, and their scopes are mismatched in breadth, so treating them as peers on a leaderboard would obscure what each is actually contributing.

paper_a_title: Towards Trustworthy Retrieval Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
paper_b_title: Trustworthiness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems: A Survey
gold_rationale: Both works are surveys on trustworthy RAG published within months of each other, and they share substantial topical overlap. Paper A organizes its analysis around reliability, privacy, safety, fairness, explainability, and accountability, while Paper B uses factuality, robustness, fairness, transparency, accountability, and privacy. The taxonomies overlap but are not identical (e.g., reliability vs factuality; safety vs robustness; explainability vs transparency). More importantly, Paper B contributes an empirical benchmark (TRC Bench) with quantitative evaluations of proprietary and open-source LLMs across its six dimensions, whereas Paper A is a pure literature roadmap with taxonomies but no original empirical results. The two are therefore comparable as survey-style contributions on the same problem space, but they diverge in evidence base and what they deliver to a reader.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head comparison would require either (a) restricting the comparison to the survey/taxonomy contributions while explicitly noting that the dimension definitions differ and need alignment, or (b) separately treating Paper B's empirical benchmark contribution as out-of-scope when comparing coverage. Reviewers should also map dimension labels across the two taxonomies (e.g., A's reliability ≈ B's factuality+robustness) before comparing coverage breadth, and should note publication timing since A could cite B but not vice versa for the most recent literature cut-off.
independent_rubric_rationale: A reader looking at the two side by side would correctly see them as overlapping overviews of the same research area, so a leaderboard placement is not wildly off. However, the dimension labels do not line up one-to-one, and only one of the two delivers original quantitative scores on a benchmark of models, which means a naive ranking that treats them as offering the same kind of deliverable would mislead someone trying to decide which to use for empirical reference numbers versus conceptual mapping of the field.

paper_a_title: Securing Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Taxonomy of Attacks, Defenses, and Future Directions
paper_b_title: RAPID: Long-Context Inference with Retrieval-Augmented Speculative Decoding
gold_rationale: Paper A is a survey/taxonomy paper organizing the literature on RAG security threats and defenses along a six-stage knowledge-access pipeline (SLOT framework, CIA properties). Paper B (judging from title) is a concrete systems contribution proposing RAPID, a retrieval-augmented speculative decoding method for long-context inference efficiency. The two papers diverge on every coordinate: the failure_type differs (adversarial security breaches vs. latency/throughput of long-context generation); evidence_assumption differs (synthesis of prior attack/defense literature vs. empirical efficiency benchmarks); intervention_point differs (whole-pipeline taxonomic mapping vs. the decoding step with draft/verify); metric_target differs (confidentiality/integrity/availability outcomes vs. speed and generation-quality metrics); action_policy differs (an organizing framework with research-direction recommendations vs. a deployable algorithm). They share only the surface term 'retrieval-augmented' and cannot be placed on a common leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid pairing would require two artifacts addressing the same problem under comparable conditions, e.g., two RAG security taxonomies/surveys with overlapping scope and threat models, or two long-context inference methods evaluated on shared benchmarks (e.g., InfiniteBench, RULER) with reported latency, throughput, and quality numbers. At minimum, the two works should share the same outcome being measured and the same kind of contribution (survey-vs-survey or method-vs-method).
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper is a literature-organizing survey about security threats and protections in retrieval-augmented generation, while the other proposes a concrete decoding-time speed-up technique that uses retrieved content to draft tokens for long-context generation. They have different research goals, different deliverables (a taxonomy and research agenda versus an algorithm with speed/quality numbers), and no shared benchmark or scoring scheme. Putting their headline results side by side on a single leaderboard would give a practitioner a false impression that the two are addressing the same question or competing for the same slot.

paper_a_title: Trust or Abstain? A Self-Aware RAG Approach
paper_b_title: PoisonedRAG: Knowledge Corruption Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Paper A (SABER) addresses naturally occurring knowledge conflicts between parametric and retrieved contextual knowledge, proposing an inference-time belief estimator that selects among trust-PK, trust-CK, trust-either, or abstain, and is judged on end-to-end QA accuracy, conflict-specific faithfulness, and risk-coverage curves on benign conflict-QA datasets. Paper B (PoisonedRAG) takes the adversary's seat: it formulates an optimization for injecting malicious passages into the corpus so the LLM emits attacker-chosen wrong answers, and reports attack success rate. The two works differ on every coordinate: the harm being studied (organic conflict vs. corpus poisoning), the corpus model (clean/conflicting vs. adversarially perturbed), where the change is applied (decision module on the LLM side vs. data injection on the index side), the evaluation quantity (accuracy/abstention quality vs. ASR), and the role taken (defender vs. attacker). They share only the surface label 'RAG.'
what_valid_comparison_requires: A common task, threat model, and evaluation. For example, SABER would need to be evaluated as a defense under PoisonedRAG-style corpus poisoning, with both works reported on the same questions, the same retriever and corpus, and the same outcome variables (e.g., ASR reduction and clean-task accuracy retention under attack, or risk-coverage under poisoning). Alternatively, PoisonedRAG would need to be re-cast as a stressor on SABER's conflict-QA benchmark with abstention-aware scoring. Without such a shared evaluation harness, only descriptive co-citation is appropriate, not ranking.
independent_rubric_rationale: Paper A is a defensive method that helps a RAG system decide which knowledge source to rely on or to say 'I don't know' when neither is trustworthy, and it is scored by answer correctness and abstention quality on benign conflict datasets. Paper B is an offensive study showing that a small number of crafted documents inserted into the corpus can make the model produce a chosen wrong answer, and it is scored by how often that manipulation succeeds. The two sit on opposite sides of the safety pipeline and report numbers that mean different things, so juxtaposing their headline results on one leaderboard would suggest a false equivalence and lead a practitioner to draw conclusions that neither paper supports.

paper_a_title: Magic Mushroom: A Customizable Benchmark for Fine-grained Analysis of Retrieval Noise Erosion in RAG Systems
paper_b_title: Why Uncertainty Estimation Methods Fall Short in RAG: An Axiomatic Analysis
gold_rationale: Paper A diagnoses generator susceptibility to heterogeneous retrieval noise, intervening through a configurable noise-injection benchmark and denoising strategies, with answer-quality metrics under controlled noise distributions. Paper B diagnoses miscalibration of uncertainty estimation methods, intervening through an axiomatic framework and a calibration function, with metrics on correlation between uncertainty scores and response correctness. The failure modes (incorrect generation vs. miscalibrated confidence), intervention points (benchmark/denoising vs. UE calibration), target metrics (QA accuracy vs. uncertainty-correctness correlation), and resulting action policies (build noise-robust RAG vs. build better UE methods) all diverge. Only the evidence_assumption (retrieved documents may be noisy/conflicting) loosely overlaps.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers would need to target the same downstream objective on shared inputs — e.g., both reporting answer correctness on the same noisy-retrieval benchmark, or both reporting uncertainty-correctness correlation under the same noise taxonomy. Shared evaluation datasets, retrievers, LLM backbones, noise/distribution conditions, and a common headline metric would be required before any leaderboard-style ranking could be meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two studies report numbers on entirely different quantities — one measures how well an RAG system answers questions when retrieved passages are corrupted in controlled ways, while the other measures how well confidence scores track answer correctness in RAG. Putting their headline numbers side by side on one leaderboard would lead a practitioner to draw spurious conclusions, because higher or lower scores in one study say nothing about progress on the problem the other study addresses.

paper_a_title: Toward Robust RALMs: Revealing the Impact of Imperfect Retrieval on Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
paper_b_title: RoseRAG: Robust Retrieval-augmented Generation with Small-scale LLMs via Margin-aware Preference Optimization
gold_rationale: Paper A is a diagnostic/evaluation study that introduces a taxonomy of imperfect-retrieval scenarios (unanswerable, adversarial, conflicting), proposes a new attack generator (GenADV) and a new metric (RAD), and characterizes failure modes without modifying the model. Paper B is a training-time method paper that fine-tunes small-scale LLMs using margin-aware preference optimization with rejection sampling, evaluated on standard open-domain QA benchmarks (e.g., HotpotQA) with EM/F1. The two works differ on nearly every coordinate: failure_type (broad taxonomy including answerability/conflict vs. retrieval noise specifically), intervention_point (none/evaluation vs. preference-optimized training of SLMs), metric_target (RAD plus scenario-specific behaviors vs. EM/F1 on QA), and action_policy (abstain/flag/contradict-detect vs. generate accurate answer). They are also scoped to different model regimes (general RALMs vs. SLMs).
what_valid_comparison_requires: A meaningful comparison would require both papers to make the same type of contribution (e.g., both proposing a robustness-enhancing method or both proposing an evaluation), evaluated on overlapping benchmarks with shared backbones, the same failure scenarios, and the same metrics. At minimum, Paper B would need to be measured under Paper A's RAD/scenario protocol, or Paper A's vulnerabilities would need to be addressed by a method comparable to RoseRAG on identical settings.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper diagnoses where retrieval-augmented systems break down across several distinct problem situations and introduces new ways to measure those breakdowns, while the other trains a small model with a preference-learning recipe and reports EM/F1 on standard QA datasets. Placing their headline numbers side by side would suggest a head-to-head ranking where none exists: the scopes, the targeted problem regimes, the model sizes, and the reported scores are not on a common scale, so a reader trying to choose between them would draw unwarranted conclusions.

paper_a_title: Hierarchical Planning for Complex Tasks with Knowledge Graph-RAG and Symbolic Verification
paper_b_title: Supportiveness-based Knowledge Rewriting for Retrieval-augmented Language Modeling
gold_rationale: Paper A targets complex multi-step task planning, using a knowledge graph as structured evidence and inserting symbolic verification at the planning/decomposition stage to validate plan steps. Paper B targets noisy or misleading passages retrieved during open-domain QA-style RAG, using unstructured retrieved text as evidence and inserting a learned rewriter (DPO-trained on a supportiveness signal) as a preprocessing module before generation. The two systems therefore differ on every coordinate: the failure they address (planning errors vs. retrieval noise), the evidence form they assume (KG triples/subgraphs vs. text passages), the pipeline locus of the fix (plan synthesis/verification vs. context rewriting), the reported metric family (plan/task success on complex-task benchmarks vs. accuracy on knowledge-intensive QA across multiple LLMs), and the policy itself (hierarchical decomposition + symbolic check vs. supportiveness-aligned text summarization). With no Paper A text snippet available, some details are inferred from the title, but the gap is wide enough on multiple coordinates that direct comparison is not warranted.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers would need to (a) tackle the same class of failure on a shared benchmark, (b) operate over the same evidence representation (either both KG-grounded or both text-passage RAG), (c) intervene at a comparable pipeline stage, (d) report a common, head-to-head metric (e.g., the same QA set or the same complex-task planning suite), and (e) ideally hold the backbone LLM and retriever constant. Absent shared benchmarks and a common pipeline locus, any side-by-side ranking is meaningless.
independent_rubric_rationale: These two systems tackle distinct problems—one decomposes and verifies multi-step plans grounded in a structured knowledge graph, while the other rewrites noisy retrieved passages so a language model can answer questions better. They consume different kinds of source information (graph-structured facts versus unstructured text), operate at different stages of the pipeline, and report numbers on different benchmark families. Placing their headline scores side by side on one leaderboard would suggest a head-to-head contest that does not exist, and a practitioner could easily pick the wrong tool for their actual use case.

paper_a_title: Overcoming the Retrieval Barrier: Indirect Prompt Injection in the Wild for LLM Systems
paper_b_title: GRACE: Reinforcement Learning for Grounded Response and Abstention under Contextual Evidence
gold_rationale: All five coordinates diverge. Paper A studies an adversarial failure type (indirect prompt injection where attackers plant malicious content in corpora), assumes a poisoned/adversarial evidence pool, intervenes at the embedding/retrieval layer by crafting trigger fragments, measures retrieval success and attack success (e.g., SSH key exfiltration ~80%), and proposes an offensive attack policy. Paper B targets benign-corpus failure modes (hallucination and ungrounded answers), assumes standard or possibly insufficient but non-adversarial retrieval, intervenes at the generator via RL fine-tuning with a gated reward, measures answer accuracy and abstention quality, and proposes a defensive generation policy. The two works share only the RAG setting label; they are not directly comparable or rankable.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both papers to address the same problem on overlapping benchmarks with shared metrics — for example, both proposing defenses against indirect prompt injection (with attack success rate and clean-task accuracy reported), or both being grounded-generation/abstention methods evaluated on the same QA benchmarks under matched retrieval conditions. As stated, one paper reports attack effectiveness on poisoned corpora while the other reports answer/abstention accuracy on standard QA, so no common axis of comparison exists.
independent_rubric_rationale: Paper A demonstrates an offensive technique that plants hidden instructions into external corpora to hijack a retrieval-augmented LLM, with headline numbers about near-perfect retrieval of poisoned content and high exfiltration success. Paper B trains an LLM with reinforcement learning to either cite supporting passages or say 'I don't know' on standard question-answering benchmarks, with headline numbers about accuracy and the balance between answering and declining. These are essentially different studies — one shows how to break a system from the outside, the other shows how to make a system more trustworthy on benign questions — and putting their headline numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would seriously mislead a practitioner about what either result means.

paper_a_title: DRAGged into Conflicts: Detecting and Addressing Conflicting Sources in Search-Augmented LLMs
paper_b_title: Rescuing the Unpoisoned: Efficient Defense against Knowledge Corruption Attacks on RAG Systems
gold_rationale: Paper A tackles naturally occurring knowledge conflicts in RAG retrieval (freshness, controversial/debatable topics, etc.) among legitimate sources, contributing a taxonomy, the CONFLICTS benchmark, and prompting-based reasoning to elicit conflict-aware responses. Paper B tackles adversarial knowledge corruption (data poisoning) and proposes RAGDEFENDER, a post-retrieval ML-based filter, evaluated by attack success rate (ASR) reduction against baselines like RobustRAG and Discern-and-Answer. The two papers differ on essentially every coordinate: the kind of breakdown they target (benign disagreement vs. malicious injection), what they assume about retrieved evidence (truthful but inconsistent vs. partially adversarial), where they act (prompt/reasoning vs. post-retrieval filtering), what they optimize (response appropriateness on a curated conflict benchmark vs. ASR under poisoning), and the operational policy (acknowledge/explain conflict vs. discard suspected passages).
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared threat model and benchmark: either (i) both systems evaluated on CONFLICTS-style natural conflict items using the same appropriateness/quality scoring, or (ii) both systems evaluated on poisoned-RAG benchmarks under matched attacker budgets using ASR and clean-task utility, with identical retrievers, generators, and adversarial passage ratios. Without a common task definition and metric, leaderboard placement is not meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works address fundamentally different problems: one studies how models should respond when honestly retrieved web sources legitimately disagree (e.g., outdated vs. current, or opinion-based), while the other studies how to protect a RAG pipeline when an attacker plants deceptive passages in the knowledge base. Their headline numbers come from different datasets, scoring schemes, and threat assumptions, so putting them side-by-side on one leaderboard would lead a practitioner to think one approach dominates the other when in fact they solve disjoint problems.

paper_a_title: RoseRAG: Robust Retrieval-augmented Generation with Small-scale LLMs via Margin-aware Preference Optimization
paper_b_title: Faithfulness-Aware Uncertainty Quantification for Fact-Checking the Output of Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Paper A (RoseRAG) targets the failure mode of small LLMs producing incorrect answers under noisy retrieval and intervenes at training time via margin-aware preference optimization on the generator, with success measured by EM/F1 on open-domain QA. Paper B (FRANQ) targets a different failure mode—undetected hallucinations in RAG outputs—and intervenes post-hoc via uncertainty quantification conditioned on faithfulness, with success measured by hallucination-detection quality on a new long-form QA dataset. The downstream policy differs as well: A produces improved answers, while B flags suspect claims. Four of the five coordinates diverge, so the two main results live in different evaluation spaces.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared task and metric setup—e.g., either (i) both systems evaluated on the same QA benchmark with EM/F1 (requiring FRANQ to be coupled to a generation policy such as abstention or rewriting), or (ii) both systems evaluated as hallucination detectors over the same RAG outputs with the same labeling protocol and detection metrics (AUROC, PRR), using matched base generators and retrievers.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper trains a small generator to give better final answers when retrieved passages are noisy, while the other adds a post-generation detector that scores whether claims are likely true. Their headline numbers describe different things on different benchmarks, so putting them side by side on a single leaderboard would lead a practitioner to draw the wrong conclusion about which system is stronger or better suited to their use case.

paper_a_title: Redefining Retrieval Evaluation in the Era of LLMs
paper_b_title: Chunk-Distilled Language Modeling
gold_rationale: Paper A targets the failure of classical IR metrics (nDCG, MAP, MRR) to predict RAG end-to-end answer accuracy, assuming an LLM-as-consumer setting, intervening at the evaluation-metric layer by proposing UDCG, with the metric target being correlation against generator accuracy across 5 datasets and 6 LLMs, and an action policy of replacing the offline IR scorer for RAG component selection. Paper B (title: 'Chunk-Distilled Language Modeling'), with no snippet provided but a clearly different topic, addresses a language modeling / generation problem via chunk-level distillation; its failure mode, evidence base, intervention site (model training/inference), target metric (presumably LM/perplexity or downstream LM quality), and resulting action policy all differ from Paper A. All five coordinates diverge, so the two headline results are not commensurable.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both works would need to share the same underlying task (e.g., either both proposing RAG retrieval evaluators or both proposing generation/LM systems), evaluate on overlapping benchmarks with the same protocol, report a comparable headline number on the same axis (e.g., both report correlation with answer accuracy on the same datasets, or both report LM quality on the same corpus), and recommend interchangeable downstream actions for a practitioner. As specified, none of these conditions hold.
independent_rubric_rationale: check: the two papers are aimed at different research questions — one is about how to score retrieval systems whose results are read by an LLM in a RAG pipeline, the other is about a chunk-distilled approach to language modeling itself. Their headline numbers live on different axes and on different tasks, so dropping them into a shared leaderboard row would give a practitioner the false impression that one approach 'beats' the other, when in reality they are not solving the same problem.

paper_a_title: LI-RAGE: Late Interaction Retrieval Augmented Generation with Explicit Signals for Open-Domain Table Question Answering
paper_b_title: DSLR: Document Refinement with Sentence-Level Re-ranking and Reconstruction to Enhance Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Based on titles and venues alone (no snippets available), Paper A (LI-RAGE) targets open-domain Table Question Answering using late-interaction retrieval over structured tables, while Paper B (DSLR) targets text-passage RAG via post-retrieval sentence-level reranking and reconstruction. The failure_type differs (table retrieval matching vs. noisy/irrelevant sentences in retrieved passages); the evidence_assumption differs (structured tabular cells vs. unstructured prose passages); the intervention_point differs (retriever architecture with explicit signals vs. post-retrieval document refinement); and the metric_target almost certainly differs (table-QA benchmarks like NQ-tables/OTT-QA vs. open-domain text QA benchmarks). The action_policy is also different in spirit (retrieve-better vs. clean-after-retrieval). They are not on a shared evaluation surface.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both systems to be evaluated on the same benchmark with the same evidence modality (e.g., either both on open-domain text QA or both on table QA), the same retriever/corpus setup, and the same end-task metrics, ideally with one paper's technique reimplemented or ablated within the other's pipeline so the contribution being compared is isolated. Without shared datasets, modality, and evaluation protocol, head-to-head ranking is not meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems address fundamentally different inputs and pipeline stages: one works with structured tables in an open-domain table QA pipeline, the other cleans up unstructured text passages before generation. Putting their headline numbers next to each other on a single leaderboard would conflate distinct task settings, corpora, and evaluation suites, leading a practitioner to draw unsupported conclusions about which approach is 'better' for retrieval-augmented generation.

paper_a_title: TrustRAG: Enhancing Robustness and Trustworthiness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper_b_title: SUGAR: Leveraging Contextual Confidence for Smarter Retrieval
gold_rationale: These papers diverge on every coordinate. TrustRAG targets an adversarial failure_type (corpus poisoning, injected malicious documents) under a threat-model evidence_assumption, places its intervention_point as a post-retrieval defensive filter (cluster filtering plus LLM self-assessment), pursues a metric_target dominated by attack resistance and robustness, and uses a fixed always-filter action_policy. SUGAR targets a benign efficiency/noise failure_type (unnecessary retrieval and distraction by irrelevant context), assumes a non-adversarial corpus, places its intervention_point at the pre-retrieval gating stage using semantic entropy, targets QA accuracy and inference efficiency, and uses an adaptive retrieve/skip/multi-step action_policy. There is essentially no shared evaluation regime or shared notion of 'improvement,' so a direct ranking is not meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require (1) a shared evaluation suite that exercises both adversarial poisoning conditions and benign efficiency/noise conditions, (2) a common threat model so both systems are stressed on the same inputs, (3) overlapping evaluation measures such as accuracy under attack, accuracy without attack, and retrieval/inference cost, and (4) compatible deployment positions (e.g., showing how a gating policy like SUGAR would behave when poisoned documents are present, or how TrustRAG's filter behaves when retrieval is optional). Without at least overlapping benchmarks and threat models, only orthogonal claims can be made.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems are solving essentially different problems on essentially different test conditions. One is being judged on resisting deliberately planted poisoned documents, while the other is being judged on knowing when to skip or expand external lookups for ordinary questions. Putting their headline numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would suggest one is 'better' than the other, when in fact a practitioner choosing between them should be choosing based on which scenario they face, not on a single comparable score.

paper_a_title: Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth: Revealing the Behavior of Large Language Models in Knowledge Conflicts
paper_b_title: GraphRAG under Fire
gold_rationale: Paper A is a controlled behavioral study of how LLMs handle benign/organic knowledge conflicts between parametric memory and external evidence, measuring receptiveness and confirmation bias using constructed counter-memory.
