Paper B is an adversarial security study proposing GRAGPOISON, a poisoning attack against GraphRAG systems that exploits shared relations in knowledge graphs, measured by attack success rate (up to 98%) and poisoning-text efficiency. The two works diverge on every coordinate: the failure being characterized (organic conflict vs. malicious poisoning), the nature of the external evidence (coherent counter-memory from elicited parametric beliefs vs. adversary-crafted text), the locus of study (LLM consumption behavior vs. graph indexing/retrieval pipeline of GraphRAG specifically), the outcome being measured (receptiveness/bias percentages vs. attack success and stealth), and the stance of the work (descriptive analysis vs. offensive method with defense discussion). They also evaluate on different system architectures (vanilla tool-augmented LLMs vs. GraphRAG variants).
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both papers to study the same threat or phenomenon (e.g., both adversarial poisoning, or both benign conflict), on overlapping system architectures (e.g., both on GraphRAG or both on standard RAG), with shared outcome measures (e.g., attack success rate on the same task, or a common receptiveness/robustness metric on the same benchmark), and a shared role (both as attack methods, both as analyses, or both as defenses). At minimum, one would need a common evaluation setup with the same datasets, models, and a metric that captures comparable quantities.
independent_rubric_rationale: Placing these two results side by side on a single leaderboard would mislead a practitioner because the two studies are addressing fundamentally different questions on different systems with different threat models. Paper A's percentages describe how a model naturally weighs conflicting context elicited from its own beliefs, while Paper B's percentages describe how often an adversary can corrupt a graph-structured retrieval pipeline. Numbers like 'receptiveness' and 'attack success rate' look superficially like comparable rates but encode incompatible quantities, so a reader could wrongly infer that one work outperforms or supersedes the other when they do not address the same problem at all.

paper_a_title: Adaptive Contrastive Decoding in Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Handling Noisy Contexts
paper_b_title: Know Or Not: a library for evaluating out-of-knowledge base robustness
gold_rationale: Paper A (ACD) targets the failure mode where retrieved context is noisy/irrelevant and distracts the LLM; it intervenes at decoding time via an entropy-weighted contrastive decoding scheme, with the action policy of producing a correct answer, measured by open-domain QA accuracy under noisy retrieval. Paper B (knowornot/PolicyBench) targets a different failure mode—answering questions whose answer is not in the knowledge base (OOKB)—and is not a generation method but an evaluation library/benchmark, where the desired action policy is abstention and the metric target is OOKB robustness (refusal correctness) on domain-specific policy QA chatbots. paper_a_title: Backdoored Retrievers for Prompt Injection Attacks on Retrieval Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
paper_b_title: Defense Against Prompt Injection Attack by Leveraging Attack Techniques
gold_rationale: Paper A is an offensive study introducing corpus poisoning and a novel backdoor attack on the dense retriever during fine-tuning, with the goal of maximizing attack success rate (ASR) for injection objectives like malicious links and DoS. Paper B is a defensive study that inverts training-free attack techniques to build prompting-based defenses on the generator LLM, with the goal of minimizing ASR against direct/indirect prompt injection. The failure_type framings differ (retriever-level corpus/fine-tuning compromise vs. instruction-following confusion in the generator), the intervention_point differs (retriever pipeline vs. LLM prompt construction), the metric_target is inverted (higher ASR is success for A, lower ASR is success for B), and the action_policy roles are opposite (attacker vs. defender). Only evidence_assumption partially overlaps in that both consider injected content reaching the LLM, but threat models still diverge.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A meaningful head-to-head would need (i) both works to occupy the same role on the attack/defense axis, (ii) target the same pipeline component under a shared threat model (e.g., both defenses evaluated against retriever-poisoning attacks, or both attacks evaluated under identical defenses), (iii) use the same datasets, retriever, and generator LLM, and (iv) report the same direction of the metric (e.g., post-defense ASR on a common benchmark such as InjecAgent or BIPIA) with matched injection objectives.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper showcases an offensive technique that aims to push a success-rate number as high as possible, while the other proposes a protective technique that aims to drive the same number as low as possible. They also operate on different parts of the pipeline (retriever training vs. generator prompting) and under different threat scenarios. Putting their headline numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would lead a practitioner to read them as commensurable scores when in fact they describe opposite goals on different components, which would seriously distort any practical takeaway.

paper_a_title: ADMIT: Few-shot Knowledge Poisoning Attacks on RAG-based Fact Checking
paper_b_title: Hidden-in-Plain-Text: A Benchmark for Social-Web Indirect Prompt Injection in RAG
gold_rationale: Paper A (ADMIT) is an offensive contribution proposing a specific few-shot knowledge poisoning attack against RAG-based fact-checking, where the failure mode is verdict flipping in the presence of credible counter-evidence, and the headline metric is Attack Success Rate (~86% at 0.93x10^-6 poisoning rate). Paper B (OpenRAG-Soc) is an evaluative/defensive contribution introducing a benchmark and harness for web-facing RAG under indirect prompt injection and retrieval poisoning via HTML/Markdown/Unicode carriers, reporting a heterogeneous bundle of attack-time outcomes, rank shifts in sparse/dense retrievers, utility, and latency, alongside deployable mitigations. The failure types differ (fact-checking verdict flips vs. web-native IPI/poisoning), the evidentiary settings differ (authoritative fact-checking corpora vs. social-web user-generated content), the points of action differ (attacker-side adversarial injection vs. benchmark plus sanitization/normalization defenses), the headline numbers are not commensurate (single ASR figure vs. multi-axis benchmark dashboard), and the contributions target opposite roles in the threat ecosystem. No common axis supports direct ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both works to instantiate the same threat model (e.g., indirect prompt injection on the same corpus), share a common retriever/LLM stack, report a single shared headline number (e.g., ASR under matched poisoning budgets), and play the same role (either both attacks evaluated under identical defenses, or both defenses evaluated against identical attacks). At minimum, Paper A's ADMIT attack would need to be run on Paper B's OpenRAG-Soc harness, or Paper B's benchmark would need to include fact-checking tasks with credible counter-evidence and report ASR-equivalent scores.
independent_rubric_rationale: The first paper reports an attack-success number for a narrow fact-checking setting where credible evidence dominates the retrieval pool, while the second paper reports a multi-dimensional benchmark score sheet (answer-time outcomes, ranking shifts, utility, latency) for web-facing RAG over social content with built-in defenses. The targets, threat carriers, datasets, and headline numbers are not commensurable, so a practitioner reading them side-by-side on one leaderboard would likely misread the 86% figure from the first as competitive with or superior to anything in the second, when in fact the two address different problems and play opposite roles (offensive technique vs. evaluation suite with mitigations).

paper_a_title: ProGRank: Probe-Gradient Reranking to Defend Dense-Retriever RAG from Corpus Poisoning
paper_b_title: On the Vulnerability of Applying Retrieval-Augmented Generation within Knowledge-Intensive Application Domains
gold_rationale: Both papers target the same threat model (corpus poisoning of dense-retriever RAG) and both propose retriever-side defenses, so the failure_type and broad intervention_point align. However, the action_policy differs substantively: Paper A is a reranking/score-suppression mechanism that preserves passages but reorders them using probe-gradient instability signals, whereas Paper B is a binary detection mechanism that flags poisoned documents. Their metric_target also diverges — Paper A reports robustness–utility trade-offs, poisoned Top-K exposure, and end-to-end attack success across three datasets and three backbones, while Paper B reports detection rates centered on a medical Q&A universal-poisoning setting (with 225 setup combinations). The evidence_assumption is narrower in B (universal poisoning, medical/PII focus) than in A (multiple attack families including trigger-based and misleading-evidence). Side-by-side comparability exists at a high level but the headline numbers do not measure the same quantity on the same workloads.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation harness with: (1) the same corpora, retrievers, and attack implementations covering both papers' threat models; (2) a common metric set that captures both detection performance (precision/recall on poisoned passages) and downstream impact (poisoned Top-K rate, attack success rate, clean-task utility); (3) treating Paper B's detector as a filter feeding Paper A's reranker (or vice versa) so each can be evaluated as a pipeline stage; (4) matched adaptive-attack protocols; and (5) reporting on at least one common domain such as medical Q&A so the domain-specific claims in B and the general claims in A overlap.
independent_rubric_rationale: A reader scanning a single leaderboard would see one paper reporting how well poisoned passages are flagged in a medical Q&A setting and another reporting reordering quality and downstream answer corruption across several general benchmarks. Because the headline numbers describe different outputs (flag-or-not vs reorder-and-keep) on different corpora, ranking them by a single column would create a false impression of head-to-head superiority, even though both target the same underlying threat and could plausibly be combined.

paper_a_title: Defending against Indirect Prompt Injection by Instruction Detection
paper_b_title: A Few Words Can Distort Graphs: Knowledge Poisoning Attacks on Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Paper A is a defense paper proposing InstructDetector to detect indirect prompt injection (IPI) in standard text-based RAG via hidden-state/gradient features, reporting detection accuracy (99.60% in-domain, 96.90% OOD) and ASR reduction (0.03%) on BIPIA. Paper B is an offense paper proposing two knowledge poisoning attacks (TKPA, UKPA) against GraphRAG by altering a few words in source text used for graph construction, reporting attack success rate (93.1%) and QA accuracy collapse (95%→50%). All five coordinates diverge: (1) failure_type differs (instruction injection in retrieved docs vs. corrupting graph construction); (2) evidence_assumption differs (adversary plants instructions at inference-time retrieval vs. adversary edits source corpus before graph build); (3) intervention_point differs (LLM-side detector vs. source-text manipulation in graph extraction pipeline); (4) metric_target differs (detection accuracy / ASR reduction on BIPIA vs. attack success / QA degradation on graph QA); (5) action_policy differs (filter suspicious documents vs. craft poisoned narratives). The papers also play opposite roles (defender vs. attacker) on different system variants (RAG vs. GraphRAG).
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers would need to address the same threat surface (e.g., both attacks on GraphRAG or both defenses against IPI), share the same target system (text-RAG or GraphRAG), use a common benchmark and threat model, and report comparable quantities (e.g., both ASR under matched attack conditions, or both detection performance against matched poisoning attacks). At minimum a shared dataset and a shared role (attack-vs-attack or defense-vs-defense) is required.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works sit on opposite sides of the security problem and on different system architectures: one is a protective tool that screens retrieved text in conventional RAG, while the other is an offensive technique that corrupts the graph built by GraphRAG by editing source documents. Their headline numbers measure different things (how well malicious snippets are caught vs. how reliably the adversary can flip answers) on different benchmarks. A practitioner who saw them side by side on a single ranked list could easily conflate a defender's success rate with an attacker's success rate, or assume the GraphRAG attack is relevant to the text-RAG defender's setting, leading to seriously wrong conclusions about which system is safer or stronger.

paper_a_title: Decide Then Retrieve: A Training-Free Framework with Uncertainty-Guided Triggering and Dual-Path Retrieval
paper_b_title: Know Or Not: a library for evaluating out-of-knowledge base robustness
gold_rationale: Paper A (DTR) is a training-free RAG method targeting answer correctness on open-domain QA, addressing indiscriminate retrieval triggering and sparse query handling, measured via EM/F1 across five QA benchmarks. Paper B (Know Or Not) is an evaluation library plus a domain benchmark (PolicyBench) targeting out-of-knowledge-base hallucination/abstention behavior in QA chatbots. The two works differ on nearly every coding-frame axis: the problem being addressed (noisy/sparse retrieval vs. inappropriate non-abstention), where the work plugs into the pipeline (a generation-time controller vs. an external evaluation harness with no model changes), the quantities being reported (accuracy-style EM/F1 vs. OOKB robustness/abstention behavior), and the prescribed system behavior (retrieve-then-answer vs. abstain-when-unsupported). There is no shared task, dataset, or scoring protocol that would allow ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation setup would be needed: either (a) running DTR's policy on PolicyBench (or a comparable OOKB-robustness suite) and reporting abstention/refusal-correctness measures alongside Know Or Not's baselines, or (b) using knowornot to construct OOKB stress tests on the five open-domain QA benchmarks DTR uses and reporting matched accuracy and abstention outcomes. At minimum the comparison requires the same underlying generator(s), retriever(s), corpora, query distribution, and outcome definitions; ideally a joint table reporting both correctness on answerable queries and abstention quality on unanswerable ones.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works study fundamentally different things. Paper A reports gains in answer correctness on standard open-domain QA suites using a controller that decides when to pull in external context, while Paper B offers an evaluation toolkit and a government-policy benchmark for whether chatbots correctly decline to answer when the knowledge base does not cover the query. Their headline numbers describe unrelated behaviors on unrelated data, so placing them in a single leaderboard would lead a practitioner to draw conclusions that the evidence does not support.

paper_a_title: Over-Searching in Search-Augmented Large Language Models
paper_b_title: QuCo-RAG: Quantifying Uncertainty from the Pre-training Corpus for Dynamic Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Paper A is a diagnostic/benchmark study of over-searching (search invoked when unnecessary, harming abstention on unanswerable queries and inflating cost) and introduces a cost-aware metric TPC together with the OverSearchQA benchmark. Paper B proposes a new dynamic-RAG triggering mechanism (QuCo-RAG) that uses pre-training corpus statistics via Infini-gram to decide when to retrieve, evaluated on multi-hop QA with EM gains over DRAGIN-style baselines. The failure modes are oriented in opposite directions (excessive retrieval vs. poorly timed/under-triggered retrieval driven by miscalibrated internal signals). The evidence assumptions differ (search-tool agents with potentially noisy retrieval vs. access to a 4T-token corpus index). The metric targets differ (TPC + abstention/accuracy on answerable/unanswerable queries vs. EM on multi-hop QA and long-form generation). The action policies differ (suppress unnecessary calls vs. trigger calls more accurately). The two papers also operate on disjoint benchmarks. A unified ranking is therefore not meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A common evaluation suite that includes both answerable and unanswerable queries, a metric that jointly captures correctness, abstention quality, and retrieval cost (e.g., TPC plus EM/F1 plus abstention accuracy), identical base LLMs and retrieval corpora, and a head-to-head test where QuCo-RAG's corpus-grounded trigger is run on OverSearchQA-style inputs while Paper A's mitigations are run on multi-hop QA. Without aligning the benchmark, the trigger/no-trigger decision space, and the scoring rule, side-by-side numbers cannot be interpreted.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works target opposite-facing problems within dynamic retrieval for LLMs: one studies when calling the search tool is wasteful or harmful and scores systems by a token-cost-vs-correctness tradeoff on a new benchmark that includes unanswerable items; the other proposes a corpus-statistics trigger and reports exact-match gains on multi-hop QA. The test sets, base models, and scoring rules barely overlap, and the headline numbers measure essentially different things. A practitioner skimming a single leaderboard that mixed these results would likely draw an unwarranted head-to-head conclusion.

paper_a_title: When to Trust: A Causality-Aware Calibration Framework for Accurate Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation.
paper_b_title: GRACE: Reinforcement Learning for Grounded Response and Abstention under Contextual Evidence
gold_rationale: Paper A targets Knowledge Graph RAG with a causality-aware calibration framework that decides when to trust an answer, implying structured KG evidence and a post-hoc/training-time calibration mechanism. Paper B targets general text-based RAG with a reinforcement-learning pipeline using a multi-stage gated reward to jointly enforce evidence grounding and explicit abstention. The evidence channel (structured KG vs unstructured text), the intervention mechanism (calibration vs RL with reward shaping), and the response policy (trust score vs explicit 'I don't know') differ substantively. Without Paper A's snippet, the exact benchmarks cannot be confirmed, but KG-RAG benchmarks (e.g., WebQSP, CWQ) and the multi-hop text QA suites typical for grounded-abstention work rarely overlap. Hence putting their headline numbers side by side would conflate different problem formulations.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both systems would need to be evaluated on the same task and dataset family (either KG-grounded QA or open-domain text RAG), use the same retriever/context, and report the same trust-or-abstain metrics (e.g., joint accuracy and abstention precision, or calibration error such as ECE). Additionally, the action interface must be comparable—e.g., both producing an explicit abstain decision or both producing a confidence score thresholded the same way—so that one leaderboard row reflects equivalent operating conditions.
independent_rubric_rationale: Paper A is built around knowledge-graph-backed question answering with a calibration-style trust score, while Paper B is built around free-text retrieval with a reinforcement-learning recipe that produces explicit 'answer' or 'I don't know' outputs. The benchmarks, the kind of supporting context, and even what the headline number means (calibrated trust vs grounded-or-abstain accuracy) are not aligned. A practitioner scanning a single leaderboard row would likely draw the wrong conclusion about which system is better for their use case.

paper_a_title: Reliable Decision‑Making via Calibration‑Oriented Retrieval‑Augmented Generation
paper_b_title: Sufficient Context: A New Lens on Retrieval Augmented Generation Systems
gold_rationale: Paper A has no text snippet available; only the title 'Reliable Decision-Making via Calibration-Oriented Retrieval-Augmented Generation' is provided. While the title hints at a calibration-focused RAG approach, we cannot identify its datasets, base models, calibration metric (e.g., ECE, Brier, selective accuracy), retrieval setup, or abstention mechanism. Paper B is well-specified: it defines a 'sufficient context' classifier, evaluates Gemini 1.5 Pro, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5, Mistral 3, and Gemma 2 stratified by context sufficiency, and reports a selective generation method that improves the correct-answer fraction among responses by 2–10%. Without Paper A's specifics, the five coordinates cannot be matched across the two works, so the comparison is underspecified rather than clearly valid or invalid.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Access to Paper A's methods and results: the datasets used (e.g., Natural Questions, HotpotQA, FreshQA), the base LLMs evaluated, the retrieval pipeline, the exact reported metric (calibration error vs. selective accuracy vs. correct-when-answered), the abstention/decision rule, and the baselines. A fair leaderboard would also need both papers to share at least one dataset, base model family, and evaluation metric (or a clear conversion between calibration and selective-answering metrics), since calibration of confidences and conditional accuracy under abstention are related but not identical targets.
independent_rubric_rationale: Because only the title of the first work is available, there is no way to know which benchmarks, base models, or headline numbers it reports. The second work gives a specific 2–10% gain in correct-answer rate among responded queries for particular model families using a sufficient-context-guided abstention rule. Without comparable details from the first work, it is impossible to judge whether placing both numbers on one leaderboard would convey an accurate or distorted picture to a practitioner.

paper_a_title: PrismRAG: Boosting RAG Factuality with Distractor Resilience and Strategized Reasoning
paper_b_title: The Curse of Helpfulness: Inverse Scaling Law in Robustness to Distractor Instructions via DistractionIF
gold_rationale: Although both papers use the word 'distractor' in a RAG context, they target fundamentally different failure modes. Paper A (PrismRAG) addresses factual errors caused by semantically semi-relevant passages mixed with gold evidence, fine-tuning with synthetic distractor-aware QA pairs plus reasoning training, and reports a 5.4% average factuality gain over 12 open-book RAG QA benchmarks. Paper B (DistractionIF) addresses a prompt-injection-like failure where models execute instruction-like text embedded in reference material instead of treating it as inert data; it uses GRPO RL and reports a 15.5% robustness gain on its own benchmark, plus an inverse-scaling claim. The evidence assumption differs (content-noise vs instruction-shaped noise), the metric differs (answer factuality vs strict data/instruction separation), and the action policy differs (synthesize correct answer vs refuse to act on embedded directives). Putting the two headline numbers on the same axis would conflate distinct robustness phenomena.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head would require either (a) evaluating PrismRAG on DistractionIF (or a comparable instruction-distractor benchmark) and DistractionIF's GRPO recipe on the same 12 RAG QA factuality benchmarks, using the same base model and decoding setup; or (b) restricting comparison to a shared subset where 'distractor' is operationalized identically and the scoring rubric (factuality vs instruction-fidelity) is unified. Without this, the two numbers measure incompatible quantities.
independent_rubric_rationale: A practitioner glancing at a single leaderboard listing '+5.4%' beside '+15.5%' would likely assume the two systems are competing on the same task, but they are not: one is improving the truthfulness of answers when retrieved passages contain semantically similar but unhelpful content, while the other is improving a model's refusal to obey command-like phrases hidden inside reference material. The benchmarks, the scoring rubrics, and the underlying problem each system is solving are different, so a direct ranking would push a reader toward an unwarranted conclusion about which approach is 'better.'

paper_a_title: Parallel Key-Value Cache Fusion for Position Invariant RAG
paper_b_title: Beyond RAG vs. Long-Context: Learning Distraction-Aware Retrieval for Efficient Knowledge Grounding
gold_rationale: Paper A (KV Fusion) targets the 'Lost in the Middle' positional bias problem by modifying the decoder architecture to inject uniform positional information across passages, with the goal of order-invariant generation. Paper B (LDAR) targets distractor-induced degradation in long-context vs. RAG settings by training an adaptive retriever that selects how many/which passages to retrieve, with the goal of a favorable performance/token-usage trade-off. The failure modes (positional bias vs. distractor-driven token-budget waste), the pipeline component being modified (generator-side KV handling vs. retriever-side selection policy), the primary metric framing (position-invariance/robustness vs. accuracy-per-token), and the operational change (architecture/training of the LM vs. training a retrieval policy) are essentially disjoint.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation protocol with the same base LLMs, the same retrieval corpus and top-k budget, the same benchmarks (overlap appears possible on NQ/TriviaQA-style QA), and metrics that capture both axes: (a) accuracy under shuffled/adversarial passage ordering and presence of distractors, and (b) accuracy as a function of token budget. Ideally the two methods would be combined or run as ablations against a common baseline so that the contribution of generator-side position handling can be separated from retriever-side selection.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems are designed to fix different bottlenecks in the RAG pipeline and report headline numbers under different operating conditions (one emphasizes order-robust answering on a fixed passage set; the other emphasizes accuracy versus token budget on long-context tasks). A practitioner reading a single leaderboard score would likely misattribute gains: thinking one approach 'beats' the other when in fact each is optimizing a different quantity on potentially different setups, and the two ideas are largely complementary rather than substitutable.

paper_a_title: Entropy-Based Decoding for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models
paper_b_title: RAFT: Adapting Language Model to Domain Specific RAG
gold_rationale: Paper A proposes a training-free decoding-time technique (entropy-based document-parallel ensemble plus contrastive decoding across layers) evaluated on open-domain QA. Paper B proposes a training-time recipe (supervised fine-tuning with distractor documents plus chain-of-thought rationales) evaluated on domain-specific corpora (PubMed, HotpotQA, Gorilla). Although both target distraction/noise in RAG (shared failure framing), they differ on the intervention point (decoding vs. fine-tuning), the resource and data assumptions (no training data vs. domain training set with distractors), the action policy (probability reweighting vs. parameter update with rationales), and the evaluation regime (general open-domain QA vs. specialized in-domain RAG). These are largely complementary rather than competing methods and cannot be ranked directly from headline numbers.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared base LLM and retriever, a common set of benchmarks (e.g., both evaluated on the same open-domain and domain-specific splits with identical retrieved contexts), matched compute/data budgets, explicit reporting of training vs. training-free regime so practitioners see the cost trade-off, and ideally an ablation that combines the two (RAFT-tuned model with entropy decoding) to show whether the gains are additive or overlapping. Without this, the two numbers belong on separate leaderboards.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two papers solve adjacent but structurally different problems with very different recipes. One simply re-weights output probabilities at generation time without touching model weights, while the other rewrites the model itself through supervised tuning on domain examples that include irrelevant passages and reasoning traces. They also report results on different benchmark families - broad open-domain question answering versus specialized domains like PubMed and Gorilla. Placing their headline scores side-by-side on a single leaderboard would hide these differences in setup, compute cost, data requirements, and target conditions, so a practitioner choosing between them based on the numbers alone would likely make a poor choice.

paper_a_title: Can Small Language Models Use What They Retrieve? An Empirical Study of Retrieval Utilization Across Model Scale
paper_b_title: END: Early Noise Dropping for Efficient and Effective Context Denoising
gold_rationale: Paper A is an explicitly diagnostic empirical study with no proposed remedy: it characterizes a utilization bottleneck in sub-7B models using an oracle-retrieval probe and a parametric-knowledge split, reporting failure rates and error-mode breakdowns. Paper B proposes a concrete technique (END) that uses a linear prober on early transformer layers to discard noisy context chunks, and reports gains in task performance and compute efficiency on general LLMs across RAG, table QA, and ICL. The two works occupy different roles in a research pipeline (measurement vs. mitigation), operate on different model-scale regimes (small models ≤7B vs. general LLMs without a scale-centric study), and report incomparable headline numbers (utilization/error rates under controlled retrieval conditions vs. accuracy/efficiency deltas from a denoising module). The evidence-assumption coordinate is also misaligned because Paper A relies on an oracle-passages condition that Paper B does not use.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation in which both works are run on the same datasets, retriever, and base models with matching prompts and metrics; in particular, Paper B's END would need to be evaluated on Paper A's oracle-retrieval and parametric-split protocol at the sub-7B scale, and Paper A would need to provide a comparable mitigation baseline. Reported headline numbers should be of the same kind (e.g., exact-match accuracy under identical retrieval conditions and the same answerability partition), and any efficiency claims should be measured under matched hardware and chunking settings.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper diagnoses a problem in small models under a controlled oracle setup, while the other proposes a chunk-dropping technique evaluated on general LLMs and different datasets. Their headline numbers measure different things and were produced under different setups, so placing them side by side on a single ranking would suggest a comparison that the underlying evidence does not support, and a practitioner choosing between them would likely draw the wrong conclusion about scope and applicability.

paper_a_title: {MIRAGE}: A Metric-Intensive Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Evaluation
paper_b_title: RAGAs: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Based on titles alone (no snippets provided), MIRAGE presents itself as a benchmark dataset with intensive metrics for RAG evaluation, while RAGAs presents itself as an automated, reference-free evaluation framework/toolkit. These are different artifact types operating at different levels of the RAG evaluation stack: one supplies what to test against, the other supplies how to compute scores. Their failure_type framings (gap in evaluation data vs gap in scalable scoring tooling) and intervention_points diverge, and their action_policies for a practitioner (download benchmark and run my system vs install library and score my outputs) differ substantially. Coding is conservative due to absent snippets.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) both works would need to deliver evaluation tooling that computes overlapping scores on a shared dataset under identical retrieval and generation conditions, or (b) both would need to deliver benchmark datasets with comparable task definitions and reference protocols. A common scaffold such as 'agreement with human judgments on a fixed RAG output set' would let the two artifacts be ranked head to head; without such a shared substrate, leaderboard placement requires explicit normalization.
independent_rubric_rationale: Putting these two side by side on a single leaderboard would mislead a practitioner because one supplies test items and reference answers to evaluate a RAG system against, while the other supplies an automated scoring toolkit that operates without references. They occupy complementary layers of a RAG evaluation pipeline rather than competing for the same slot, so a single ranked number across them would not represent a meaningful head-to-head result.

paper_a_title: ReEval: Automatic Hallucination Evaluation for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models via Transferable Adversarial Attacks
paper_b_title: Redefining Retrieval Evaluation in the Era of LLMs
gold_rationale: Paper A (ReEval) addresses hallucination behavior of the generation component under transferable adversarial perturbations of the retrieval context; its failure_type is generator hallucination, its evidence_assumption is that adversarially rewritten contexts expose latent unfaithfulness, its intervention_point is a probing/testing harness, its metric_target is hallucination rate under perturbation, and its action_policy is to use those probes for model auditing. Paper B (UDCG) addresses misalignment between offline retrieval scoring and downstream RAG answer accuracy; its failure_type is ranking-evaluation misalignment, its evidence_assumption is that end-to-end answer accuracy is the correct supervisory signal for retrieval scoring, its intervention_point is the offline IR scoring formula (positional discount plus utility/distraction labels), its metric_target is correlation between the proposed score and answer accuracy across datasets/LLMs, and its action_policy is to replace nDCG/MAP/MRR with UDCG for retriever evaluation in RAG. None of the five coordinates align, so a head-to-head ranking is not meaningful. (Note: no snippet was available for Paper A, so confidence is moderate.)
what_valid_comparison_requires: A meaningful comparison would require both works to target the same RAG evaluation question on the same units. For example, both would need to (a) evaluate the same component (retriever-only, generator-only, or end-to-end), (b) report the same outcome variable (e.g., hallucination rate, or correlation with answer accuracy, or answer-quality delta), (c) use overlapping datasets and LLM backbones, and (d) describe interventions of the same type (either both proposing new scoring schemes, or both proposing probing/auditing harnesses). Absent that, any leaderboard juxtaposition is category-mixing.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works tackle different problems inside RAG evaluation: one probes how the generator behaves when its supporting passages are adversarially rewritten, while the other proposes a ranking-quality score for the retriever that is tuned to correlate with downstream answer accuracy. Their headline numbers describe different phenomena on different scales (perturbation-induced unfaithfulness vs. correlation with end-to-end accuracy), so placing them side by side on one leaderboard would push a practitioner toward unjustified 'A beats B' or 'B beats A' conclusions about RAG evaluation quality.

paper_a_title: MTRAG-UN: A Benchmark for Open Challenges in Multi-Turn RAG Conversations
paper_b_title: RAGLAB: A Modular and Research-Oriented Unified Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Paper A is a multi-turn RAG benchmark dataset (666 tasks, 6 domains) targeting model weaknesses on unanswerable, underspecified, non-standalone questions and unclear responses. Paper B is a modular research framework/toolkit for building and comparing RAG pipelines. The two contribute fundamentally different artifacts: an evaluation suite vs. a research infrastructure. They do not share a common dependent variable, evaluation protocol, or system-level deliverable, so a head-to-head ranking is not meaningful. Even the failure type each addresses differs (model weakness on hard conversational inputs vs. lack of unified experimentation tooling).
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both works would need to be the same class of contribution under a shared yardstick — e.g., either two benchmarks scoring overlapping RAG capabilities on matched test sets, or two toolkits implementing the same set of pipelines with reported usability/performance numbers under identical conditions. Minimally, one would need to define a common task, dataset, and scoring rule that both papers actually report, which is absent here.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper releases a curated multi-turn conversational test collection emphasizing tricky question types and reports model struggles on it; the other delivers a modular software toolkit meant to standardize how researchers build and run retrieval-augmented generation pipelines. Their headline outputs describe different kinds of objects — a dataset with difficulty findings versus a reusable codebase — so placing their main numbers side-by-side on one leaderboard would leave a practitioner confused about what is even being scored, and likely lead to drawing conclusions that neither paper supports.

paper_a_title: Generating Leakage-Free Benchmarks for Robust RAG Evaluation
paper_b_title: Judge as A Judge: Improving the Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation through the Judge-Consistency of Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Paper A targets the failure type of knowledge leakage in RAG benchmarks (questions solvable from parametric memory), with the intervention at the benchmark construction stage via type-constrained entity replacement on a reasoning graph; its metric target is benchmark discriminativeness (leakage reduction, preserved reasoning difficulty) and revealed variability across RAG systems. Paper B (judging from the title; no snippet available) targets a different failure type—unreliable LLM-as-judge evaluation—with the intervention on the judging/scoring side via a judge-consistency mechanism, and its metric target is evaluator reliability/agreement rather than benchmark quality. The two works address orthogonal stages of the RAG evaluation pipeline (data construction vs. evaluator design), so their headline numbers cannot be placed on a common axis. Confidence is moderated by the absence of Paper B's text snippet, but the title is sufficiently explicit to characterize the contribution.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head comparison would require both papers to (1) target the same evaluation deficiency (either benchmark contamination/leakage OR judge unreliability, not one of each), (2) be evaluated on a shared testbed with identical RAG systems, retrieval corpora, and seed datasets, (3) report a common quantitative target such as correlation with human judgments, discrimination between RAG methods, or a calibrated reliability score, and (4) hold the other pipeline stage fixed (e.g., use the same judge when comparing benchmarks, or the same benchmark when comparing judges). Without these alignments, any leaderboard ranking conflates improvements in test-set quality with improvements in scoring fidelity.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works address different stages of the RAG evaluation pipeline: one rebuilds the question set so models cannot answer from memory, while the other reworks how an LLM scores RAG outputs by checking judge agreement. Their headline numbers measure different things—how cleanly a benchmark separates RAG systems versus how consistently a judge scores them—so a practitioner reading a single leaderboard entry per paper would likely treat them as competing solutions to the same problem when they are actually complementary, and could pick the wrong tool for their needs.

paper_a_title: Whose Facts Win? LLM Source Preferences under Knowledge Conflicts
paper_b_title: Rethinking All Evidence: Enhancing Trustworthy Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Conflict-Driven Summarization
gold_rationale: Paper A studies inter-context knowledge conflicts focused specifically on source credibility (government, newspaper, person, social media) using synthetic sources, and proposes a fine-tuning approach whose headline numbers are a 79.2% reduction in repetition bias and 72.5% retention of original source preferences across 13 open-weight LLMs. Paper B addresses a broader problem of reconciling parametric and retrieved evidence using a CARE-RAG pipeline with conflict-driven summarization (3B distilled summarizer) and QA Repair, evaluated by QA accuracy on revised QA benchmarks. The failure modes (source-credibility manipulation vs. mixed internal/external noise), evidence setups (synthetic source-attributed passages vs. natural retrieval + parametric), intervention granularity (LoRA-style fine-tune vs. multi-stage pipeline with distillation and data repair), reported metrics (bias-reduction/preference-retention vs. QA accuracy), and decision objects (which source to trust vs. final synthesized answer) all differ. There is no shared benchmark or metric on which the two could be ranked.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation on the same conflict benchmark with a common metric, e.g., end-to-end QA accuracy under controlled inter-context conflicts that include source attribution and repetition variants, applied to both Paper A's fine-tuned models and Paper B's CARE-RAG pipeline, using the same base LLMs and the same set of retrieval/parametric contexts. Alternatively, both methods could be evaluated on Paper A's source-preference and repetition-bias diagnostics, or both on Paper B's revised QA datasets, with identical retrieval corpora and prompts.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works study different phenomena within knowledge conflicts and report headline numbers that are not on the same scale or task. Paper A's percentages describe how much source-credibility behavior shifts under repetition and how much it is preserved after training, while Paper B's results are downstream question-answering scores on cleaned benchmarks. Placing these numbers in one leaderboard would invite a practitioner to treat them as alternatives to each other when in fact they target unrelated outcomes on incompatible setups, so the side-by-side ranking would seriously mislead.

paper_a_title: Context-DPO: Aligning Language Models for Context-Faithfulness
paper_b_title: FaithfulRAG: Fact-Level Conflict Modeling for Context-Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Both papers target the same failure_type (LLM unfaithfulness to provided context under knowledge conflict in RAG-style settings) and share a similar action_policy goal (produce context-grounded answers). However, the intervention_point differs fundamentally: Paper A modifies model weights via DPO alignment using preference pairs of faithful vs. stubborn responses, while Paper B operates at inference-time by identifying fact-level conflicts and invoking a self-thinking reasoning process without weight updates. The evidence_assumption also likely differs: Paper A evaluates on its own ConFiQA benchmark (synthetically constructed knowledge-conflict QA), while Paper B's snippet refers to 'extensive experiments' and 'state-of-the-art' comparisons on unspecified (likely different) benchmarks. The metric_target framings differ as well: Paper A reports relative improvement percentages (35%-280%) on open-source models, whereas Paper B frames results as outperforming SOTA, with no shared headline metric visible in the snippet.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head comparison would require (1) evaluating both methods on the same benchmark suite (e.g., ConFiQA plus the benchmarks used by Paper B), (2) using the same backbone LLMs and reporting identically-defined faithfulness metrics (e.g., memorization rate, faithfulness accuracy), (3) explicitly accounting for the training-time vs inference-time intervention asymmetry, including compute cost, applicability to closed-source models, and whether the DPO-aligned model is used as the backbone for the inference-time framework, and (4) controlling for differences in conflict construction (synthetic counterfactual vs naturally occurring retrieval conflicts).
independent_rubric_rationale: A practitioner browsing a single leaderboard with both headline numbers would get a partly misleading impression. The two systems address the same context-grounding problem in retrieval-augmented question answering, so a side-by-side ranking is tempting, but they operate at different stages of the pipeline (weight tuning versus inference-time reasoning) and appear to be measured on different test sets with different score definitions. Without harmonized backbones, datasets, and scoring, any direct ranking would conflate genuine quality differences with setup differences and would hide the practical trade-offs (cost of preference data and tuning vs added latency from explicit reasoning steps) that determine which approach is preferable in deployment.

paper_a_title: Position: Retrieval-augmented systems can be dangerous medical communicators
paper_b_title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
gold_rationale: Paper A is a position paper arguing that retrieval-augmented systems pose communicative safety risks in medical settings; its failure_type concerns pragmatic/clinical miscommunication, its evidence_assumption is argumentative with illustrative cases, its intervention_point is system design guidance for medical RAG, its metric_target is safety/appropriateness in healthcare communication, and its action_policy is normative recommendations. Paper B is an empirical study showing that LLM accuracy on multi-document QA and key-value retrieval degrades when relevant information appears in the middle of a long context; its failure_type is positional accuracy degradation, its evidence_assumption is controlled benchmark experiments, its intervention_point is context construction/positioning, its metric_target is task accuracy as a function of document position, and its action_policy is prompt-engineering implications. The two diverge on every coordinate, so no shared axis exists for direct comparison or ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both papers to address a shared question (e.g., both empirically evaluating retrieval-augmented LLMs on the same clinical-QA benchmark), to use the same evidence type (e.g., both quantitative benchmark results), to report on the same outcome scale (e.g., accuracy or safety scores on overlapping tasks), and to recommend interventions at compatible points in the pipeline. As is, one is a normative position piece in the medical domain and the other is a general empirical analysis of long-context behavior, so they cannot share a leaderboard.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper presents an argumentative stance about safety risks of retrieval-augmented systems used as medical communicators, while the other reports empirical accuracy results on how language models handle information placed at different positions inside long prompts. They tackle different questions, use different kinds of evidence (normative argument vs benchmark scores), and report outcomes on incompatible scales, so putting their headline results side by side on a single leaderboard would seriously mislead a practitioner trying to draw conclusions from such a ranking.

paper_a_title: KnowPO: Knowledge-aware Preference Optimization for Controllable Knowledge Selection in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
paper_b_title: Why So Gullible? Enhancing the Robustness of Retrieval-Augmented Models against Counterfactual Noise
gold_rationale: Both papers nominally address 'knowledge conflicts' in RAG, but they frame the failure differently. Paper A (KnowPO) targets conflicts between the LM's parametric knowledge and retrieved external evidence, with intervention via preference optimization (DPO-style) on the generator and a custom conflict-construction protocol. Paper B (Why So Gullible?) targets inter-document conflicts caused by counterfactual/misleading content within the retrieved set, intervening via a separately fine-tuned discriminator or GPT-3.5 prompting, evaluated on ODQA with MACNOISE. Evidence assumptions differ (Paper A treats retrieval as the authoritative side to adhere to; Paper B explicitly rejects the relevance=truth assumption among retrieved docs). Datasets, base models, and primary metrics likely differ as well. There is some thematic overlap (noise robustness in retrieved context), so the pair is not fully orthogonal, but a head-to-head ranking would conflate distinct problem formulations.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared conflict-type taxonomy (separating parametric-vs-retrieved from intra-retrieval conflicts), evaluation on a common benchmark suite that contains both conflict varieties (e.g., MACNOISE plus the KnowPO conflict set), identical base LMs and retrieval pipelines, and a unified metric (e.g., accuracy under controlled conflict ratios) reported on identical splits. Reporting headline percentage gains relative to differing baselines, as both papers do, would also need to be normalized.
independent_rubric_rationale: Both works tackle reliability of retrieval-augmented language models when retrieved text is problematic, but they target distinct sub-problems: one centers on tension between a model's internal knowledge and retrieved content, while the other centers on contradictions among the retrieved documents themselves. Their training recipes, datasets, and evaluation suites differ enough that side-by-side placement on a single leaderboard would give a practitioner a misleading sense of which system is stronger for any given deployment scenario, though the broader topic overlap means the comparison is not entirely meaningless.

paper_a_title: Hierarchical Planning for Complex Tasks with Knowledge Graph-RAG and Symbolic Verification
paper_b_title: RAG4GFM: Bridging Knowledge Gaps in Graph Foundation Models through Graph Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Based solely on titles (no snippets supplied), the two papers operate in different problem regimes. Paper A targets hierarchical task planning for complex tasks, with knowledge-graph retrieval coupled to symbolic verification as the intervention surface; the failure being remediated is planning errors in long-horizon tasks. Paper B targets graph foundation models, where the failure is missing/incomplete knowledge in the GFM and retrieval augmentation is inserted at the model's reasoning surface over graph data. Although both invoke 'RAG' over graph-structured evidence, the failure_type differs (plan correctness vs. GFM knowledge coverage), the intervention_point differs (planner loop with symbolic checking vs. GFM inference pipeline), and the metric_target almost certainly differs (task/plan success vs. node/edge/graph-level benchmarks). Without snippets, the evidence_assumption and action_policy comparison is harder to lock down, but at least three coordinates already diverge.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A defensible head-to-head would need (i) a shared task family (either both on planning benchmarks or both on GFM downstream tasks), (ii) overlapping datasets and evaluation protocols, (iii) the same outcome measures reported with comparable splits, and (iv) either matched baselines or a controlled ablation isolating the graph-RAG component on the same backbone.
independent_rubric_rationale: Title-level reading suggests the two works live in different research neighborhoods: one centers on hierarchical planning for long-horizon problems with symbolic checking, the other on closing knowledge gaps inside graph foundation models. Putting their headline numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would likely mislead a practitioner because the underlying tasks, datasets, and benchmark conventions are unlikely to align, so any apparent ranking would reflect domain choice rather than the relative strength of either approach.

paper_a_title: Entity-Focused Dense Passage Retrieval for Outside-Knowledge Visual Question Answering
paper_b_title: Quebec Automobile Insurance Question-Answering With Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Based on titles and venues (no snippets supplied), the two works target disjoint problem settings. Paper A addresses outside-knowledge Visual Question Answering, where the input is an image plus question and the system retrieves textual passages using entity-focused dense retrieval; the failure mode is poor passage recall when visual entities are not well represented in DPR encodings, evidence is multimodal (image + Wikipedia-scale corpus), the intervention point is the retriever, the metric target is OK-VQA-style answer accuracy plus retrieval recall, and the action policy is an entity-aware dense retriever. Paper B addresses closed-domain legal/insurance QA over Quebec automobile insurance documents using RAG; the failure mode is hallucination or unfaithful generation in a regulated narrow domain, evidence is text-only domain corpora, the intervention point spans retrieval + generation, the metric target is generation quality on insurance questions, and the action policy is a domain-specific RAG pipeline. All five coordinates differ, so the two headline results cannot be placed on a shared leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A meaningful comparison would require either (a) both systems being evaluated on the same QA benchmark with identical inputs, corpora, and scoring, or (b) reframing the comparison narrowly around a shared methodological claim (e.g., entity-aware retrieval techniques vs. domain-adapted retrieval) tested on the same dataset and modality. Given the divergence in modality (multimodal vs. text-only), domain (open-world VQA vs. Quebec insurance), and pipeline scope (retrieval-only vs. retrieval+generation), no fair head-to-head ranking is possible without substantial re-running of one system in the other's setting.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two papers tackle fundamentally different problems: one answers questions that pair an image with the need for external world knowledge, while the other answers text-only questions about a specific body of Quebec automobile insurance documents. Their datasets, input modalities, target domains, and evaluation protocols have essentially no overlap, so placing their headline numbers side-by-side on a single leaderboard would lead a practitioner to draw conclusions about relative quality that the underlying tasks do not support.

paper_a_title: Think-on-Graph 2.0: Deep and Faithful Large Language Model Reasoning with Knowledge-guided Retrieval Augmented Generation
paper_b_title: ReFIR: Grounding Large Restoration Models with Retrieval Augmentation
gold_rationale: Paper A (Think-on-Graph 2.0) tackles LLM reasoning hallucinations in knowledge-intensive QA by tightly coupling knowledge-graph traversal with retrieval-augmented generation, evaluated on multi-hop QA benchmarks with QA accuracy and reasoning faithfulness. Paper B (ReFIR) tackles hallucination/ungroundedness in large image restoration models by retrieving visually similar reference images, evaluated on image restoration benchmarks with image-quality scores (e.g., PSNR/SSIM/perceptual quality). All five coordinates diverge: the failure mode lives in different modalities (text reasoning vs. visual restoration), the evidence sources are structured KG triples vs. retrieved reference images, the pipeline insertion points are different (graph-guided reasoning steps vs. restoration backbone conditioning), and the evaluation targets share no common scale or benchmark. The only superficial commonality is the word 'retrieval-augmented.'
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers would need to address the same task on shared benchmarks with comparable evaluation protocols. A direct ranking would require either (a) restricting comparison to a common retrieval-augmentation paradigm question on a shared task they both perform, or (b) treating them as instances of a general RAG-grounding strategy and comparing only at a conceptual/qualitative level rather than via a leaderboard. As stated, no shared task, benchmark, or scoring scale exists between text QA over KGs and image restoration.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works live in entirely different modalities and problem spaces: one is language reasoning over knowledge graphs for question answering, the other is visual restoration of images using reference look-ups. Their reported numbers come from disjoint benchmarks on incompatible scales, so placing them side by side on a single leaderboard would suggest a comparison that simply does not exist and could lead a practitioner to draw conclusions about relative quality or progress that have no basis.

paper_a_title: TRACE: Grounding Time Series in Context for Multimodal Embedding and Retrieval
paper_b_title: Unified Generative and Discriminative Training for Multi-modal Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Based solely on titles (no snippets provided), Paper A targets time-series-centric multimodal embedding for retrieval, while Paper B targets unifying generative and discriminative objectives in general-purpose MLLMs. The failure_type differs (poor cross-modal alignment for time series vs. fragmented training paradigms in MLLMs), the intervention_point differs (embedding/representation pipeline vs. training objective composition for an LLM backbone), the metric_target almost certainly differs (retrieval recall/precision on time-series multimodal benchmarks vs. standard MLLM generation/discrimination benchmarks), and the action_policy a practitioner would take differs (deploy a specialized retriever vs. adopt a new MLLM training recipe). They are not natural leaderboard neighbors.

Without overlapping benchmarks, shared backbones, or a common downstream task framing, any head-to-head ranking would not reflect comparable capabilities. A snippet-level confirmation of evaluation suites would also be required to upgrade confidence.

Putting their headline numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would suggest a comparison that the underlying tasks and benchmarks do not support, leading a practitioner to draw conclusions about relative quality that are not warranted.

paper_a_title: Chunk-Distilled Language Modeling
paper_b_title: Context Tuning for Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: No text snippets were provided for either paper, leaving all five coordinates inferable only from titles. From titles alone, Paper A ('Chunk-Distilled Language Modeling') appears to modify the LM itself by distilling retrieved chunks into the model, while Paper B ('Context Tuning for Retrieval Augmented Generation') appears to operate on the retrieved context fed to an unchanged generator. These suggest different intervention points and likely different failure modes (generative knowledge gaps vs. noisy/irrelevant retrieved context), but the specific datasets, evaluation metrics, and baselines cannot be confirmed without the actual text. A conservative gold label is therefore 'underspecified' rather than 'invalid', because the surface mismatch is plausible but not verifiable.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To upgrade to a 'valid' or 'partial' verdict, we would need: (1) confirmation that both papers evaluate on at least one overlapping benchmark with the same metric definition; (2) matched or comparable base LM scales and retrieval corpora; (3) clarity on whether the comparison is end-task QA quality, perplexity, factuality, or latency, since A and B likely optimize different objectives; (4) the actual reported headline numbers and baselines; (5) confirmation that the unit of improvement (chunk-level model distillation vs. context-selection tuning) is being scored against the same reference system.
independent_rubric_rationale: With no excerpts available and only titles to rely on, there is not enough basis to judge whether a side-by-side leaderboard entry of the two headline results would mislead a practitioner. The titles hint that the two works modify different stages of a retrieval-augmented pipeline and probably report different evaluation setups, which would normally favor a 'partly' or 'misleading' label, but without the texts confirming benchmarks, baselines, and reported numbers, a confident rubric label cannot be assigned.

paper_a_title: Cooperative Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Question Answering: Mutual Information Exchange and Ranking by Contrasting Layers
paper_b_title: Separate the Wheat from the Chaff: Winnowing Down Divergent Views in Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Paper A provides no text snippet, only a title indicating a cooperative RAG approach involving 'mutual information exchange' and 'ranking by contrasting layers.' Paper B's WinnowRAG is described as a two-stage clustering plus critic-LLM filtering pipeline tested on undisclosed (in snippet) datasets. Without Paper A's specifics on datasets, retrievers, backbone LLMs, baselines, evaluation metrics, and the precise denoising mechanism, none of the five coordinates can be confidently matched or contrasted. While both target the broad problem of noisy retrievals in QA, this surface overlap is insufficient to determine whether the experimental setups, evaluation protocols, and design contributions are comparable.

A meaningful comparison would need both works to be evaluated on overlapping benchmarks with the same retriever and LLM backbone, reporting the same metric, and ideally addressing the same regime (e.g., open-domain multi-hop with high-k retrieval where noise dominates).

A side-by-side leaderboard placement could be either reasonable or grossly misleading depending on facts that are simply not in evidence, so a reliable judgment about whether a reader would be led astray cannot be formed.

paper_a_title: RankRAG: Unifying Context Ranking with Retrieval-Augmented Generation in LLMs
paper_b_title: xRAG: Extreme Context Compression for Retrieval-augmented Generation with One Token
gold_rationale: Based on titles alone (no snippets available), the two systems target orthogonal weaknesses of RAG pipelines. RankRAG addresses noisy or poorly ordered retrieved passages by unifying re-ranking and answer generation inside one LLM, so its primary headline numbers reflect end-task quality gains attributable to better context selection. xRAG addresses prompt length and serving cost by collapsing a passage into essentially a single embedding token via a projector aligned to a frozen LLM, so its headline numbers are an accuracy-vs-compression trade-off relative to a full-context baseline. The two thus differ on what is treated as the core defect of vanilla RAG (poor ordering vs. prohibitive context length), where in the pipeline they modify behavior (joint ranker-generator at decoding vs. encoder-side compression), what they primarily optimize against (downstream QA accuracy with longer ranked inputs vs. accuracy retention at extreme token budgets), and the runtime behavior of the resulting system (multi-passage reranking then generation vs. one-token-per-passage generation). They may share QA benchmarks such as NQ or TriviaQA, but a single leaderboard cell would suppress these very different cost/quality contracts.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A fair head-to-head would need (1) the same base LLM, retriever, and corpus; (2) matched evaluation suites with both accuracy and efficiency reported (input tokens consumed, latency, FLOPs, memory); (3) a Pareto view rather than a single scalar, because one method spends more compute for quality while the other spends quality for compute; (4) ablations that hold the number and form of retrieved passages constant; and (5) explicit statement of whether the comparison question is 'best accuracy at any cost' or 'best accuracy at a fixed token/latency budget'. Without these, ranking them on one number is not meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems are pursuing different goals: one is trying to squeeze more answer quality out of retrieved passages by reordering them, while the other is trying to make retrieval-augmented generation drastically cheaper by shrinking each passage to almost nothing. If a practitioner saw their headline numbers side by side on one leaderboard, they would likely read it as 'A beats B' or vice versa on quality, and miss that the two are operating under very different cost budgets and were never aiming at the same target. Picking between them based on such a ranking would lead to wrong deployment decisions in most realistic settings.

paper_a_title: SEER: Self-Aligned Evidence Extraction for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper_b_title: Neuro-RIT: Neuron-Guided Instruction Tuning for Robust Retrieval-Augmented Language Model
gold_rationale: Paper A's text snippet is unavailable, so its exact benchmarks, base model, retriever, noise protocol, and reported scores cannot be verified. From titles alone, Paper A (SEER) appears to operate at the evidence-extraction stage upstream of generation via self-alignment, while Paper B (Neuro-RIT) modifies the generator LLM internally through attribution-based neuron mining plus two-stage instruction tuning. These are clearly different intervention points with different underlying assumptions about how to handle noisy retrieved context, and without confirmed shared benchmarks/base models the comparability cannot be established.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Matched base LLM (size and family), identical retriever and retrieval corpus with the same top-k and document-ordering protocol, the same QA benchmarks and splits, identical noise/distractor injection regimes for robustness tests, the same evaluation metric definitions (EM/F1/accuracy), shared baselines reported under the same conditions, and disclosure of training data and compute for the tuning-based system versus inference-time overhead for the extraction-based system.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems target different stages of a retrieval-augmented pipeline: one reshapes what context reaches the model upstream, while the other rewires how the generator itself processes context via targeted parameter updates. Even if both report numbers on similar QA datasets, dropping single headline scores side-by-side on one leaderboard would likely mislead a practitioner because the base models, retrievers, noise conditions, and training budgets are probably not aligned, and Paper A's setup cannot be independently confirmed here.

paper_a_title: Towards Secure Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Comprehensive Review of Threats, Defenses and Benchmarks
paper_b_title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
gold_rationale: Paper A is a survey of security threats (data poisoning, adversarial attacks, membership inference) and defenses (encryption, differential privacy, sanitization) for RAG pipelines, with evaluation framed around security benchmarks. Paper B is the seminal Lewis et al. RAG paper that introduces the retrieval-augmented generation architecture and benchmarks it on knowledge-intensive NLP tasks (open-domain QA, fact verification, etc.) using task-quality scores. The two works diverge on every coordinate of the frame: the kind of failure they target (security breach vs. knowledge gap / hallucination), the underlying assumptions about what counts as evidence of progress, where they apply changes in the pipeline, the quantitative targets they report, and the operational policy they recommend. There is no shared leaderboard or shared task on which their headline numbers live.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both works to address the same RAG question on overlapping benchmarks — e.g., both reporting attack success rate / defense effectiveness on a common security testbed, or both reporting task accuracy on a common knowledge-intensive QA suite under matched retrievers and generators. Additionally, Paper A would need to contribute its own empirical results rather than only synthesizing prior literature, and both would need to share evaluation protocols, datasets, and threat or task definitions.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper is a literature review about defending retrieval-augmented systems from adversaries and privacy leaks, while the other is the original architectural proposal evaluated on open-domain question answering and fact verification quality. Their headline numbers describe completely different phenomena and live in different evaluation worlds, so dropping them next to each other in a single ranked table would lead a practitioner to draw conclusions that neither paper actually supports.

paper_a_title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Comprehensive Survey of Architectures, Enhancements, and Robustness Frontiers
paper_b_title: LLM-Oriented Information Retrieval: A Denoising-First Perspective
gold_rationale: Both items are non-empirical survey/perspective papers rather than systems with measured results. Paper A is a broad taxonomic survey of RAG architectures, enhancements, and robustness, covering retriever-centric, generator-centric, hybrid, and robustness-oriented designs with comparative analyses drawn from the literature. Paper B is a position/perspective paper arguing that denoising is the primary bottleneck and proposing a four-stage framework (inaccessible→undiscoverable→misaligned→unverifiable) plus a pipeline-organized taxonomy of signal-to-noise techniques. They differ in failure_type framing (broad RAG limitations vs. noise as the central pathology), in intervention_point scope (full taxonomy vs. denoising-first across stages), in metric_target (no shared benchmark numbers in either, only narrative synthesis), and in action_policy (descriptive taxonomy vs. prescriptive denoising-first agenda). There is no shared evaluation surface that would let one rank or directly compare them.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require either (a) both papers reporting head-to-head results on the same benchmark(s) using comparable retrievers, generators, and noise/robustness protocols, or (b) restricting the comparison to a clearly scoped sub-question (e.g., 'taxonomic coverage of denoising techniques in RAG') with an explicit rubric for survey quality. Since both are non-empirical synthesis pieces with different theses (comprehensive overview vs. denoising-first agenda), only a scoped qualitative comparison of coverage, framing, and recency would be defensible — not a leaderboard-style ranking.
independent_rubric_rationale: Neither paper reports its own experimental numbers; both are synthesis pieces with different scopes and theses. Placing them side by side on a single leaderboard would suggest a head-to-head comparison that the documents do not support, and a practitioner could easily mistake one paper's broader taxonomic reach for empirical superiority or mistake the other's sharper denoising thesis for a narrower technique rather than a perspective. Direct ranking would mislead readers about what each paper is even trying to deliver.

paper_a_title: Towards Trustworthy Retrieval Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
paper_b_title: Trustworthiness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems: A Survey
gold_rationale: Both works are surveys on trustworthy RAG and share a meaningful overlap in scope (fairness, accountability, privacy appear in both). However, their failure_type taxonomies diverge: Paper A organizes around reliability, privacy, safety, fairness, explainability, accountability, while Paper B uses factuality, robustness, fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy. The evidence_assumption also differs: Paper A is a pure literature roadmap, whereas Paper B couples its survey with an original benchmark (TRC Bench) and empirical evaluations of proprietary and open-source LLMs. Their metric_target therefore differs in kind — qualitative taxonomy/roadmap vs. taxonomy plus quantitative benchmark results. They are not non-comparable, but they cannot be placed in a single ranking without significant caveats.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require (1) aligning the two trustworthiness taxonomies onto a shared set of dimensions or explicitly mapping non-overlapping ones (e.g., A's 'reliability/safety' vs B's 'factuality/robustness'); (2) restricting the comparison to the survey-coverage axis (breadth, recency, citation set, downstream applications) rather than empirical performance, since only Paper B reports measurements; and (3) treating Paper B's benchmark contribution as an additional artifact rather than a competing claim to Paper A's roadmap. Comparison on benchmark performance is not possible because Paper A produces no such numbers.
independent_rubric_rationale: A practitioner placing these side by side on one list would see two surveys of trustworthy RAG that look like substitutes, but they actually deliver different things: one provides a conceptual roadmap with six trust dimensions, while the other provides a six-dimension framework plus an original evaluation suite with empirical numbers across multiple LLMs. Their dimension labels overlap only in part (e.g., reliability vs. factuality, safety vs. robustness, explainability vs. transparency are related but not identical concepts), so treating them as interchangeable references — or ranking them by empirical scores — would mislead the reader, though both remain legitimate entries in the same topic area.

paper_a_title: Securing Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Taxonomy of Attacks, Defenses, and Future Directions
paper_b_title: RAPID: Long-Context Inference with Retrieval-Augmented Speculative Decoding
gold_rationale: Paper A is a survey/taxonomy organizing the literature on RAG security (attacks on confidentiality, integrity, availability across a knowledge-access pipeline) and produces a conceptual framework (SLOT). Paper B is a systems/inference paper proposing retrieval-augmented speculative decoding to accelerate long-context generation. The two works tackle entirely different problems (adversarial robustness/taxonomy vs. decoding efficiency), use different forms of evidence (literature mapping vs. inference benchmarks), operate at different points (cross-pipeline conceptual framing vs. token-level decoding loop), optimize different outcomes (taxonomic coverage and threat-model clarity vs. latency/throughput with quality preservation), and yield different deliverables (a research-organizing framework vs. a deployable decoding algorithm). They share only the RAG keyword.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers would need to target the same problem class with a common evaluation protocol — for example, both proposing methods for the same RAG security objective (or both proposing inference-efficiency methods) and reporting results on shared benchmarks with overlapping baselines and metrics. A taxonomy paper and a decoding-acceleration method cannot be placed on a common leaderboard without redefining what is being measured.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works are about different things inside the broader RAG area: one surveys and categorizes the security literature, while the other proposes a concrete decoding technique to make long-context generation faster. There is no shared yardstick on which their headline numbers or contributions can be lined up, so placing them side by side on one leaderboard would give a practitioner a false sense that one is 'better' than the other when they are not even answering the same question.

paper_a_title: Trust or Abstain? A Self-Aware RAG Approach
paper_b_title: PoisonedRAG: Knowledge Corruption Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Paper A (SABER) targets naturally occurring knowledge conflicts between parametric and retrieved contextual knowledge, building an inference-time defensive estimator that decides among trust-PK, trust-CK, trust-either, or abstain, scored by end-to-end accuracy, conflict faithfulness, and risk-coverage curves. Paper B (PoisonedRAG) targets adversarial corruption of the knowledge database by injecting malicious passages, scored by attack success rate against chosen target answers. The two works occupy opposite roles in the threat model (defender vs. attacker), assume different sources of error (benign noise/conflict vs. crafted poison), operate at different stages of the pipeline (post-retrieval decision logic vs. pre-retrieval data injection), optimize different objective functions, and report incommensurable headline numbers. All five coordinates diverge, so no shared axis exists for ranking them.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require either (i) evaluating SABER as a defense under PoisonedRAG-style poisoning and reporting attack success rate or accuracy-under-attack, or (ii) running PoisonedRAG against a SABER-protected RAG pipeline using the same backbones, datasets, retriever, and poisoning budget, with both papers reporting the same accuracy or robustness number on the same benchmark. Absent such a shared evaluation protocol—same threat model, same dataset, same backbone, same scoring function—the two headline results cannot be co-tabulated.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper reports how well a defensive selection-and-abstention module preserves answer correctness when retrieved passages naturally disagree with model memory; the other reports how often an adversary can flip answers by seeding the corpus with crafted passages. Putting a ~90% attack-success number next to an accuracy or risk-coverage improvement on the same leaderboard would suggest these systems are doing comparable work, when in fact one is building a shield against benign confusion and the other is wielding a weapon against an undefended pipeline. A practitioner glancing at a unified table would draw wrong conclusions about which technique helps or harms which scenario.

paper_a_title: Magic Mushroom: A Customizable Benchmark for Fine-grained Analysis of Retrieval Noise Erosion in RAG Systems
paper_b_title: Why Uncertainty Estimation Methods Fall Short in RAG: An Axiomatic Analysis
