gold_rationale: Paper A targets generation-quality degradation caused by heterogeneous retrieval noise, introducing a configurable benchmark and evaluating generators plus denoising strategies on QA accuracy under varied noise distributions. Paper B targets a different failure mode entirely: that uncertainty estimation methods do not reliably reflect correctness in RAG, and it proposes an axiomatic framework plus a calibration function evaluated by axiom satisfaction and correlation between uncertainty and correctness. The two works disagree on every coordinate: the failure being studied (noise-induced wrong answers vs. miscalibrated confidence), the evidence stance (noise taxonomy reflects realistic retrieval vs. five axioms capture desired UE behavior), the locus of change (benchmark/generator/denoiser vs. UE scoring/calibration), the headline metric (QA accuracy under noise vs. UE-correctness correlation/axiom coverage), and the proposed policy (controlled benchmarking vs. axiomatic diagnosis plus calibration). No common leaderboard exists.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared task and metric on the same dataset under matched RAG conditions. For example, both methods would need to be evaluated on retrieval-noise-rich QA with either (a) a common end-task accuracy metric and identical generators, or (b) a common selective-prediction / abstention metric that ties uncertainty thresholds back to answer correctness under controlled noise injection. Without such a shared benchmark and evaluation target, the headline numbers measure incomparable quantities.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works tackle different problems in RAG with no overlapping evaluation. Paper A reports how generation quality degrades when retrieved passages contain various kinds of misleading content, while Paper B reports how well confidence scores track answer correctness after retrieval is added. Their headline numbers describe different quantities on different setups, so a reader who saw them ranked together would draw unwarranted conclusions about which approach is better for RAG.

paper_a_title: Toward Robust RALMs: Revealing the Impact of Imperfect Retrieval on Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
paper_b_title: RoseRAG: Robust Retrieval-augmented Generation with Small-scale LLMs via Margin-aware Preference Optimization
gold_rationale: Paper A is a diagnostic/benchmarking study that catalogs three distinct imperfect-retrieval scenarios (unanswerable, adversarial, conflicting), introduces a generative adversarial attack (GenADV) and a custom Robustness under Additional Document (RAD) metric, and aims to characterize where RALMs break. Paper B is a method paper that proposes a training-time margin-aware preference optimization pipeline (multi-turn prompting + rejection sampling + contrastive selection) specifically for small-scale LLMs, evaluated with standard EM/F1 on three open-domain QA benchmarks. While both nominally address robustness to imperfect retrieval, the evidence assumption is the only coordinate that roughly aligns. The intervention point (no model change vs. preference-optimization training), metric target (RAD/detection rates vs. EM/F1), and action policy (diagnose vulnerabilities vs. ship a trained SLM) differ fundamentally, so any direct numerical comparison or ranking is not meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both works would need to share (i) the same target model family/scale (e.g., both evaluate SLMs or both evaluate large RALMs), (ii) the same evaluation suite covering the same imperfect-retrieval scenarios, (iii) the same scoring procedure (either both report RAD-style robustness under adversarial/unanswerable/conflicting documents, or both report EM/F1 on identical QA benchmarks with matched retrievers), and (iv) comparable contribution types — either two diagnostic studies measuring vulnerability, or two training/inference methods proposing fixes with shared baselines.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper is a diagnostic study that catalogs how retrieval-augmented models stumble across several problematic document scenarios and proposes a custom robustness score, while the other is a training-recipe paper for small models reporting standard exact-match and F1 numbers on open-domain QA benchmarks. They target different model scales, run on different datasets, and report different scoring schemes, so putting their headline numbers side-by-side on one leaderboard would lead a practitioner to draw conclusions about relative quality that the underlying experiments simply do not support.

paper_a_title: Hierarchical Planning for Complex Tasks with Knowledge Graph-RAG and Symbolic Verification
paper_b_title: Supportiveness-based Knowledge Rewriting for Retrieval-augmented Language Modeling
gold_rationale: Based on titles and Paper B's abstract (Paper A has no snippet), the two works address distinct problem settings. Paper A targets hierarchical planning for complex tasks, combining knowledge-graph RAG with symbolic verification — the failure mode is plan correctness/feasibility for multi-step tasks, and the intervention is at the planner/verifier level over a structured KG evidence base. Paper B targets noisy/misleading retrieved passages in standard RALM pipelines and intervenes by training a DPO-aligned 'supportiveness'-based rewriter over unstructured text, evaluated on six knowledge-intensive QA-style benchmarks across four LLMs. The metric targets (plan/task success vs. QA accuracy), evidence assumptions (KG vs. retrieved text), and intervention points (planner+verifier vs. post-retrieval rewriter) differ substantively. Confidence is held at 3 because Paper A's snippet is unavailable, limiting fine-grained verification of its exact benchmarks and metrics.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both systems to be evaluated on a shared benchmark with the same evidence source modality (e.g., both on a KG-grounded multi-step task or both on text-based knowledge-intensive QA), the same backbone LLM(s), the same retrieval corpus and retriever, and the same scoring protocol (e.g., exact-match/F1 for QA, or task success rate for planning). Additionally, ablations isolating the contribution of the rewriter vs. the planner+verifier on a common task would be needed before placing the two methods on a single leaderboard.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two papers tackle different problem types: one builds a multi-step planner over a structured knowledge graph with symbolic checking, while the other rewrites retrieved text passages to better support QA-style generation. They use different inputs, different evaluation suites, and different success criteria, so placing their headline numbers side-by-side on one leaderboard would suggest a head-to-head winner that does not actually exist and would likely steer a practitioner toward the wrong tool for their use case.

paper_a_title: Overcoming the Retrieval Barrier: Indirect Prompt Injection in the Wild for LLM Systems
paper_b_title: GRACE: Reinforcement Learning for Grounded Response and Abstention under Contextual Evidence
gold_rationale: Paper A is an offensive security study targeting indirect prompt injection in RAG/agentic pipelines; its failure_type is adversarial corpus poisoning, its evidence_assumption is an attacker with embedding-API access and write access to the external corpus, its intervention_point is the document/corpus side (trigger+attack fragment construction), its metric_target is retrieval rate and end-to-end attack success (e.g., SSH-key exfiltration ~80%), and its action_policy is a black-box attack algorithm. Paper B is a defensive RL training method for grounded answering and abstention; its failure_type is hallucination and ungrounded answering under insufficient evidence, its evidence_assumption is a benign retriever returning mixed-sufficiency contexts, its intervention_point is generator fine-tuning via multi-stage gated rewards, its metric_target is answer accuracy plus calibrated abstention, and its action_policy is producing grounded answers or explicit 'I don't know'. The two works share only the RAG substrate; every coordinate diverges.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head would require both papers to address the same failure mode (e.g., either both attacking retrieval or both improving grounding under adversarial/noisy contexts), operate on a shared threat or evidence model, intervene at compatible pipeline stages, and report at least one common headline number (e.g., attack-success-rate of poisoned content versus abstention-on-poisoned-content for a defense, on a shared benchmark and embedding model). Without an overlapping setup such as evaluating GRACE-style abstention against IPI-poisoned corpora, no meaningful ranking is possible.
independent_rubric_rationale: Placed side by side on one leaderboard, a practitioner would be seriously misled: one paper reports how often a hidden adversarial document gets pulled in and hijacks the model, while the other reports how often a model gives a correct grounded answer or politely declines on benign question-answering benchmarks. The headline numbers measure different worlds (offense versus reliability), use different datasets and threat conditions, and have no shared baseline, so any direct ordering would suggest a comparison that does not exist.

paper_a_title: DRAGged into Conflicts: Detecting and Addressing Conflicting Sources in Search-Augmented LLMs
paper_b_title: Rescuing the Unpoisoned: Efficient Defense against Knowledge Corruption Attacks on RAG Systems
gold_rationale: Paper A addresses naturally occurring knowledge conflicts in RAG (temporal shifts, debatable/controversial queries, differing perspectives) where all sources may be legitimate, and proposes a taxonomy plus prompting strategies whose success is judged by response appropriateness per conflict type. Paper B addresses adversarial knowledge corruption (data poisoning) where attackers inject malicious passages into the retrieval pool, and proposes a lightweight post-retrieval filter judged by Attack Success Rate reduction. The failure modes (benign disagreement vs. malicious injection), the evidence model (all legitimate vs. partially adversarial), the pipeline stage of the fix (generation-time prompting vs. post-retrieval filtering), the success metric, and the desired model behavior (nuanced multi-perspective answers vs. discard-and-answer-from-clean-set) all differ. They cannot be placed on a shared leaderboard.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both systems would need to be evaluated on the same problem scope (either natural conflict resolution or adversarial corruption defense), using a shared benchmark with comparable ground-truth labels, the same retrieval pipeline and base LLMs, and a common scoring criterion (e.g., both judged on ASR under poisoning, or both judged on conflict-type-appropriate response quality on a benchmark like CONFLICTS). At minimum, Paper B would need to be run on natural-conflict data or Paper A's prompting approach would need to be evaluated under poisoning attacks with ASR reporting.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works look superficially similar because both involve 'conflicts' among retrieved passages in RAG, but they target fundamentally different scenarios. One handles genuine disagreement among legitimate sources (outdated info, debatable topics) and aims to produce well-calibrated, possibly multi-perspective answers. The other defends against attackers who deliberately seed the corpus with poisoned passages and aims to discard them before answering. A practitioner glancing at a shared leaderboard could easily pick the wrong tool: deploying the poisoning-defense filter on a debatable-opinion query would suppress legitimate minority viewpoints, and using the conflict-acknowledgment prompting on a poisoned corpus would amplify attacker content. The headline numbers (response-quality scores vs. attack-success-rate) are not on the same scale or about the same phenomenon.

paper_a_title: RoseRAG: Robust Retrieval-augmented Generation with Small-scale LLMs via Margin-aware Preference Optimization
paper_b_title: Faithfulness-Aware Uncertainty Quantification for Fact-Checking the Output of Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Paper A (RoseRAG) targets answer-quality degradation in small LLMs caused by noisy retrieved passages, training the generator with margin-aware preference optimization and reporting Exact Match / F1 on short-form open-domain QA (HotpotQA etc.). Paper B (FRANQ) targets hallucination detection in long-form RAG outputs by post-hoc uncertainty quantification conditioned on faithfulness to the retrieved context, evaluated on a new long-form factuality/faithfulness dataset using detection-style scores. The two systems address different problems (generate better answers vs. flag unreliable claims), operate at different stages of the pipeline (training-time generator alignment vs. inference-time detection), and report incompatible metrics on different benchmarks. There is no shared task definition that would let one be ranked above the other.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both systems would need to be evaluated on the same benchmark with a shared output type and metric. For example: (a) run RoseRAG's generator under FRANQ's hallucination-detection setup with matching faithfulness/factuality annotations and a common detection metric (AUROC/PRR), or (b) measure end-task QA quality (EM/F1 or long-form factuality score) when FRANQ-based filtering/abstention is layered onto the same SLM backbone used by RoseRAG, on the same datasets and retrieval pipeline. Shared LLM size class, retriever, corpus, and prompt format would also be required.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two papers solve different problems within the RAG space: one trains a small generator to produce better short answers under noisy retrieval, while the other adds a post-hoc reliability score to long-form generations to flag likely errors. Their reported numbers come from different datasets, different output formats, and different evaluation procedures, so placing them in a single leaderboard row would invite an apples-to-oranges ranking that a practitioner could easily misread as one system being superior to the other.

paper_a_title: Redefining Retrieval Evaluation in the Era of LLMs
paper_b_title: Chunk-Distilled Language Modeling
gold_rationale: Paper A targets retrieval evaluation in RAG, introducing UDCG to better correlate ranking quality with downstream LLM answer accuracy across 5 datasets and 6 LLMs. Paper B, based on its title 'Chunk-Distilled Language Modeling,' addresses a fundamentally different problem: training or inference of language models via chunk-level distillation, presumably optimizing perplexity or generation quality rather than ranking correlation. The failure_type (misaligned IR metric vs. LM efficiency/quality), intervention_point (evaluation layer vs. model architecture/training), metric_target (correlation with answer accuracy vs. likely LM-quality measures), and action_policy (adopt new ranking metric vs. adopt new LM technique) all diverge. The two contributions live in different stages of a system pipeline and optimize different objectives, so a direct comparison is not meaningful. Paper B has no text snippet, but the title is unambiguous enough to conclude topical mismatch.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers would need to address a shared problem class (e.g., either both proposing RAG evaluation methodology, or both proposing LM/RAG generation techniques) with a common downstream benchmark, identical evaluation protocol, and overlapping baselines. Specifically, a comparable pair to Paper A would be another RAG evaluation metric measured by correlation with end-to-end answer accuracy on the same datasets and LLMs; a comparable pair to Paper B would be another language modeling or retrieval-augmented LM technique measured on perplexity or generation quality on shared corpora.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works tackle distinct problems at different layers of the stack: one redefines how to score ranked retrieval outputs for LLM consumers, while the other concerns how a language model itself is built or distilled using text chunks. They report results in incommensurable units on different tasks, so placing their headline numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would suggest a head-to-head contest that does not exist and would lead a reader to draw conclusions that the underlying experiments do not support.

paper_a_title: LI-RAGE: Late Interaction Retrieval Augmented Generation with Explicit Signals for Open-Domain Table Question Answering
paper_b_title: DSLR: Document Refinement with Sentence-Level Re-ranking and Reconstruction to Enhance Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Paper A (LI-RAGE) addresses retrieval enhancement for open-domain Table QA, where evidence consists of structured tables and the contribution operates at the retrieval stage via late interaction with explicit signals. Paper B (DSLR) addresses post-retrieval document refinement via sentence-level re-ranking and reconstruction for general (unstructured) text RAG. These differ in evidence type (tables vs. free text), pipeline stage (retrieval vs. post-retrieval filtering), and almost certainly in benchmarks/metrics (Table QA datasets like NQ-tables/OTT-QA vs. open-domain QA datasets such as NQ/TriviaQA/HotpotQA). Without snippets confirming any shared benchmark, a direct head-to-head ranking is not meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Shared evaluation conditions: (1) the same evidence modality (either both on tables or both on unstructured passages), (2) overlap in benchmark datasets and matched train/test splits, (3) the same end-task metric (e.g., EM/F1 on a single QA benchmark), (4) the same retriever-generator backbone so the contribution of the proposed component is isolated, and (5) clarity that both methods operate on the same pipeline stage or are evaluated end-to-end so stage differences do not confound the score.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works tackle different sides of RAG: one is built around searching over tables for open-domain table question answering, while the other cleans up already-retrieved passages of free text. Putting their headline numbers next to each other on a single leaderboard would likely lead a practitioner to draw the wrong conclusion, because the inputs, datasets, and pipeline roles are different enough that the scores are not really speaking about the same task.

paper_a_title: TrustRAG: Enhancing Robustness and Trustworthiness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper_b_title: SUGAR: Leveraging Contextual Confidence for Smarter Retrieval
gold_rationale: TrustRAG (A) targets adversarial corpus poisoning, presupposes an attacker who injects malicious passages, intervenes by cluster filtering plus self-assessment after retrieval, optimizes attack-resistance/robust accuracy, and always retrieves but cleanses. SUGAR (B) targets unnecessary or noisy retrieval in benign settings, presupposes a clean (but possibly irrelevant) corpus, intervenes by gating whether to retrieve at all using semantic entropy, optimizes standard QA accuracy and inference efficiency, and adaptively chooses no/single/multi-step retrieval. All five coordinates diverge, so the works are not on the same problem axis.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared benchmark would require (i) a common threat/noise model (either both evaluated under PoisonedRAG-style adversaries or both under clean adaptive-RAG QA suites such as NQ/HotpotQA), (ii) overlapping evaluation outcomes (e.g., both reporting accuracy and attack success rate, or both reporting accuracy plus retrieval-call efficiency), (iii) matched retrievers, corpora, and base LLMs, and (iv) an apples-to-apples baseline like vanilla RAG so each method's delta is measured against the same reference. Without harmonizing the threat model and outcome variables, no leaderboard ranking is meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems are solving different problems: one is a defense against attackers who plant poisoned passages in the corpus, while the other is an efficiency-oriented adaptive retrieval gate driven by the model's own uncertainty. They use different threat conditions, different evaluation goals (robustness under attack vs. QA accuracy plus call savings), and different points in the pipeline. A practitioner placing their headline numbers side-by-side on a single leaderboard would draw conclusions that have no shared basis.

paper_a_title: Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth: Revealing the Behavior of Large Language Models in Knowledge Conflicts
paper_b_title: GraphRAG under Fire
gold_rationale: Paper A is a behavioral investigation of how LLMs reconcile their parametric memory with naturally-occurring counter-memory in tool/retrieval-augmented settings, using a controlled framework to elicit memory and construct conflicting evidence, and reporting receptiveness vs. confirmation-bias rates on general LLM+RAG configurations. Paper B is an adversarial security paper that designs GRAGPOISON, a poisoning attack specifically targeting GraphRAG's graph-indexed retrieval, reporting attack success rate and poisoning-text efficiency. The threat models (benign epistemic conflict vs. malicious corpus poisoning), target systems (generic RAG vs. GraphRAG variants), evaluation outcomes (uptake/bias rates vs. ASR), and research goals (descriptive behavioral study vs. offensive method plus defense discussion) diverge across every coordinate.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared system under test (e.g., both on GraphRAG or both on vanilla RAG), a shared scenario class (either both adversarial poisoning or both benign knowledge conflict), and aligned outcome variables (e.g., both reporting how often the model adopts the external snippet over its prior, computed on matched queries). Without at least system + scenario + outcome alignment, any leaderboard placement conflates fundamentally different phenomena.
independent_rubric_rationale: Placing these two side by side would mislead a practitioner: one paper characterizes how models negotiate truthful but conflicting context in ordinary retrieval pipelines, while the other reports how an attacker can rig a graph-structured knowledge store to flip answers. The headline numbers describe entirely different phenomena on different stacks, so reading them as comparable scores would distort what each result actually says about system reliability.

paper_a_title: Adaptive Contrastive Decoding in Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Handling Noisy Contexts
paper_b_title: Know Or Not: a library for evaluating out-of-knowledge base robustness
gold_rationale: Paper A proposes a decoding-time technique (Adaptive Contrastive Decoding) targeting answer correctness in open-domain QA when retrieved context is noisy but the query is in principle answerable. Paper B is an evaluation library plus benchmark (knowornot / PolicyBench) targeting whether LLMs appropriately abstain on out-of-knowledge-base queries. The two works diverge on what counts as a failure (wrong answer under distractor context vs. answering at all when no supporting evidence exists), on the evidence regime (in-scope retrieval with noise vs. deliberately out-of-scope queries), on the locus of contribution (model decoding modification vs. evaluation tooling and benchmark), on what is scored (QA correctness vs. abstention/OOKB robustness), and on the desired model behavior (answer better vs. refuse to answer). Only the 'evidence_assumption' coordinate has any overlap, and even there the regimes differ.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head comparison would require (1) a shared task definition that includes both answerable-with-noise and unanswerable/OOKB queries, (2) a shared scoring scheme that jointly rewards correct answers and correct abstentions (e.g., a selective-QA or risk-coverage metric), (3) running Paper A's ACD inside Paper B's evaluation pipeline on PolicyBench (or running an abstention-capable variant of ACD on the same dataset), and (4) matched models, retrievers, prompts, and decoding budgets. Without these, the methods sit in disjoint evaluation frames.
independent_rubric_rationale: Dropping the headline numbers of these two works into a single leaderboard would seriously mislead a practitioner. One paper reports gains on answering open-domain questions when retrieved passages contain distractors; the other reports how well systems decline to respond when the knowledge base does not actually cover the query. A reader scanning a unified table would not see that the two systems are being judged on incompatible goals (getting the right answer vs. correctly refusing), on different datasets, and with different success criteria, and could easily conclude one is 'better' than the other when they are addressing essentially different problems.

paper_a_title: Generating Leakage-Free Benchmarks for Robust RAG Evaluation
paper_b_title: Superposition Prompting: Improving and Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Paper A (SeedRG) is a benchmark-generation pipeline that addresses knowledge leakage in RAG evaluation; its failure type is unreliable evaluation due to parametric-memory contamination, its intervention point is the benchmark/data layer, its metric targets are leakage reduction and discriminative power across RAG systems, and its deliverable is an evaluation artifact. Paper B (Superposition Prompting) is a prompting/inference-time technique aimed at improving accuracy and latency of RAG; its failure type is suboptimal RAG quality/speed, its intervention point is the prompt-construction/inference layer, its metric targets are answer quality and runtime, and its deliverable is a method to deploy. The two contributions operate at different layers of the RAG stack and report fundamentally different quantities, so a direct head-to-head ranking is not meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both works to deliver the same kind of contribution evaluated on the same axis — e.g., both being RAG methods evaluated on a shared, leakage-controlled benchmark with matched retrievers, generators, and reported under the same accuracy/latency definitions. Alternatively, Superposition Prompting could be re-evaluated on SeedRG-generated tasks alongside other RAG methods, but this still would not put the benchmark itself and the method on the same leaderboard.
independent_rubric_rationale: Paper A delivers a leakage-controlled evaluation dataset whose headline numbers describe how much contamination is removed and how clearly RAG systems can then be distinguished, while Paper B delivers a prompting/inference technique whose headline numbers describe answer quality and speed improvements over baseline RAG pipelines. These are different kinds of deliverables measured on different quantities, so a practitioner who saw their top-line scores listed together on one leaderboard would likely draw incorrect conclusions about which is 'better,' since neither is a substitute for the other.

paper_a_title: RAG-SR: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Neural Symbolic Regression
paper_b_title: HippoRAG: Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for Large Language Models
gold_rationale: judgment based on titles only since no snippets were provided. The two papers share the 'RAG' label but operate in entirely disjoint problem spaces. Paper A targets neural symbolic regression — recovering closed-form mathematical expressions fitting numerical data — using retrieval over an expression library. Paper B targets long-term memory for LLMs in knowledge-intensive QA, using a neurobiologically inspired indexing structure over text corpora. All five coordinates diverge: the failure modes addressed (poor symbolic search vs. weak multi-hop knowledge integration), the underlying evidence (regression datasets vs. text/QA corpora), the intervention point (expression generation loop vs. memory indexing and retrieval), the metric targets (regression error / expression quality vs. QA accuracy / multi-hop reasoning), and the recommended action policy each support are unrelated.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head comparison would require both systems to be evaluated on the same task family (e.g., both on symbolic regression benchmarks like SRBench, or both on multi-hop QA like MuSiQue / 2WikiMultiHopQA), under matched retrieval corpora, comparable backbone models, and a shared primary metric. Absent any common benchmark, dataset, or task definition, no leaderboard placement can be meaningfully constructed.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works tackle fundamentally different problems — discovering mathematical formulas that fit numerical data versus equipping language models with durable knowledge stores for question answering. Because they share only the surface-level 'retrieval-augmented' branding, putting their headline numbers side by side on one ranking would strongly suggest a comparability that does not exist, and a practitioner skimming such a table could easily draw unfounded conclusions about which approach is 'better'.

paper_a_title: Safeguarding RAG Pipelines with GMTP: A Gradient-based Masked Token Probability Method for Poisoned Document Detection
paper_b_title: Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
gold_rationale: Paper A (GMTP) targets adversarial corpus poisoning in RAG, defending retrieval via gradient-based masked token probability filtering, with success measured by poisoned-document detection/filtering rates and preserved retrieval quality under attack. Paper B addresses personalization of agents via editable memory graphs over user data, with success measured by personalization or response quality on benign user contexts. The two operate on disjoint problem framings (security vs. personalization), assume different threat/data conditions (adversarial injections vs. trusted user memory), modify different pipeline stages (pre-retrieval filtering vs. memory-graph construction/editing), optimize incomparable metrics, and produce different system behaviors. Note: Paper B snippet is unavailable, but the title is unambiguous enough about scope to support an invalid verdict rather than underspecified.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared task and evaluation setting where both methods are run on the same RAG benchmark under the same conditions, with a common metric of interest. For example, evaluating GMTP and the memory-graph personalization system on identical poisoned-corpus benchmarks with end-task accuracy under attack, or on identical personalization benchmarks with and without injected adversarial documents. Without such overlap in problem definition, threat model, evaluation corpus, and headline metric, any side-by-side ranking would be meaningless.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems address fundamentally different goals on different data regimes: one protects retrieval against adversarial injections, the other tailors agent responses to a user's editable memory. Their headline numbers come from incompatible benchmarks and score different things, so placing them next to each other on a single leaderboard would lead a practitioner to draw conclusions about relative quality that the underlying experiments do not support.

paper_a_title: Seeing through the Conflict: Transparent Knowledge Conflict Handling in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper_b_title: Cordon-MAS: Defending RAG against Knowledge Poisoning via Information-Flow Control
gold_rationale: Paper A (TCR) targets naturally occurring knowledge conflicts between parametric memory and benign-but-inconsistent retrieved evidence, with a soft-prompt signal injected into a single generator and headline numbers in conflict-detection F1 (+5–18), knowledge-gap recovery (+21.4 pp), and misleading-context override reduction (−29.3 pp) across seven QA-style benchmarks. Paper B (Cordon-MAS) targets adversarial Confundo-style poisoning under an attacker threat model, with an architectural multi-agent compartmentalization that forbids the synthesizer from ever reading raw untrusted text, evaluated by attack success rate reduction (−92.4%) on five BEIR datasets. The threat models, problem definitions, scoring quantities, and structural changes to the RAG pipeline differ on all five coordinates, so the two results are not on a shared axis.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared benchmark in which both natural conflicts and Confundo-style poisoned passages appear in the retrieved set, plus a common evaluation suite reporting both clean-task quality (e.g., conflict-resolved accuracy, knowledge-gap recovery) and adversarial ASR under matched retriever, corpus, attacker budget, and base LLM. Both systems would need to be run end-to-end in the same harness with identical inputs and the same set of outcome scores, including overhead/latency, before any ranking could be drawn.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems are solving different problems on different test beds with different scoring quantities: one reports how well a generator reconciles ordinary contradictions between memory and retrieved text, while the other reports how often an attacker-crafted document still steers the final answer. Putting a ‘−29.3 pp override’ number next to a ‘−92.4% attack success rate’ number on a single leaderboard would invite a practitioner to read one as ‘better’ than the other, when in fact neither result speaks to the scenario the other addresses, and a system that wins on one column could easily lose badly on the other.

paper_a_title: Robust Fine-tuning for Retrieval Augmented Generation against Retrieval Defects.
paper_b_title: SeRTS: Self-Rewarding Tree Search for Biomedical Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Based on titles alone (no snippets provided), Paper A targets a robustness failure mode (defective/noisy retrieved passages) and intervenes via train-time robust fine-tuning of the generator, with an action policy of producing answers more tolerant to corrupted evidence on general RAG benchmarks. Paper B targets a retrieval-quality failure mode in the biomedical domain and intervenes at inference time via a self-rewarding tree search procedure, with an action policy of iteratively exploring retrieval paths to improve biomedical QA metrics. The intervention_point differs (training vs. inference search), the failure_type differs (defect tolerance vs. better retrieval discovery), metric_target likely differs (general RAG vs. biomedical-specific benchmarks), and the action policies are fundamentally different (parameter update vs. test-time search). Evidence_assumption is also likely different (assume noisy retrieval given vs. assume retrieval can be improved by search).
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both works would need to be evaluated on overlapping benchmarks within the same domain (e.g., both on biomedical RAG or both on a shared general QA suite), use comparable base models and retrievers, and either be reframed as solving the same problem (e.g., both reported under a retrieval-noise robustness protocol or both under a retrieval-improvement protocol) with matched compute budgets so that train-time vs. test-time gains can be normalized.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works tackle different slices of retrieval augmented generation: one adjusts the generator during training to tolerate flawed retrieved passages across general settings, while the other adds a self-rewarding search loop at answering time for biomedical question answering. Putting their headline scores on one leaderboard would hide differences in domain, evaluation setup, and where the improvement is produced, so a practitioner could easily pick the wrong system for their actual use case.

paper_a_title: Detecting Hallucination and Coverage Errors in Retrieval Augmented Generation for Controversial Topics
paper_b_title: Magic Mushroom: A Customizable Benchmark for Fine-grained Analysis of Retrieval Noise Erosion in RAG Systems
gold_rationale: Paper A (per title) targets detection of hallucination and coverage errors in RAG outputs specifically for controversial topics — a classification/detection task over generated responses. Paper B is a benchmark that stress-tests end-to-end RAG generation under four categories of synthetically configured retrieval noise (single- and multi-hop QA), reporting generator and denoising-strategy performance dynamics. The failure modes (post-hoc error detection vs. noise-induced answer degradation), evidence regimes (curated controversial-topic retrievals vs. configurable noisy contexts), targets of measurement (detector quality vs. answer quality under noise), and operational responses (flag/abstain vs. denoise/generate) differ substantially. Paper A's text snippet is unavailable, which limits certainty but the title-level scope mismatch is clear.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both works would need to (1) share a task formulation (either error detection on the same generated outputs, or answer quality on the same QA set under matched retrieval conditions), (2) use overlapping datasets including the controversial-topic distribution and/or Magic Mushroom noise configurations, (3) report a common scoring criterion (e.g., detection F1, or answer correctness under identical noise mixtures), and (4) align on generator models and retrieval pipelines so the leaderboard entry reflects the same underlying system behavior.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two studies pursue different questions on different inputs: one (paper A, judging from its title) is about spotting wrong or unsupported statements in answers to politically contentious questions, while the other builds a stress-test corpus of plausible-looking but misleading retrieved passages and reports how well generators and denoisers cope as noise grows. Putting their headline numbers in a single ranked table would suggest a head-to-head comparison that does not exist; a practitioner could easily draw the wrong conclusion about which system is 'better' for RAG reliability.

paper_a_title: Retrieval augmented text-to-SQL generation for epidemiological question answering using electronic health records
paper_b_title: Neuro-RIT: Neuron-Guided Instruction Tuning for Robust Retrieval-Augmented Language Model
gold_rationale: Paper A targets text-to-SQL generation over electronic health record databases for epidemiological questions, where the failure mode is producing incorrect SQL against a structured EHR schema and the evidence source is database-grounded clinical data with retrieved exemplars. Paper B targets open-domain QA where the generator LLM degrades under noisy/irrelevant passages, the evidence is unstructured retrieved text, the intervention is neuron-level instruction tuning of the generator, and the metric is QA accuracy under noise. The failure being mitigated, the form of evidence, the locus of modification (retrieval augmentation pipeline vs. neuron-targeted tuning), the evaluation target (executable SQL/answer correctness on EHR vs. textual QA accuracy under perturbed contexts), and the deployment recipe all diverge. No shared benchmark or output format exists to align them.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared task formulation (e.g., both producing SQL on EHR or both doing open-domain text QA), evaluation on a common benchmark with the same retrieval setup and noise conditions, identical metrics (execution accuracy or exact-match/F1 under the same perturbation protocol), and matched base LLMs so that the contribution of retrieval-augmentation vs. neuron-guided tuning could be isolated on equivalent inputs.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems solve essentially different problems: one generates database queries over clinical records for epidemiology, while the other improves open-domain question answering robustness to noisy passages. They use different inputs, different output formats, different domains, and different evaluation suites, so juxtaposing their headline numbers on a single leaderboard would give a practitioner a false sense that one approach is 'better' than the other when they are not addressing the same need.

paper_a_title: PR-Attack: Coordinated Prompt-RAG Attacks on Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Large Language Models via Bilevel Optimization
paper_b_title: Retrieval Augmented Generation or Long-Context LLMs? A Comprehensive Study and Hybrid Approach
gold_rationale: Paper A studies adversarial security of RAG, proposing a bilevel-optimization attack that injects poisoned texts plus a backdoor trigger, reporting attack success rate and stealth under an adversarial threat model. Paper B is a benign efficiency/quality study contrasting RAG with long-context LLMs and proposing a hybrid routing scheme, reporting QA quality and cost trade-offs on standard benchmarks. The two works diverge on every coordinate: the failure being addressed (knowledge-base poisoning vs. choosing between RAG and long-context), the evidentiary setting (adversary-controlled corpus vs. clean benchmark corpora), where the change is applied (prompt+corpus injection vs. system-level architecture choice), the outcome being optimized (ASR/stealth vs. QA accuracy/cost), and the downstream guidance (defender awareness vs. deployment architecture selection). No common axis exists on which their headline numbers could be ranked.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would need both papers to operate in the same regime: either (a) both evaluating defense/attack robustness of RAG vs. long-context architectures under a shared adversarial protocol with attack success rate and clean-task utility, or (b) both evaluating clean-task QA quality and cost on identical datasets, retrievers, and models. Minimally, they must share threat model, evaluation corpora, and the dependent variable being reported.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two headline results describe different worlds: one quantifies how often an attacker can hijack outputs by tampering with the knowledge store, the other quantifies answer quality and serving cost between two clean architectural choices. A reader scanning a single leaderboard with both numbers would conflate a security-threat score with a quality/efficiency score and reach unfounded conclusions about which system is 'better.'

paper_a_title: Beyond Black-Box Interventions: Latent Probing for Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper_b_title: FlippedRAG: Black-Box Opinion Manipulation Adversarial Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation Models
gold_rationale: The two papers diverge on every coordinate of the coding frame. Paper A addresses contextual unfaithfulness (the LLM generating responses inconsistent with retrieved evidence), assumes a benign-but-noisy or knowledge-conflicting corpus, intervenes inside the LLM via latent probing and attention-head modulation (a white-box defensive method), and is evaluated on accuracy and faithfulness metrics for QA. Paper B addresses an adversarial security vulnerability (opinion manipulation), assumes an attacker who can inject poisoned documents into the retrieval corpus, intervenes at the corpus/retrieval level via transfer attacks from a surrogate retriever (a black-box offensive method), and is evaluated on attack success rate, opinion polarity shift, and user cognition shift on controversial topics. They solve different problems with opposite framings (defense vs. attack), so no headline number from one maps onto the other.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both papers to target the same problem (e.g., both improving RAG robustness, or both attacking RAG), share an evaluation setup (same datasets, same threat or noise model, same retriever/generator stack), report a shared primary outcome (e.g., faithfulness/accuracy under a defined corruption, or attack success rate under a defined adversary), and operate at comparable access levels (both white-box or both black-box, or carefully bridged via ablation). At minimum a defensive method like ProbeRAG would need to be evaluated against a poisoning attack like FlippedRAG (or vice versa) on overlapping benchmarks and metrics.
independent_rubric_rationale: Putting these two head-line results in a single leaderboard would seriously mislead a practitioner. One paper reports gains in answer accuracy and trustworthiness when retrieved passages are noisy or conflict with the model's prior knowledge; the other reports how much an adversary can shift opinion polarity by poisoning the document store of a black-box system. The headline numbers are denominated in incompatible currencies and reflect opposing goals (making a system better for users versus making a system worse for users), so any ranking between them would convey a false equivalence.

paper_a_title: Chunk-Distilled Language Modeling
paper_b_title: Over-Searching in Search-Augmented Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Paper A (Chunk-Distilled Language Modeling) addresses general language modeling quality via a training-time chunk distillation method (judged from title only — no snippet supplied). Paper B is a systematic evaluation of over-searching behavior in search-augmented LLMs at inference time, introducing the Tokens-Per-Correctness metric and the OverSearchQA benchmark. The two papers target distinct failure types (LM generation/perplexity quality vs. unnecessary tool invocation), report on different evaluation targets (likely modeling quality vs. TPC/accuracy/abstention), intervene at different stages (training/distillation vs. inference-time tool decisions and retrieval composition), and propose different policy levers. Confidence is limited because Paper A's snippet was unavailable.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers would need to (a) target the same task family — for example, knowledge-intensive QA with optional retrieval; (b) report results on overlapping benchmarks; (c) use commensurate evaluation measures, such as accuracy plus a comparable efficiency or cost measure; (d) operate at a shared point in the pipeline (both training-time, or both inference-time); and (e) be framed against the same problem definition (e.g., both attempting to reduce unnecessary retrieval, or both attempting to improve LM quality with chunk-based augmentation).
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works address different research questions in different parts of the LLM pipeline. Paper A appears to be about improving language generation quality through a chunk-based distillation training scheme, while Paper B is a behavioral study of when retrieval-augmented systems invoke external search tools too often, accompanied by a new benchmark and a cost-aware scoring scheme. They are evaluated on different tasks under different criteria, so combining their headline numbers on a single leaderboard would suggest a comparison that does not actually exist and would mislead a practitioner about which system is better for any concrete deployment choice.

paper_a_title: Multilingual Retrieval Augmented Generation for Culturally-Sensitive Tasks: A Benchmark for Cross-lingual Robustness
paper_b_title: Robust Fine-tuning for Retrieval Augmented Generation against Retrieval Defects.
gold_rationale: Based on titles alone (no snippets provided), Paper A is a benchmark contribution targeting cross-lingual robustness on culturally-sensitive queries in multilingual RAG, while Paper B is a fine-tuning method targeting robustness to retrieval defects (likely noisy, irrelevant, or counterfactual passages) in a generic, presumably monolingual RAG setting. The failure modes being characterized differ (cultural/language drift vs. corrupted retrieval), the evidence regimes differ (multilingual corpora across cultures vs. perturbed retrieval pools), the intervention points differ (none/evaluation-only vs. generator fine-tuning), the measured outcomes differ (cross-lingual cultural fidelity vs. defect-resilient answer quality), and the deliverables differ (a dataset/benchmark vs. a trained model recipe). None of the five coordinates align well enough to support a head-to-head ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both works to (a) target the same robustness phenomenon (e.g., either retrieval-noise resilience or cross-lingual cultural fidelity), (b) evaluate on overlapping benchmarks and languages with comparable retrieval pipelines and base generators, (c) report the same primary outcome on the same task, and (d) provide either a directly applicable mitigation method (so the benchmark paper would need a method) or shared evaluation of the method on the cultural benchmark. Without one of these bridges, ranking them on a single leaderboard is not meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works tackle different problems in the RAG space: one studies how systems behave across languages and cultural contexts and offers a dataset to probe that, while the other proposes a training recipe to make a generator more tolerant of degraded retrieved passages in a generic setting. If a practitioner saw a single combined ranking, they would likely infer that the two systems were solving the same problem and pick a 'winner' on numbers that were never produced under comparable conditions, leading to a poor choice for either use case.

paper_a_title: Unified Generative and Discriminative Training for Multi-modal Large Language Models
paper_b_title: Accelerating Inference of Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Sparse Context Selection
gold_rationale: Based on titles alone (no snippets provided), the two works target fundamentally different problem settings. Paper A concerns a training-time unification of generative and discriminative objectives for multi-modal LLMs, presumably evaluated on vision-language benchmarks. Paper B concerns inference-time acceleration of retrieval-augmented generation via sparse context selection, presumably evaluated on RAG QA benchmarks with latency/throughput as primary outcomes. The five coordinates diverge: the problem being addressed (multi-modal capability gap vs. RAG inference cost), the empirical evidence base (MLLM benchmarks vs. RAG corpora), where the change is made (training procedure vs. inference-time context pruning), what is being optimized (task accuracy across modalities vs. speed/efficiency at iso-quality), and the deployment scenario the recommendation supports.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A meaningful side-by-side comparison would require both works to address the same problem class (e.g., both proposing inference-time efficiency techniques for the same model family on overlapping benchmarks, or both proposing training schemes evaluated on shared multi-modal tasks), use compatible evaluation suites with shared baselines, and report outcomes on the same primary axes (e.g., quality at matched compute, or speedup at matched accuracy). None of these conditions appear satisfied here.
independent_rubric_rationale: If a practitioner saw the headline numbers from these two papers placed on a single leaderboard, they would likely draw incorrect conclusions, because the works solve unrelated problems on different data with different success criteria. One concerns how a multi-modal model is taught to handle both producing and discriminating content; the other concerns how to make a retrieval-based pipeline faster at serving time. Ranking them together has no operational meaning for a downstream user choosing between them.

paper_a_title: CPA-RAG: Covert Poisoning Attacks on Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Large Language Models
paper_b_title: Divide-Then-Align: Honest Alignment based on the Knowledge Boundary of RAG
gold_rationale: Paper A is an offensive security study proposing a black-box adversarial framework (CPA-RAG) that poisons the retrieval corpus to induce target answers, evaluated by Attack Success Rate. Paper B is a defensive alignment study (DTA) that post-trains the LLM with DPO across four knowledge-boundary quadrants so the system can abstain with 'I don't know,' evaluated by accuracy plus appropriate abstention. The two works diverge on every coordinate: the problem they treat (corpus-poisoning vulnerability vs. hallucination under knowledge-boundary uncertainty), what they assume about evidence (corpus can be injected with crafted texts vs. retrievals may be noisy/absent), where the change is applied (external knowledge base vs. model weights via preference optimization), what is being scored (ASR for adversarial success vs. honesty-aware QA quality), and the orientation of the work (attack feasibility vs. trustworthiness improvement). There is no shared task, dataset use, or scoring axis that would let one rank or compare them directly.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A meaningful comparison would require both papers to address a common task with a shared evaluation protocol—for example, evaluating DTA's abstention behavior under CPA-RAG-style poisoned corpora on the same datasets, using paired scores such as ASR plus correct-abstention rate. Without overlapping benchmarks, threat models, and unified scoring (e.g., honest-answer rate on clean queries and refusal-or-correctness rate on poisoned queries), the two systems target disjoint problems and cannot be placed on the same leaderboard.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works pursue opposite goals on different evaluation dimensions: one reports how often crafted documents can flip RAG answers to an adversary-chosen target, while the other reports how well a fine-tuned model balances correct answers with appropriate 'I don't know' responses. Placing their headline numbers side by side on one leaderboard would invite practitioners to read them as comparable scores when in fact they measure unrelated phenomena, with no shared task, dataset slice, or scoring convention. A reader could easily mistake a high score in one for a stronger system than the other, which would be a serious misreading.

paper_a_title: Cutting Off the Head Ends the Conflict: A Mechanism for Interpreting and Mitigating Knowledge Conflicts in Language Models
paper_b_title: A Few Words Can Distort Graphs: Knowledge Poisoning Attacks on Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Paper A studies knowledge conflicts between parametric memory and retrieved context in standard LLMs, proposing a defensive mechanism (PH3) that prunes attention heads to control whether the model favors memory or context, measured by controllability deltas (+44.0% / +38.5%) and open-domain QA. Paper B studies adversarial knowledge poisoning on GraphRAG, proposing two attack algorithms (TKPA, UKPA) operating on the source text used during graph construction, measured by attack success rate (93.1%) and QA degradation (95% to 50%). The failure modes (benign conflict vs. adversarial poisoning), the locus of operation (internal attention heads vs. external corpus text), the metric semantics (defensive control gain vs. offensive degradation), and the stance (mitigation vs. attack) are all incommensurate. Even the evidence assumption differs: Paper A treats both memory and context as potentially correct sources to be balanced, while Paper B treats the corpus as untrusted and manipulable. There is no shared task, model family pipeline (GraphRAG vs. standard RAG/LLM), or benchmark on which a head-to-head numeric comparison would be meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both papers to operate on the same system (e.g., both on GraphRAG or both on standard RAG), share the same threat or task model (both defensive or both offensive, evaluated under a common adversary or conflict generation protocol), use the same QA benchmark with identical retrieval setup and base LLM, and report a commensurable headline number (e.g., post-defense accuracy under poisoning, or attack success rate against a defended system). Ideally one paper's method would be applied as a defense against the other's attack, or both would be evaluated on a shared knowledge-conflict benchmark with matched baselines.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works tackle entirely different problems on different system types: one is about steering an LLM's preference between its own memory and a passage it was given, while the other is about adversaries rewriting source text to corrupt a knowledge graph used by GraphRAG. Their headline numbers describe opposite goals (defending and balancing vs. breaking) on different pipelines and datasets, so placing 44%/38.5% next to 93.1%/50% on a single leaderboard would lead a practitioner to draw conclusions the experiments do not support.

paper_a_title: FiD-Light: Efficient and Effective Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
paper_b_title: SURE-RAG: Sufficiency and Uncertainty-Aware Evidence Verification for Selective Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Paper A (FiD-Light) targets efficient retrieval-augmented text generation, modifying the FiD decoder to trade compute for generation quality (no snippet available, but title and venue make the scope clear). Paper B (SURE-RAG) targets evidence sufficiency verification with a three-way SUPPORTED/REFUTED/INSUFFICIENT decision and selective answering, evaluated as Macro-F1 and risk-at-coverage on HotpotQA-RAG v3 against DeBERTa pooling, a GPT-4o judge, and a concat cross-encoder. The two works address different failure modes (decoder cost vs unverified support), operate at different pipeline stages (generation vs post-retrieval verification), optimize different metric targets (efficiency plus QA quality vs Macro-F1 with abstention), and adopt incompatible answering policies (always answer vs answer-or-abstain). The evidence assumptions also diverge: A treats retrieved passages as usable input, B treats them as possibly insufficient or conflicting.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers would need to share a problem framing (e.g., both selective RAG answering with abstention, or both efficient RAG generation), the same datasets and splits, the same primary metric defined the same way, and matched decision policies (both forced-answer or both selective with the same coverage). Without that alignment, headline numbers from the two systems describe different tasks and cannot be ranked on one leaderboard.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems pursue different goals: one improves the speed-quality balance of a generation pipeline, while the other decides whether retrieved passages justify answering or warrant staying silent. Their headline numbers describe different tasks, different datasets, and different decision spaces, so a side-by-side leaderboard would give a practitioner the wrong impression that the two compete on the same problem.

paper_a_title: The LiveRAG Challenge at SIGIR 2025
paper_b_title: Multi-Hop Paragraph Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
gold_rationale: Paper A is a venue/challenge overview describing the LiveRAG competition at SIGIR 2025, which centers on end-to-end retrieval-augmented generation over a designated live corpus and reports community competition outcomes across multiple participating teams. Paper B is a 2019 single-system methods paper proposing a specific recurrent multi-hop paragraph retriever evaluated on open-domain QA benchmarks (e.g., HotpotQA-style multi-hop retrieval). The two operate on different tasks (full RAG generation vs. retrieval-only), different corpora and time horizons (live 2025 web/Fineweb-style data vs. static 2019 Wikipedia-style corpora), different evaluation paradigms (multi-team leaderboard for generation quality vs. retrieval recall/precision), and different document genres (event overview vs. method contribution). No text snippets were supplied, but the title-level signals are strong enough to conclude direct comparison is not meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both works would need to address the same task definition (either retrieval-only or end-to-end RAG), share an aligned corpus and query set, use the same scoring protocol (e.g., Recall@k for retrieval, or answer correctness/faithfulness for RAG), and report a single comparable system-level result. A challenge overview paper would have to be replaced by results from one specific participating system, and that system would need to have been evaluated on a benchmark overlapping Paper B's setting (multi-hop open-domain QA).
independent_rubric_rationale: Putting a community competition summary next to a single-model retrieval proposal on one leaderboard would mislead a practitioner. The two works tackle different problems (end-to-end generation with retrieved context vs. paragraph retrieval for multi-hop questions), rely on different corpora separated by six years, and play different roles in the literature—one reports aggregate outcomes from many teams under a 2025 live-data setup, the other reports a single 2019 model on standard multi-hop QA test sets. Any side-by-side ranking would conflate these distinct setups.

paper_a_title: Backdoored Retrievers for Prompt Injection Attacks on Retrieval Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
paper_b_title: Defense Against Prompt Injection Attack by Leveraging Attack Techniques
gold_rationale: Paper A is an offensive contribution that introduces corpus poisoning and a novel backdoor against the dense retriever's fine-tuning, reporting attack success rates for harmful-link insertion, unauthorized-service promotion, and denial-of-service prompts. Paper B is a defensive contribution that repurposes training-free prompt-injection attack templates at the LLM inference layer to reduce attack success rate against an already-injected prompt. The two works sit on opposite sides of the threat model (attacker vs. defender), modify different components (retriever fine-tuning/corpus vs. LLM prompt wrapping), and their headline numbers move in opposite directions (higher ASR is the goal in A, lower ASR in B). No common axis exists to rank them.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (i) both papers report defense effectiveness against the same indirect prompt-injection attacks on RAG under identical retriever/LLM stacks, datasets, and ASR definition, or (ii) both papers report attack effectiveness against a shared, undefended RAG baseline using the same corpus, queries, and injection goals. Additionally, the locus of modification (retriever fine-tuning vs. LLM prompt-time defense) and the assumed attacker capabilities (data-supply-chain access vs. content-only injection) would need to be matched or explicitly bridged.
independent_rubric_rationale: Placing these two headline results on one leaderboard would mislead a practitioner. One paper's number reports how often a tampered retrieval component can be made to surface attacker-chosen content, while the other's number reports how often a wrapping technique around the language model suppresses unwanted behavior once content has already been injected. The two numbers concern different stages of the pipeline, rely on different threat setups, and move in opposite preferred directions, so a side-by-side ranking would not reflect any real performance comparison.

paper_a_title: ADMIT: Few-shot Knowledge Poisoning Attacks on RAG-based Fact Checking
paper_b_title: Hidden-in-Plain-Text: A Benchmark for Social-Web Indirect Prompt Injection in RAG
gold_rationale: Paper A (ADMIT) is an offensive few-shot poisoning technique evaluated on RAG-based fact-checking pipelines, measuring attack success rate (ASR) for flipping verdicts when authentic supporting/refuting evidence dominates the retrieval pool. Paper B (OpenRAG-Soc) is a defensive benchmark for social-web indirect prompt injection and retrieval poisoning, with web-native carriers (HTML/Markdown/Unicode) and built-in mitigations, reporting rank shifts, utility, and latency. The two diverge on essentially every coordinate: the failure mode (verdict flipping in fact-checking vs. instruction injection through web carriers), evidence assumption (credible curated evidence pool vs. user-generated social web content), intervention point (semantically aligned injected documents vs. carrier-based injection plus sanitization defenses), reported metrics (ASR vs. rank shifts/utility/latency), and stance (attack-only vs. attack-plus-defense benchmark).
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both works would need to evaluate on a shared corpus and threat model — for example, applying ADMIT-style injected documents to the OpenRAG-Soc harness, or running OpenRAG-Soc's IPI carriers against the fact-checking benchmarks ADMIT uses — and report a common metric (e.g., ASR under identical retriever/LLM stacks, with and without the same defenses). Without aligning the task (fact-checking verdict vs. generation under IPI), the corpus, the retriever/LLM stack, and the metric, the two headline numbers cannot be placed on one axis.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works address quite different slices of RAG security. The first develops an offensive technique aimed at verdict-style truthfulness pipelines and reports an aggregate success percentage on credibility-oriented corpora. The second is a reproducible web-facing benchmark with sanitization defenses, reporting ranking changes, utility, and latency on a social corpus. Their headline numbers come from incompatible setups, threat scenarios, and scoring harnesses, so dropping them into a single leaderboard would give a practitioner a false sense of which approach is stronger or more dangerous.

paper_a_title: ProGRank: Probe-Gradient Reranking to Defend Dense-Retriever RAG from Corpus Poisoning
paper_b_title: On the Vulnerability of Applying Retrieval-Augmented Generation within Knowledge-Intensive Application Domains
gold_rationale: Both papers address the same failure_type — corpus poisoning of dense-retriever RAG — and both intervene at the retriever side, so the topic overlaps substantially. However, the intervention mechanisms diverge: Paper A is a probe-gradient reranker that reorders Top-K passages while preserving content, whereas Paper B is a detection-based filter triggered by embedding-deviation patterns. The metric_target also differs: Paper A reports defense strength plus a robustness–utility trade-off across three datasets, three retriever backbones, and several attack families, while Paper B reports detection rates on 225 setup combinations focused largely on medical Q&A and a universal-poisoning threat. The action_policy (rerank vs. detect-and-remove) and the evidence_assumption about attacker scope (broad attack families incl. trigger-based and adaptive vs. universal poisoning with targeted-information payloads) are not aligned. These coordinate mismatches make any single-number leaderboard placement only partially meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Shared benchmark corpora and retriever backbones; a common threat model expressing both universal-poisoning and the broader attack families (PoisonedRAG, GASLITE, trigger-based, misleading-evidence); a unified evaluation protocol that reports both end-to-end attack success rate after defense and detection precision/recall on the same poisoned/clean splits; matched Top-K and generator configurations; and consistent clean-query utility reporting so robustness–utility trade-offs can be compared head-to-head.
independent_rubric_rationale: Both works tackle defending RAG pipelines against attacker-injected passages and both modify the retrieval stage, so they sit in the same general space. But one reorders retrieved passages using gradient-based stress tests while the other flags and removes suspicious documents using embedding-pattern detectors, and they report fundamentally different headline numbers (defense strength plus clean-query utility across many attack families vs. detection rates concentrated on medical-domain universal poisoning). A practitioner reading a leaderboard that lined up their top reported numbers side-by-side would get a partly misleading picture of which one is actually stronger for their deployment, because the underlying tasks, attacker scopes, and success scores are not on the same scale.

paper_a_title: Defending against Indirect Prompt Injection by Instruction Detection
paper_b_title: A Few Words Can Distort Graphs: Knowledge Poisoning Attacks on Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Paper A is a defense paper proposing InstructDetector for Indirect Prompt Injection on standard RAG, evaluated on BIPIA with detection accuracy (99.60%/96.90%) and reduced ASR (0.03%). Paper B is an attack paper proposing two knowledge poisoning attacks (TKPA, UKPA) against GraphRAG's LLM-driven graph construction step, reporting attack success rate (93.1%) and QA accuracy collapse (95%->50%). The papers differ on every coordinate: defense vs. attack role, IPI document-level injection vs. graph-extraction poisoning, standard RAG vs. GraphRAG architecture, document filtering vs. source-text rewriting, and defender-favoring vs. attacker-favoring metrics. Neither shares a benchmark, threat model, or pipeline, and there is no common quantity to rank.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both works would need to share (1) the same RAG variant (either standard RAG or GraphRAG, not one of each), (2) the same role on the attack-defense axis, (3) a common threat model and corpus, and (4) a shared evaluation metric such as ASR under matched attacks on matched models. At minimum, a comparison would require pairing Paper A's defense against Paper B's attacks on GraphRAG, or pairing Paper B's attacks against a GraphRAG-targeted defense baseline.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper builds a protective tool that filters injected text from a standard retrieval pipeline, while the other crafts a new offensive technique that subtly rewrites source text to corrupt graph-structured retrieval pipelines. Their headline numbers describe opposite goals on different underlying systems with no shared benchmark, so a practitioner reading them on one leaderboard would draw seriously wrong conclusions about which approach 'wins' or even what is being measured.

paper_a_title: Decide Then Retrieve: A Training-Free Framework with Uncertainty-Guided Triggering and Dual-Path Retrieval
paper_b_title: Know Or Not: a library for evaluating out-of-knowledge base robustness
gold_rationale: Paper A proposes DTR, a training-free RAG method that uses generation uncertainty to gate retrieval and a dual-path retrieval mechanism, evaluated on five open-domain QA benchmarks with EM and F1 against standard RAG baselines. Paper B presents knowornot, a library/methodology for evaluating out-of-knowledge-base (OOKB) robustness — i.e., whether LLMs abstain on queries outside the knowledge base — and demonstrates it via the PolicyBench benchmark. The failure_type differs (retrieval noise / sparse query handling vs. hallucination on OOKB queries / abstention behavior). The intervention_point differs (a new RAG pipeline vs. an evaluation framework/library). The metric_target differs (EM/F1 on open-domain QA vs. OOKB robustness / abstention rates on domain-specific QA chatbots). The action_policy differs (adaptive retrieval triggering and evidence selection vs. systematic synthetic-question generation and judging pipeline). The evidence_assumption also diverges (general open-domain corpora vs. closed domain-specific knowledge bases with explicit out-of-scope partitions). No shared dataset, baseline, or scoring scheme overlaps.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A meaningful comparison would require both works to target the same problem on a shared benchmark with comparable scoring — for example, running DTR's selective-retrieval pipeline through knowornot's OOKB evaluation on PolicyBench (measuring abstention behavior), or, conversely, having Paper B report EM/F1 on the same open-domain QA datasets DTR uses. At minimum, an overlapping benchmark, identical generator models, and a common evaluation protocol (either QA accuracy or abstention/OOKB robustness scored the same way) would be needed before placing results side-by-side.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two papers tackle fundamentally different problems with non-overlapping evaluation regimes. Paper A reports exact-match and F1 gains on open-domain QA from a new adaptive RAG pipeline, while Paper B contributes an evaluation library and a policy-domain benchmark focused on whether models correctly decline to answer when the knowledge base lacks support. A practitioner viewing these headline numbers on one leaderboard would conflate accuracy improvements on standard QA with abstention/robustness behavior on out-of-scope queries, drawing conclusions neither paper supports.

paper_a_title: Over-Searching in Search-Augmented Large Language Models
paper_b_title: QuCo-RAG: Quantifying Uncertainty from the Pre-training Corpus for Dynamic Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Paper A studies over-searching: search-augmented LLMs invoking retrieval when they should answer from parametric knowledge or abstain on unanswerable queries; it proposes Tokens-Per-Correctness on the new OverSearchQA benchmark and explores query/retrieval-level mitigations to suppress unnecessary search and improve abstention. Paper B studies the orthogonal/opposite issue in dynamic RAG: ill-calibrated internal-confidence triggers that miss needed retrievals, and replaces them with Infini-gram corpus-frequency and entity co-occurrence signals, reporting EM gains on multi-hop QA. The two works define different failure conditions, evaluate on different datasets, and report incompatible headline numbers (TPC/abstention vs. EM). No shared trigger-decision evaluation exists to align them.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation setting with (i) a common pool of both answerable and unanswerable queries, (ii) a unified retrieval-trigger policy comparison (when retrieval is invoked, when withheld, when abstention is chosen), (iii) the same backbone models and retriever, and (iv) joint reporting of both correctness/abstention quality and cost-efficiency (e.g., TPC plus EM/F1) so each system's trigger decisions are scored under identical conditions.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works examine quite different problems in retrieval-augmented generation. One looks at unnecessary tool invocations and how models behave on questions they should refuse to answer, reporting a cost-versus-correctness ratio on a new benchmark centered on abstention. The other targets better timing of when to pull in evidence during multi-hop generation, reporting exact-match gains on standard multi-hop QA. Placing their headline numbers side by side on one leaderboard would imply a head-to-head ranking that the experiments do not support, because the test sets, scoring schemes, and target behaviors differ substantially, and a practitioner would likely draw the wrong conclusion about which approach is 'better.'

paper_a_title: When to Trust: A Causality-Aware Calibration Framework for Accurate Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation.
paper_b_title: GRACE: Reinforcement Learning for Grounded Response and Abstention under Contextual Evidence
gold_rationale: Paper A snippet is unavailable, but its title clearly scopes the work to Knowledge-Graph RAG with a causality-aware calibration framework for deciding when to trust retrieved KG facts. Paper B targets generic text RAG and uses reinforcement learning with a multi-stage gated reward to jointly train grounded answering and abstention, with data constructed from heterogeneous retrievers. The evidence_assumption differs (structured KG triples vs unstructured retrieved passages from heterogeneous retrievers). The intervention_point differs (post-hoc/inference-time calibration vs RL fine-tuning of the generator). The metric_target differs (calibration/trust accuracy on KG-RAG vs overall accuracy plus answer-vs-abstain balance on QA benchmarks B reports). The action_policy differs (trust/no-trust gating over KG-derived answers vs evidence-extraction-then-answer-or-IDK). Even granting that both touch the 'reliability of RAG' theme, the underlying tasks, training regimes, and likely benchmark suites do not line up.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Shared retrieval substrate (both KG-RAG or both passage-RAG, or an explicit cross-modality protocol), evaluation on a common benchmark suite with identical splits, a shared definition and metric for abstention/trust (e.g., selective accuracy, coverage-risk curves, calibration error), and matched base LLMs and inference budgets. Without aligning these, headline numbers from each paper measure different constructs.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems operate over different kinds of retrieved knowledge (a structured graph versus general retrieved passages) and are trained or adjusted in very different ways, so their reported headline numbers almost certainly come from different test suites and reflect different notions of 'reliability.' A practitioner skimming a combined leaderboard would likely draw an unwarranted ordering between them and pick the wrong tool for their deployment setting.

paper_a_title: Reliable Decision‑Making via Calibration‑Oriented Retrieval‑Augmented Generation
paper_b_title: Sufficient Context: A New Lens on Retrieval Augmented Generation Systems
gold_rationale: Paper A provides only a title ('Reliable Decision-Making via Calibration-Oriented Retrieval-Augmented Generation') with no text snippet available. While the title suggests a calibration-focused RAG approach that might thematically overlap with Paper B's selective generation / abstention framework, none of the five coordinates can be verified for Paper A: the targeted error mode, the framing of retrieved evidence, where in the pipeline the change is made, the headline numeric target, and the downstream policy (e.g., abstain vs. answer) are all unknown. Paper B is well-specified: it introduces a sufficient-context classifier, evaluates Gemini/GPT/Claude/Mistral/Gemma on QA datasets, and reports a 2–10% improvement in the fraction of correct answers among responded queries via a guided-abstention selective generation method. Without Paper A's details, a principled judgment of comparability cannot be reached, so a conservative 'underspecified' verdict is warranted.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Access to Paper A's abstract/method section to identify: (1) the specific reliability failure being addressed (miscalibration vs. hallucination vs. over-answering), (2) the assumed role of retrieved evidence (sufficiency, relevance, calibration signal), (3) where the change is applied (retriever, generator, post-hoc selector), (4) the headline metric and dataset (e.g., ECE, selective accuracy, coverage-risk, answer correctness on Natural Questions/HotpotQA), and (5) the downstream behavior (abstention, confidence thresholding, re-retrieval). Both papers would also need shared base models, datasets, and an aligned operating point (e.g., matched coverage) to be placed on one leaderboard.
independent_rubric_rationale: With only a title from Paper A, there is no way to know what numbers, datasets, base models, or evaluation protocol it reports. A practitioner could be misled or could be fine — there simply is not enough information from one side of the pair to decide.

paper_a_title: PrismRAG: Boosting RAG Factuality with Distractor Resilience and Strategized Reasoning
