paper_b_title: The Curse of Helpfulness: Inverse Scaling Law in Robustness to Distractor Instructions via DistractionIF
gold_rationale: Although both papers invoke 'distractor robustness' in RAG-like settings, they operationalize the failure mode in incompatible ways. PrismRAG (A) targets factuality degradation caused by semi-relevant retrieved passages mixed with gold evidence, intervening via supervised fine-tuning on synthetic distractor QA pairs plus reasoning-centric training, and measuring average factuality across 12 open-book RAG QA benchmarks (+5.4%). DistractionIF (B) targets a distinct failure mode: instruction-like fragments embedded in reference text (editorial notes, format directives, UI residue) that the model erroneously treats as commands; it intervenes via GRPO reinforcement learning and measures instruction-following robustness on its own DistractionIF benchmark (+15.5%). The notion of 'distractor', the evaluation suites, the scoring rubrics, and the policy the model is asked to enact (synthesize a factual answer vs. execute the user's task while ignoring embedded directives) all differ. The two reported deltas live on non-overlapping axes and cannot be ranked.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (i) run both methods on a shared benchmark suite that includes both semantically-confusing retrieval distractors and embedded instruction-like noise, with a unified scoring protocol; (ii) restrict comparison to a common subset where the distractor definitions coincide (e.g., evaluate PrismRAG on DistractionIF and DistractionIF's GRPO model on the 12 RAG QA benchmarks using identical base models and decoding settings); or (iii) reframe results in a shared evaluation frame such as 'percentage of prompts in which the model resists distraction-induced behavior change' computed identically on overlapping data. Matched base models, matched training budgets, and matched judge/scoring pipelines would also be required.
independent_rubric_rationale: Putting these two numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would deceive a practitioner. The shared vocabulary of 'distractor robustness in RAG' hides that the two works study substantively different problems: one is about confusing irrelevant passages corrupting factual QA answers, the other is about reference text containing directive-like phrases that the model wrongly obeys instead of the user's request. The benchmarks, scoring criteria, and tasks have essentially no overlap, so a 5.4-point gain on one is not commensurable with a 15.5-point gain on the other, and a reader would likely draw the wrong conclusion about which approach is 'better' for their use case.

paper_a_title: Parallel Key-Value Cache Fusion for Position Invariant RAG
paper_b_title: Beyond RAG vs. Long-Context: Learning Distraction-Aware Retrieval for Efficient Knowledge Grounding
gold_rationale: Paper A targets the 'Lost in the Middle' positional bias failure mode and intervenes at the decoder/KV-cache architecture level, with the headline metric being position invariance and robustness to passage ordering on NQ/TriviaQA/POPQA. Paper B targets a different failure mode (distraction from irrelevant passages plus token inefficiency in long-context vs RAG) and intervenes at the retriever level by learning a distraction-aware retrieval policy, with headline metrics centered on the performance vs token-usage trade-off across six knowledge-intensive benchmarks. The action policies (KV fusion architecture vs trained retriever) and the evaluation framings are largely orthogonal, so a single leaderboard ranking would conflate methods that solve different sub-problems and could even be complementary.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation protocol with overlapping benchmarks, the same backbone LLM(s), an identical retriever (or matched retrieval budget), and a common metric set covering both ordering-sensitivity/robustness and token-efficient accuracy. Ideally one would also report a combined system (LDAR retrieval feeding into a KV-Fusion decoder) to disentangle the contribution of each component.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems target different bottlenecks in the RAG pipeline: one reshapes how an LLM consumes already-retrieved passages so its answer does not depend on ordering, while the other learns which passages to send to a standard LLM to balance coverage against irrelevant content. Their headline numbers are computed under different evaluation framings (ordering-robustness on three QA sets vs efficiency-accuracy curves on six benchmarks across multiple backbones), so a practitioner reading a unified leaderboard would likely draw the wrong conclusion about which approach is 'better' rather than recognizing they address complementary issues.

paper_a_title: Entropy-Based Decoding for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models
paper_b_title: RAFT: Adapting Language Model to Domain Specific RAG
gold_rationale: Paper A proposes a training-free, inference-time decoding procedure (entropy-based document-parallel ensemble plus layer-wise contrastive decoding) applied to an off-the-shelf LLM, and evaluates on open-domain QA. Paper B proposes a supervised fine-tuning recipe (RAFT) that bakes distractor-robustness and CoT citation behavior into model weights using domain-specific training data, evaluated on PubMed, HotpotQA, and Gorilla. The two solutions operate at fundamentally different points in the pipeline (decoder vs. weights), presume different resource budgets (no training data vs. domain training set), and largely report on non-overlapping evaluation suites in different settings (general open-domain vs. domain-specific RAG). A direct leaderboard ranking would conflate these distinct regimes.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both methods would need to be evaluated on a shared benchmark suite using the same base model and the same retriever/corpus, with matched prompts and retrieval depth. Reporting should disclose training cost and data requirements so readers can separate inference-time gains from train-time gains, and ideally a hybrid (RAFT-trained model + entropy decoding) baseline should be included to test orthogonality. Without this, headline numbers cannot be placed on a single axis.
independent_rubric_rationale: These two works take very different routes to improve retrieval-augmented question answering. One adjusts how the model produces tokens at generation time without any extra training, while the other reshapes the model itself through supervised fine-tuning on specialized data. They also report results on largely non-overlapping benchmark suites and presume different resource budgets and deployment scenarios (general open-domain vs. specialized domain). Putting their headline numbers side by side in a single ranking would obscure these substantial setup differences, and a practitioner would likely draw the wrong conclusion about which approach is preferable for their use case.

paper_a_title: Can Small Language Models Use What They Retrieve? An Empirical Study of Retrieval Utilization Across Model Scale
paper_b_title: END: Early Noise Dropping for Efficient and Effective Context Denoising
gold_rationale: Paper A is a diagnostic study isolating context utilization in small models (≤7B) using an oracle-retrieval condition and a parametric-knowledge split; it does not propose a method and reports failure-mode rates (irrelevant generation, parametric-answer destruction). Paper B proposes END, a method that segments input and uses early-layer linear probes to drop noisy chunks, then reports performance and efficiency gains across LLMs. The intervention_point differs (none vs. early-layer chunk dropping), the action_policy differs (avoid deploying RAG at small scale vs. apply END to improve RAG), and the metric_target differs (utilization failure rates conditioned on oracle/parametric splits vs. end-task accuracy and compute). Even the failure_type framing is asymmetric: A locates the bottleneck inside sub-7B models' ability to extract answers, while B treats noise in the input as the bottleneck regardless of scale. Evidence_assumption partially overlaps (both acknowledge distraction by context) but A guarantees an answer-bearing passage while B targets noisy mixtures.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared benchmark with matched model scales (including sub-7B), matched retrieval conditions (including an oracle/answer-bearing setting), and a common metric set covering both utilization failure modes (irrelevant generation, parametric-answer destruction) and end-task accuracy/efficiency. END would need to be evaluated on small models under Paper A's oracle and parametric-split protocol, and Paper A would need to add a denoising baseline (e.g., END) to test whether its diagnosed bottleneck is mitigated. Without such alignment, performance numbers in B do not bear on the bottleneck A measures, and A's pessimistic conclusion does not bear on whether B's method helps.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two papers look superficially related because both discuss noisy or distracting context in RAG, but placing their headline numbers side-by-side on one leaderboard would mislead a practitioner. One paper is a diagnostic report whose central numbers are rates at which small models mishandle context (including under an idealized retrieval setup), while the other reports gains from a new chunk-dropping technique on different models, datasets, and evaluation goals. A reader comparing them could wrongly conclude that the second paper's gains refute the first paper's pessimistic findings about small models, or that the first paper's bottleneck applies to systems already using the second paper's technique, when neither inference is supported by the reported evidence.

paper_a_title: {MIRAGE}: A Metric-Intensive Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Evaluation
paper_b_title: RAGAs: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Both papers concern RAG evaluation but appear to address different aspects of the problem: MIRAGE presents itself as a benchmark (test data plus evaluation protocols), while RAGAs presents itself as an automated evaluation framework (methodology for scoring RAG outputs). Without text snippets, the specific failure_type addressed, evidence_assumption, intervention_point in the RAG pipeline, metric_target definitions, and recommended action_policy cannot be verified. The titles alone suggest complementary contributions rather than directly competing ones, but conservative coding requires marking this underspecified given the absence of textual evidence to confirm the coordinate values.
what_valid_comparison_requires: To be directly comparable, both papers would need to report headline numbers of the same kind on the same task and dataset, using compatible evaluation protocols, against overlapping baseline systems. A benchmark contribution (datasets + reference scores) and an evaluation-methodology contribution (new scoring functions) usually answer different research questions and should be cited as complementary rather than ranked head-to-head. Verification would also require checking whether either paper reports results on the other's setup.
independent_rubric_rationale: With no text excerpts available from either paper, the specific headline numbers that would be placed side by side on a shared leaderboard cannot be identified. The titles suggest one paper contributes a testbed with reference scores while the other contributes a scoring framework, which would typically produce different kinds of numerical claims that are not directly rankable, but this cannot be confirmed at the snippet level provided here.

paper_a_title: ReEval: Automatic Hallucination Evaluation for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models via Transferable Adversarial Attacks
paper_b_title: Redefining Retrieval Evaluation in the Era of LLMs
gold_rationale: Paper A (ReEval) targets hallucination behavior in the generator component of RAG by automatically synthesizing transferable adversarial test cases; its headline outcome concerns whether LLMs hallucinate under perturbed evidence. Paper B (UDCG) targets the retrieval-side scoring problem, proposing a new IR-style measure with LLM-oriented position discounting and distractor penalties, evaluated by correlation with end-to-end answer accuracy across five datasets and six LLMs. The two studies diagnose different breakdowns in the RAG pipeline, operate at different stages (probe-set construction vs. ranking-quality scoring), report incompatible headline quantities (hallucination rates vs. metric–accuracy correlation), and prescribe different downstream uses (stress-testing LLMs vs. choosing a retrieval evaluator). No shared baseline, dataset protocol, or outcome variable links them.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both works would need a shared task definition and a common dependent variable—for example, both reporting either (a) hallucination/accuracy on the same RAG benchmark using a fixed generator and retriever, or (b) correlation with end-to-end answer correctness for an evaluation tool. They would also need overlapping datasets, comparable baseline systems, and a common operational role (either both as evaluation methodologies for retrievers, or both as stress tests of generators). Without at least one matched dependent variable computed under the same protocol, no leaderboard cell is meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works address different stages of the retrieval-augmented generation pipeline: one builds an automatic adversarial pipeline to probe how often language models produce unfaithful answers, while the other defines a new ranking-quality score for the retriever and shows it tracks downstream answer correctness better than classical alternatives. Their headline numbers describe distinct phenomena measured on distinct quantities, so placing them side by side on a single leaderboard would lead a practitioner to draw conclusions about systems that were never evaluated under comparable conditions.

paper_a_title: MTRAG-UN: A Benchmark for Open Challenges in Multi-Turn RAG Conversations
paper_b_title: RAGLAB: A Modular and Research-Oriented Unified Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Paper A (MTRAG-UN) is a benchmark dataset of 666 tasks across 6 domains targeting specific weaknesses in multi-turn RAG conversations (unanswerable, underspecified, nonstandalone questions, unclear responses). Paper B (RAGLAB) is a modular software framework/toolkit for RAG research. These artifacts have fundamentally different purposes: one supplies evaluation data and difficulty categories, the other supplies a unified codebase for building and running RAG pipelines. They do not produce commensurable scores and they target different objects of study. Note: Paper B snippet is missing, but the title is sufficient to identify it as a framework paper rather than a benchmark with reportable accuracy numbers comparable to Paper A.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) both papers would need to be benchmarks measuring overlapping phenomena (e.g., both reporting model performance on multi-turn RAG with shared metrics like recall, faithfulness, answerability detection on common test sets), or (b) both would need to be frameworks/methods evaluated on the same benchmark with the same scoring protocol. Additionally, the Paper B snippet should be available to confirm any reported numerical results before any side-by-side ranking is attempted.
independent_rubric_rationale: A practitioner who placed the two headline results on a single leaderboard would be led astray, because one work delivers an evaluation suite full of hard conversational cases while the other delivers a research toolkit for assembling RAG systems. Any number lifted from one would not mean the same thing as a number lifted from the other, so a head-to-head ranking would not communicate useful information about which is better.

paper_a_title: Generating Leakage-Free Benchmarks for Robust RAG Evaluation
paper_b_title: Judge as A Judge: Improving the Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation through the Judge-Consistency of Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Paper A (SeedRG) targets benchmark data contamination/knowledge leakage and intervenes at the benchmark-generation stage via reasoning-graph-based entity replacement, with metrics around leakage reduction and discriminative power across RAG systems. Paper B targets the reliability of LLM-as-judge evaluation and intervenes at the scoring stage via judge-consistency, with metrics presumably around judge agreement/quality. These address different problems at different stages of the RAG evaluation pipeline, so their headline numbers are not on the same axis. (Note: Paper B has no snippet provided, but the title is explicit enough to support this judgment with moderate-high confidence.)
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) both works would need to address the same stage of RAG evaluation—e.g., both producing benchmarks or both producing evaluator/scoring methods—and report results on a shared testbed with the same primary outcome, or (b) one would need to be re-cast as an ablation/component inside the other (e.g., run Paper B's judge on Paper A's generated benchmarks) so a head-to-head number is meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works improve different layers of the RAG evaluation pipeline: one rebuilds the test set to avoid memorized answers, the other refines how an LLM judge scores responses. If their headline results were placed on one leaderboard, a practitioner would likely treat them as rival approaches when they are actually complementary, and could easily pick the wrong tool for their problem.

paper_a_title: Whose Facts Win? LLM Source Preferences under Knowledge Conflicts
paper_b_title: Rethinking All Evidence: Enhancing Trustworthy Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Conflict-Driven Summarization
gold_rationale: Paper A studies inter-context source credibility preferences (government vs newspaper vs person vs social media) using synthetic, metadata-controlled sources, reporting source preference (SP) scores and repetition-bias reduction (79.2%) via a fine-tuning fix. Paper B proposes CARE-RAG, a pipeline that performs conflict-driven summarization over parametric and retrieved evidence and is evaluated on revised QA datasets for end-task correctness. The two diverge on every coordinate: the targeted failure (source-credibility/repetition bias vs general parametric-vs-retrieval conflict), the evidence setup (synthetic labeled sources vs real retrieval passages), the locus of change (model fine-tuning vs added summarization stage with QA Repair), the headline metric (SP score and bias reduction vs QA accuracy), and the policy goal (preserve a credibility hierarchy vs maximize answer correctness).
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared test bed and shared scoring would be needed: e.g., both systems evaluated on the same conflicting-evidence QA benchmark with identical retrieval, reporting the same accuracy-style score; or both reporting source-preference behavior on the synthetic-source framework. Without a common task definition and common numeric scale, side-by-side ranking is not meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works examine different slices of the knowledge-conflict landscape with non-overlapping numbers. One reports how strongly models lean toward institutional vs personal source labels in a synthetic setup and how a fine-tune curbs repetition-driven flips; the other reports end-task question-answering correctness for a summarization pipeline on revised QA datasets. Putting their headline figures on one leaderboard would tell a practitioner nothing useful about which is better for any shared use case and would likely cause a wrong choice.

paper_a_title: Context-DPO: Aligning Language Models for Context-Faithfulness
paper_b_title: FaithfulRAG: Fact-Level Conflict Modeling for Context-Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Both papers target the same underlying problem (LLM unfaithfulness to retrieved context under knowledge conflict in RAG) and share similar framing about parametric vs. contextual knowledge. However, they differ structurally: Paper A is a training-time alignment method (DPO on faithful/stubborn preference pairs) and introduces its own benchmark (ConFiQA), while Paper B is an inference-time reasoning framework that identifies fact-level conflicts and runs a self-thinking pass without modifying weights. Paper A's headline 35–280% improvement is reported on its own ConFiQA benchmark with open-source models; Paper B's headline 'outperforms SOTA' is on unspecified (likely different) benchmarks. The shared problem makes the comparison tempting, but the differing pipeline stage and likely different evaluation suites prevent a clean head-to-head ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Evaluation of both methods on an overlapping benchmark suite (e.g., ConFiQA plus the benchmarks used in FaithfulRAG), using the same base LLMs and the same set of baselines, with explicit recognition that one approach modifies model parameters while the other is training-free — so cost, deployability, and compatibility (the two could be stacked) should be reported alongside raw faithfulness scores.
independent_rubric_rationale: A practitioner glancing at one combined leaderboard would likely be partly misled: both works claim large gains on context-faithfulness in conflict scenarios, but one is a weight-updating training recipe with a self-built evaluation set, while the other is a prompting/reasoning pipeline that leaves weights untouched and is tested elsewhere. The two numbers are not on a common scale and the techniques are arguably complementary rather than competing, so a single ranking would hide deployment cost, base-model dependence, and benchmark mismatch.

paper_a_title: Position: Retrieval-augmented systems can be dangerous medical communicators
paper_b_title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
gold_rationale: Paper A is a position paper arguing that retrieval-augmented systems pose communication and safety risks in medical settings; its failure_type concerns pragmatic/clinical communication harm, its evidence_assumption is argumentative-normative drawing on prior literature, its intervention_point is system design and deployment policy for medical RAG, its metric_target is qualitative safety/communicative adequacy, and its action_policy is high-level recommendations to developers and clinicians. Paper B is an empirical benchmarking study of how decoder LLMs use information located at different positions within long contexts; its failure_type is position-dependent utilization (U-shaped curve), evidence_assumption is controlled multi-document QA and key-value retrieval experiments, intervention_point is context construction/document ordering, metric_target is task accuracy as a function of input position and length, and action_policy is prompt/context engineering guidance. All five coordinates diverge, so no shared yardstick exists for ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation setting would be needed, e.g., both papers measuring the same outcome (such as factual accuracy or safety-of-response) on the same medical-RAG benchmark under matched retrieval and context conditions, with comparable quantitative scores and aligned definitions of what counts as success or harm.
independent_rubric_rationale: Paper A is a normative position piece warning about safety risks of retrieval-augmented systems used to communicate medical information to patients, while Paper B is a controlled empirical study quantifying how decoder language models utilize information placed at different positions within long context windows on QA and key-value tasks. The two works ask different questions, produce different kinds of outputs (recommendations vs. accuracy curves), and target different user concerns. Placing their headline results side by side on one leaderboard would seriously mislead a practitioner because the numbers and claims are not commensurable and pertain to unrelated phenomena.

paper_a_title: KnowPO: Knowledge-aware Preference Optimization for Controllable Knowledge Selection in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
paper_b_title: Why So Gullible? Enhancing the Robustness of Retrieval-Augmented Models against Counterfactual Noise
gold_rationale: Both papers sit in the broad area of RAG robustness under conflicting/noisy retrieved evidence, but they operationalize the problem differently. Paper A (KnowPO) targets conflict between an LLM's internal parametric knowledge and external retrieved content, training with preference optimization on a constructed conflict dataset, and reports a relative gain (~37%) on its own conflict benchmark plus OOD sets. Paper B (Discern-and-Answer) targets conflict AMONG retrieved documents (counterfactual noise within the retrieved set), proposes a discriminator fine-tune or GPT-3.5 prompting pipeline, and evaluates on open-domain QA with the new MACNOISE dataset. The failure modes (intra-context vs. parametric-vs-context), training/intervention strategies (DPO-style preference learning vs. discriminator/prompting), and evaluation suites differ enough that a single ranking is not well-defined, although the high-level motivation overlaps.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation protocol using the same benchmark(s) covering both intra-context counterfactual noise and parametric-vs-context conflict, the same base LLM(s) and retriever, identical metrics (e.g., EM/F1 on matched ODQA splits, plus a conflict-handling accuracy), and matched compute/data budgets so that the preference-optimization approach and the discriminator/prompting approach are stressed on identical inputs.
independent_rubric_rationale: Both works aim at making retrieval-augmented systems more reliable when retrieved passages disagree, so a practitioner skimming a combined leaderboard would get the right general topic. However, the two studies are stressing different kinds of disagreement (internal-vs-external versus document-vs-document), use different training recipes, and report numbers on different test suites, so a raw side-by-side ranking would mix apples and oranges and could mislead someone choosing a method for a specific deployment scenario.

paper_a_title: Hierarchical Planning for Complex Tasks with Knowledge Graph-RAG and Symbolic Verification
paper_b_title: RAG4GFM: Bridging Knowledge Gaps in Graph Foundation Models through Graph Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: No text snippets were supplied, so judgment relies on titles. Paper A targets hierarchical planning for complex tasks, combining KG-RAG with symbolic verification—implying plan-execution or task-decomposition evaluation. Paper B targets knowledge gaps in Graph Foundation Models via graph-RAG, implying standard graph-learning evaluation (e.g., node/edge/graph-level prediction). The kinds of errors they remedy, where in the pipeline they inject retrieved graph context, and the success criteria differ substantively. Both nominally use graph-structured retrieval, but that surface similarity does not make the headline results commensurable.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Shared task family (either both on planning/agentic benchmarks or both on graph-learning benchmarks), overlapping datasets, and harmonized evaluation criteria (e.g., plan success rate vs. classification accuracy cannot be merged). Additionally, comparable base models or retrievers, and matched compute/retrieval budgets, would be needed before any leaderboard-style ranking is meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works appear to live in different problem spaces—one about multi-step plan generation for complex tasks with verifier checks, and the other about enriching graph foundation models with retrieved subgraph context. Reporting their headline numbers side-by-side on one leaderboard would invite a practitioner to treat them as alternatives for the same use case, which they are not, and would likely produce unwarranted conclusions about which approach is 'better.'

paper_a_title: Entity-Focused Dense Passage Retrieval for Outside-Knowledge Visual Question Answering
paper_b_title: Quebec Automobile Insurance Question-Answering With Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Paper A addresses outside-knowledge visual question answering, a multimodal task where the system must combine image understanding with retrieved textual knowledge (e.g., Wikipedia-style passages) to answer general questions about images. Paper B addresses a specialized legal/insurance QA task in a single text modality, focused on a narrow Quebec automobile insurance corpus using a RAG pipeline. The problem framings differ (multimodal knowledge gap vs. domain-specific document QA), the evidence corpora differ (open-domain encyclopedic knowledge vs. closed insurance regulation texts), the technical loci differ (entity-aware dense retriever for VQA vs. end-to-end RAG with generative LLM for legal text), and the evaluation regimes almost certainly differ (OK-VQA-style answer accuracy and retrieval Recall@k vs. domain-specific QA quality measures, likely including human or expert judgment). Placing the two headline numbers side by side would not reflect a like-for-like comparison.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid head-to-head would require both systems to be evaluated on the same benchmark with the same input modality, the same retrieval corpus, the same answer evaluation protocol, and a shared task definition. Minimally, one would need either (i) both systems run on an OK-VQA-style multimodal benchmark, or (ii) both run on a Quebec insurance QA benchmark with matched documents and scoring. Without such shared ground, only loose conceptual contrast (e.g., 'both use retrieval-augmented QA') is defensible, not ranking.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems target very different tasks: one answers general questions about images by pulling encyclopedic text, while the other answers narrow Quebec automobile insurance questions from a closed legal corpus. They use different inputs (image plus text vs. text only), different reference corpora, different evaluation datasets, and almost certainly different scoring scales. A practitioner seeing them on a single leaderboard would draw incorrect conclusions about which approach is 'better,' because the numbers are not on a shared scale and the systems are not solving the same problem.

paper_a_title: Think-on-Graph 2.0: Deep and Faithful Large Language Model Reasoning with Knowledge-guided Retrieval Augmented Generation
paper_b_title: ReFIR: Grounding Large Restoration Models with Retrieval Augmentation
gold_rationale: judgment based on titles only (no snippets provided). Paper A targets shallow or hallucinated reasoning in large language models and intervenes inside an LLM's iterative reasoning loop using a knowledge graph plus retrieved documents as evidence, evaluated on text QA-style correctness. Paper B targets degraded outputs of large image restoration models and intervenes inside an image restoration pipeline using retrieved reference images as evidence, evaluated on image-quality metrics. The two works differ on every coordinate: the kind of error being fixed, the form of retrieved evidence, the model class being augmented, the metric family, and the operational policy. There is no shared benchmark on which both could be ranked.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both systems would need to address the same task family (e.g., both text reasoning or both image restoration), augment comparable base model classes, use evidence of compatible type, and be scored on the same benchmark with the same metric. At minimum, a shared retrieval-augmentation benchmark with identical inputs, ground truth, and scoring protocol would be required before any leaderboard-style ranking could be meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works live in different modalities (language reasoning over knowledge graphs versus image restoration with reference images), solve different end-user problems, and would be scored with entirely different numbers on entirely different benchmarks. Placing their headline results side by side on one leaderboard would suggest a comparison that does not exist and would likely lead a practitioner to draw unsupported conclusions about which approach is 'better'.

paper_a_title: TRACE: Grounding Time Series in Context for Multimodal Embedding and Retrieval
paper_b_title: Unified Generative and Discriminative Training for Multi-modal Large Language Models
gold_rationale: adjudication based on titles only; no text snippets were provided for either paper. Paper A targets time-series multimodal embedding and retrieval (a representation/retrieval problem grounded in temporal data and context). Paper B targets a unified generative+discriminative training recipe for general multi-modal LLMs (a training-objective problem on vision-language MLLMs). At the title level the two works appear to address different failure types, intervene at different points in the pipeline (retriever vs. training loss), and almost certainly report on different benchmarks and metric families. However, since the actual evaluation suites, modalities, and headline numbers are not visible, a firm 'invalid' verdict cannot be defended; 'underspecified' is the conservative call.
what_valid_comparison_requires: At minimum: (1) confirmation that both systems are evaluated on at least one shared benchmark using an identically defined metric, (2) overlap in modality coverage (time series vs. image/text), (3) matched task framing (retrieval recall vs. generative/discriminative VL scores), and (4) comparable backbone scale and training-data conditions. The papers' abstracts, results tables, and benchmark lists would be needed to verify any of these.
independent_rubric_rationale: With no abstracts or result excerpts available, I cannot verify whether the two systems were ever measured on a common testbed. The titles alone hint that one work concerns retrieval over time-series content while the other concerns training recipes for general multi-modal large language models, which would normally live on different leaderboards, but this surface signal is not strong enough on its own to issue a definitive call.

paper_a_title: Chunk-Distilled Language Modeling
paper_b_title: Context Tuning for Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: No text snippets are available for either paper, so claims, benchmarks, baselines, and headline numbers are unknown. From titles alone, both papers concern retrieval/knowledge integration with LMs, but Paper A appears to modify the LM generation pathway by distilling/storing chunks, while Paper B appears to tune the retrieval/context construction stage for RAG. These look like different intervention points on different problem framings, and without snippets the evaluation targets and reported metrics cannot be confirmed to align. Conservative judgment is underspecified rather than valid or invalid.

independent_rubric_rationale: Without any snippet content showing tasks, datasets, baselines, or numbers from either paper, it is not possible to judge whether placing their headline results side by side on one leaderboard would mislead a practitioner. The titles hint at related but distinct techniques in the retrieval-augmented space, which raises concern, but there is no concrete evidence to support a safe, partly, or misleading label.

paper_a_title: Cooperative Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Question Answering: Mutual Information Exchange and Ranking by Contrasting Layers
paper_b_title: Separate the Wheat from the Chaff: Winnowing Down Divergent Views in Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Paper A has no text snippet available; only its title is given. While both works clearly target noise in retrieved documents within RAG for QA, Paper A's title points to a cooperative mutual-information design with contrastive-layer ranking, whereas Paper B (WinnowRAG) is a two-stage clustering plus critic-LLM filtering pipeline. Without Paper A's body text, the specific noise model it addresses, the assumptions about retrieved evidence, where exactly it intervenes (representation level vs. document level), the QA benchmarks/metrics reported, and the operating policy (e.g., agentic loop vs. single pass) cannot be verified. All five coordinates are therefore unresolved on the A side, even though Paper B is reasonably clear on each.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Access to Paper A's abstract/methods section to confirm (1) the noise/error mode it targets in retrieval, (2) what it assumes about the candidate document set, (3) whether it modifies retrieval scoring, decoding internals, or post-hoc selection, (4) the QA datasets and headline metrics, and (5) the deployment pipeline (single-shot vs. iterative, agentic vs. layer-contrast). Once known, both papers would need to share at least one common benchmark, retriever, base LLM family, and metric definition before being placed on a shared leaderboard.

Paper B is described clearly enough on its own, but with one side essentially blank, there is no way to judge whether putting the two headline results next to each other on a single leaderboard would give a practitioner a wrong impression of which approach is stronger or where each is appropriate.

paper_a_title: RankRAG: Unifying Context Ranking with Retrieval-Augmented Generation in LLMs
paper_b_title: xRAG: Extreme Context Compression for Retrieval-augmented Generation with One Token
gold_rationale: Based on titles alone (no snippets supplied), RankRAG and xRAG address distinct problems in RAG. RankRAG targets the quality problem of poor context ranking and instruction-tunes a single LLM to jointly rank retrieved passages and generate answers, with success measured primarily by downstream QA accuracy. xRAG targets the efficiency problem of long retrieved context and trains a projector to compress retrieved documents into a single embedding token, with success measured along an accuracy-vs-compression frontier. The diagnosed bottleneck, the place in the RAG pipeline being modified, the operational policy at inference, and the primary success criterion all differ, so a single leaderboard ranking is not meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both systems would need to be evaluated on a shared benchmark under matched retrieval, with both axes reported: end-task accuracy and inference cost (tokens consumed, latency). Even then, fair side-by-side reading requires treating them as complementary axes (ranking quality vs. context compression) rather than as substitutes, and ideally evaluating a stacked variant (compressed-then-ranked or ranked-then-compressed) before declaring one superior.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems are aimed at different goals within retrieval-augmented generation: one tries to lift answer quality by getting the model to reorder retrieved passages before answering, while the other tries to slash the cost of feeding retrieved content into the model by squeezing it into a single embedding. A practitioner who saw their headline numbers in a single ranked table would likely treat them as competitors, when in reality they trade along different axes (quality vs. efficiency) and could plausibly be combined, so a direct leaderboard comparison would give a distorted picture.

paper_a_title: SEER: Self-Aligned Evidence Extraction for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper_b_title: Neuro-RIT: Neuron-Guided Instruction Tuning for Robust Retrieval-Augmented Language Model
gold_rationale: Both papers target the same failure mode (RAG performance degradation under noisy/irrelevant retrieved contexts) and likely evaluate on overlapping QA benchmarks, so the metric_target is plausibly aligned. However, they intervene at very different points: SEER (A) is an input-side, self-aligned evidence extraction approach that refines what the generator sees, whereas Neuro-RIT (B) is a parameter-side intervention that performs neuron-level instruction tuning of the generator itself. Their evidence assumptions also diverge (extractable evidence spans vs. separable relevance-encoding neurons), and their action policies are not substitutable. Paper A's snippet is unavailable and Paper B's listed arXiv ID/date (2026) cannot be verified, further limiting confidence. A leaderboard-style direct ranking would conflate two orthogonal, potentially complementary strategies.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Matched base LLM(s), the same retriever and retrieval corpus, identical QA benchmarks with the same noise/irrelevance injection protocol, the same set of metrics (e.g., EM/F1) computed under the same prompting setup, and ideally an ablation that decouples context refinement from model-side tuning so the two approaches are evaluated on the same axis (or shown to be combinable rather than competing).
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems try to solve the same robustness problem in RAG but via fundamentally different mechanisms — one reshapes the context fed to the generator, the other reshapes the generator's internal weights at a fine-grained level. Putting their headline numbers side by side on one leaderboard would let a practitioner see relative scores, but it would obscure that the techniques operate on different parts of the pipeline, likely use different base models and evaluation protocols, and could in principle be stacked rather than chosen between. That gives a partly misleading picture rather than an outright wrong or fully safe one.

paper_a_title: Towards Secure Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Comprehensive Review of Threats, Defenses and Benchmarks
paper_b_title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
gold_rationale: Paper A is a survey/review paper cataloguing security threats, defenses, and benchmarks for RAG systems (data poisoning, adversarial attacks, membership inference, encryption, differential privacy, etc.). Paper B is the original Lewis et al. RAG method paper introducing a novel retrieval-augmented architecture and reporting empirical results on knowledge-intensive NLP benchmarks (open-domain QA, fact verification, etc.). These two works disagree on every coordinate: the failure_type addressed differs (security/privacy vulnerabilities vs. knowledge-intensive task accuracy/hallucination), the evidence_assumption differs (synthesized literature review vs. controlled empirical benchmark results), the intervention_point differs (defensive mechanisms across the RAG pipeline vs. a single proposed model architecture), the metric_target differs (security/robustness criteria vs. EM/F1 and generation quality on NLP benchmarks), and the action_policy differs (taxonomic guidance for future security work vs. a deployable model recipe). No common axis exists on which to rank them.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both papers to address the same problem (e.g., either both being RAG security surveys, or both proposing/evaluating a RAG method on the same NLP benchmark suite with shared metrics). At minimum, a shared evaluation dimension and overlapping evidence type would be needed before either ranking or head-to-head comparison could be meaningful.
independent_rubric_rationale: Placing a security-focused survey of RAG threats and defenses next to the foundational paper that introduced RAG for knowledge-intensive NLP tasks on a single leaderboard would seriously confuse a practitioner. The two works answer fundamentally different questions, use incompatible kinds of evidence, and report numbers (when present) on entirely disjoint scales. Any side-by-side ranking would suggest a contest that does not exist.

paper_a_title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Comprehensive Survey of Architectures, Enhancements, and Robustness Frontiers
paper_b_title: LLM-Oriented Information Retrieval: A Denoising-First Perspective
gold_rationale: Both papers are non-empirical synthesis works addressing retrieval for LLMs, so they share topical territory (RAG, hallucination mitigation, retrieval quality). However, they diverge sharply on coordinates. Paper A is a broad comprehensive survey cataloging architectures (retriever-centric, generator-centric, hybrid, robustness-oriented) and enhancements across retrieval, filtering, decoding, and efficiency. Paper B is a perspective/position paper with a thesis-driven framing: denoising as the primary bottleneck, organized around a four-stage challenge framework (inaccessible→undiscoverable→misaligned→unverifiable). The evidence basis (broad synthesis vs. argued perspective), the recommended policy (taxonomic mapping vs. denoising-first prescription), and the success criteria (retrieval/QA performance trade-offs vs. signal-to-noise/verifiability) differ enough that placing the two side by side as equivalents would distort what each is trying to deliver.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Either (a) both works share genre (e.g., two comprehensive surveys of RAG with comparable taxonomy scope and inclusion criteria), or (b) they are framed as alternative syntheses of the same sub-question (e.g., denoising-focused review vs. broader review explicitly compared on coverage of the denoising literature, with date ranges, paper inclusion lists, and topical scope normalized). A direct ranking would also require an explicit dimension of comparison (coverage breadth, recency, taxonomic granularity, prescriptive guidance) rather than treating them as interchangeable references.
independent_rubric_rationale: A practitioner browsing both would find genuinely overlapping material on retrieval for language models, but the two pieces serve different purposes: one is a wide-angle reference catalog, the other is a thesis-driven essay advocating a particular lens on the field. Treating them as head-to-head entries on the same list would obscure that mismatch in genre and scope, though it would not produce an outright wrong takeaway, since both are credible reading on adjacent ground.

paper_a_title: Towards Trustworthy Retrieval Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
paper_b_title: Trustworthiness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems: A Survey
gold_rationale: Both are surveys on trustworthy RAG published within months of each other, with substantial topical overlap. However, they organize the space using partially different taxonomies: Paper A uses reliability, privacy, safety, fairness, explainability, accountability (6 dimensions); Paper B uses factuality, robustness, fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy (6 dimensions). Only three dimensions overlap directly (fairness, accountability, privacy). More importantly, Paper B contributes an empirical benchmark (TRC Bench) with model evaluations, while Paper A is purely a literature taxonomy/roadmap without empirical evaluation. The evidence bases and contribution types differ meaningfully, even though both target the same broad domain.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid direct comparison would require either (1) restricting the comparison to the shared dimensions (fairness, accountability, privacy) and comparing taxonomic depth and citation coverage, or (2) treating them as complementary references rather than substitutes, noting that only Paper B provides empirical benchmark results. A leaderboard-style ranking would need a common evaluation axis such as breadth of literature surveyed, taxonomy granularity per shared dimension, or empirical contribution, applied consistently.
independent_rubric_rationale: Both works are literature overviews on the same broad topic and overlap in several organizing categories, so a practitioner consulting both would gain largely complementary coverage. However, treating them as equivalent on a single ranking could mislead in two ways: their organizing dimensions only partially align, and one of them additionally provides a quantitative model evaluation suite that the other lacks. A reader who assumed the two contributions were of the same type and scope would draw partly incorrect conclusions about what each delivers.

paper_a_title: Securing Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Taxonomy of Attacks, Defenses, and Future Directions
paper_b_title: RAPID: Long-Context Inference with Retrieval-Augmented Speculative Decoding
gold_rationale: Paper A is a security-oriented taxonomy survey of attacks and defenses in RAG, organized around adversarial threats to a knowledge-access pipeline. Paper B (based on title) is an empirical systems/method paper proposing retrieval-augmented speculative decoding to accelerate long-context inference. The two diverge on every coordinate: the failure_type differs (security/CIA violations vs. inference inefficiency/quality on long contexts); the evidence_assumption differs (adversarial corpus and prompt model vs. benign throughput/accuracy benchmarks); the intervention_point differs (pipeline-wide defenses and threat modeling vs. token-level draft/verify decoding); the metric_target differs (attack success, defense coverage, CIA properties vs. latency, accuracy, perplexity on long-context tasks); and the action_policy differs (a survey/taxonomy with future-direction guidance vs. a deployable decoding algorithm). There is no shared leaderboard or evaluation surface on which a meaningful comparison or ranking could be made.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers would need to target the same problem class (e.g., both addressing RAG security, or both addressing long-context inference efficiency/quality), share a common evaluation protocol with the same datasets and outcome measures, and produce artifacts of the same kind (e.g., two competing defenses evaluated under matched threat models, or two decoding methods evaluated on matched long-context benchmarks). None of these conditions hold here.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works address entirely different research questions: one catalogues adversarial threats and protective mechanisms for retrieval-augmented systems, while the other proposes a decoding scheme to speed up long-context generation. They share no common benchmark, problem statement, or success criterion, so placing their headline results side by side on one leaderboard would give a practitioner a false impression that they are alternative solutions to the same need.

paper_a_title: Trust or Abstain? A Self-Aware RAG Approach
paper_b_title: PoisonedRAG: Knowledge Corruption Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Paper A (SABER) is a defense-oriented method targeting natural PK/CK knowledge conflicts and unreliability; its failure_type is conflict-induced hallucination, its evidence_assumption is non-adversarial but possibly unreliable retrieved context, its intervention_point is inference-time belief estimation over already-retrieved evidence, its metric_target is end-to-end QA accuracy plus risk-coverage / abstention quality, and its action_policy is a 4-way choice among trust-PK / trust-CK / trust-either / abstain. Paper B (PoisonedRAG) is an offensive attack paper: failure_type is an adversarial security vulnerability of the corpus, evidence_assumption is an attacker injecting crafted malicious passages into the knowledge database, intervention_point is the retrieval corpus itself (data-poisoning), metric_target is attack success rate against target questions plus defense bypass, and action_policy is generating and injecting poisoned passages (with defenses as a secondary axis). All five coordinates diverge, and the two systems are not even on the same side of the problem (defender/abstainer vs. attacker).
what_valid_comparison_requires: A meaningful comparison would require both papers to be evaluated on the same task setup: e.g., run SABER as a defense against PoisonedRAG-style poisoned corpora and report a shared metric such as accuracy or attack-success-rate under the same retriever, LLM backbone, datasets, and poisoning budget. Alternatively, both would need to report results on a common knowledge-conflict-plus-poisoning benchmark with matched threat models. Without such a shared evaluation protocol, headline numbers (90% ASR vs. accuracy/abstention gains) refer to incompatible quantities.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper offers a defensive technique that lets the model choose among trusting its own memory, trusting the retrieved passage, or saying 'I don't know,' and reports correctness and selective-answering quality. The other paper is an offensive study that injects crafted poisoned passages into the corpus and reports how often the model is forced into the attacker's chosen wrong answer. Their headline numbers describe opposite goals on different evaluation pipelines, so a practitioner seeing them side by side on one leaderboard would draw incorrect conclusions about what either system delivers.

paper_a_title: Magic Mushroom: A Customizable Benchmark for Fine-grained Analysis of Retrieval Noise Erosion in RAG Systems
paper_b_title: Why Uncertainty Estimation Methods Fall Short in RAG: An Axiomatic Analysis
gold_rationale: The two papers address fundamentally distinct research problems within the RAG ecosystem. Paper A (Magic Mushroom) targets retrieval noise erosion: it builds a benchmark with four categories of misleading-but-surface-relevant noise and evaluates generators plus denoising strategies on QA accuracy under controlled noise distributions. Paper B (Axiomatic UE in RAG) targets uncertainty estimation: it proposes five axioms describing how UE scores should behave when retrieved documents are added, shows existing UE methods violate them, and proposes a calibration function judged by correlation between uncertainty and correctness. The failure modes (noise-induced wrong answers vs. miscalibrated confidence), assumed evidence regimes (heterogeneous noise categories vs. supportive/conflicting retrieved docs), points of change (benchmark design + denoiser choice vs. UE calibration), measured outcomes (answer correctness under noise vs. UE-correctness correlation and axiom satisfaction), and recommended next steps (build noise-robust generators/denoisers vs. build axiom-satisfying UE methods) all diverge. No coordinate aligns sufficiently to support direct comparison or ranking.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both papers to share at least the same outcome being scored and the same kind of system change being proposed, e.g., both reporting QA accuracy under matched retrieval-noise conditions on overlapping datasets and LLMs, or both reporting UE-correctness correlation on the same RAG configurations. Minimally, one would need a common benchmark, identical evaluation metric, and comparable system components (generator, retriever, and either denoiser or UE module) so that a leaderboard entry reflects the same underlying quantity.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works speak to disjoint practitioner questions. One asks how well a generator preserves answer quality when retrieved passages are deceptive; the other asks how well a confidence score tracks correctness once retrieval is added to the prompt. Putting their headline numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would conflate answer quality with confidence calibration, and a reader could easily infer a ranking that has no operational meaning, leading to wrong tooling choices.

paper_a_title: Toward Robust RALMs: Revealing the Impact of Imperfect Retrieval on Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
paper_b_title: RoseRAG: Robust Retrieval-augmented Generation with Small-scale LLMs via Margin-aware Preference Optimization
gold_rationale: Paper A is a diagnostic/benchmarking study that introduces an adversarial attack generator (GenADV) and a novel robustness metric (RAD) to characterize how RALMs handle three distinct problematic retrieval regimes (unanswerable, adversarial, conflicting), with desired model behavior including abstention and conflict signaling. Paper B is a training-method paper proposing RoseRAG, which uses margin-aware preference optimization (rejection sampling + contrastive preference selection) on small-scale LLMs and evaluates with standard EM/F1 on three open-domain QA benchmarks under generic noisy-retrieval conditions. The two works diverge on the type of retrieval imperfection studied, on whether any model-side change is made (none vs. training-time preference optimization), on the headline metric (novel RAD vs. EM/F1), and on the expected model behavior (detect/abstain vs. produce correct answer). These divergences prevent placing their main numbers side-by-side as comparable evidence.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared evaluation protocol: the same backbone model family and scale, the same retriever and top-K corpus, the same task instances drawn from the same scenario mix (unanswerable / adversarial / conflicting / clean), and a common scoring rule (either RAD-style robustness with abstention credit, or EM/F1 with explicit handling of unanswerables). Ideally Paper B's trained SLM would be evaluated on Paper A's GenADV/RAD suite, and Paper A's diagnosed baselines would be re-scored under Paper B's QA benchmarks, before any leaderboard ranking.
independent_rubric_rationale: A practitioner skimming a single leaderboard with these two headline numbers would draw the wrong conclusion. One paper reports a new robustness score it invented over scenarios it constructed, while the other reports standard QA accuracy on small models trained with a new optimization recipe on different benchmarks. The datasets, scoring rules, model scales, and expected output behaviors (including whether saying 'I don't know' counts as correct) do not line up, so a ranked side-by-side would suggest a head-to-head winner that does not actually exist.

paper_a_title: Hierarchical Planning for Complex Tasks with Knowledge Graph-RAG and Symbolic Verification
paper_b_title: Supportiveness-based Knowledge Rewriting for Retrieval-augmented Language Modeling
gold_rationale: Paper A addresses hierarchical planning for complex multi-step tasks using a knowledge graph as the evidence base, with symbolic verification as the corrective mechanism, and is presumably measured on task completion or plan validity. Paper B addresses noisy/misleading retrieved passages in standard RALM pipelines, with a learned rewriter trained via DPO against a supportiveness signal, evaluated on six knowledge-intensive QA-style benchmarks. The two works diverge on every coordinate: the problem they fix (bad plans vs. unhelpful retrieved text), the evidence modality (structured KG vs. unstructured retrieved passages), the place of intervention (planner with symbolic check vs. pre-generation rewrite stage), the success metric (complex task execution vs. QA performance), and the policy itself (search/verify loop vs. preference-optimized rewriting). Even allowing for the missing snippet on Paper A, the title alone fixes its task family clearly enough to rule out direct comparability.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both systems to be run on a shared benchmark suite, with identical retrievers/KGs where possible, the same base LLM, matched compute and prompt budget, and a single primary outcome metric (e.g., end-task success on a complex-task benchmark that both pipelines can plausibly attempt, or a knowledge-intensive QA suite where the planner is reduced to a single-step retriever). Without such shared conditions, the reported numbers live in different evaluation regimes.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems target different problem settings, use different forms of supporting information, and are scored on different benchmark families. Placing their headline numbers side by side on one leaderboard would suggest a head-to-head ordering that does not exist, and a practitioner choosing between them based on such a table would likely pick the wrong tool for their use case.

paper_a_title: Overcoming the Retrieval Barrier: Indirect Prompt Injection in the Wild for LLM Systems
paper_b_title: GRACE: Reinforcement Learning for Grounded Response and Abstention under Contextual Evidence
gold_rationale: Paper A is an offensive/red-team study on indirect prompt injection: it crafts trigger fragments to guarantee retrieval of poisoned content and reports attack success rates (e.g., ~80% SSH key exfiltration, near-100% retrieval) across embedding models and benchmarks. Paper B is a defensive training method (RL with a multi-stage gated reward) that teaches a model to ground answers in evidence or abstain, measured by overall accuracy and the balance between answering and refusing on QA benchmarks. The failure_type (adversarial corpus poisoning vs. ungrounded/hallucinated answers), evidence_assumption (attacker-controllable corpus vs. mixed-sufficiency retrieved context), intervention_point (crafted attack fragment in the corpus vs. RL fine-tuning of the generator), metric_target (retrieval/attack success vs. answer accuracy and abstention quality), and action_policy (maximize hijacked behavior vs. answer-or-abstain) all diverge. No common benchmark, threat model, or scoring metric connects them.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A shared task setup where both works are evaluated on the same RAG pipeline, the same corpus and queries, and a common metric — for example, running Paper B's GRACE-trained generator as a defense against Paper A's IPI attack and reporting attack success rate and grounded-answer/abstention accuracy under identical retrievers, corpora, and adversary budgets. Absent that, any leaderboard comparison would conflate offense and defense numbers measured on disjoint benchmarks.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two papers pursue opposite goals on different problem setups: one quantifies how often an adversary can hijack a retrieval-augmented system, while the other reports question-answering quality and willingness to refuse on standard QA benchmarks. Their headline numbers live on incompatible scales and conditions, so juxtaposing them on a single leaderboard would lead a practitioner to draw conclusions that neither paper supports.

paper_a_title: DRAGged into Conflicts: Detecting and Addressing Conflicting Sources in Search-Augmented LLMs
paper_b_title: Rescuing the Unpoisoned: Efficient Defense against Knowledge Corruption Attacks on RAG Systems
gold_rationale: Paper A targets naturally occurring knowledge conflicts among legitimate retrieved sources (e.g., temporal/freshness mismatches, controversial-topic disagreements) and proposes a taxonomy plus prompting-based reasoning, measured by response quality/appropriateness on the CONFLICTS benchmark. Paper B targets adversarial data-poisoning of the corpus and proposes a post-retrieval lightweight ML filter (RAGDEFENDER), measured by Attack Success Rate reduction against baselines like RobustRAG and Discern-and-Answer. The threat model, the assumption about whether retrieved passages are benign or attacker-controlled, where in the pipeline the change is made, the evaluation metric, and the desired system behavior all diverge. None of the five coordinates align, so a head-to-head comparison is not meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both works would need a shared threat model (either benign source disagreement or adversarial poisoning), a common benchmark containing the same type of conflicting/poisoned passages, the same evaluation metric (e.g., either appropriateness/coverage of conflicting answers, or ASR/clean accuracy under attack), and ideally overlapping baselines and LLM backbones. Minimally, one paper would need to be re-evaluated under the other's setting (e.g., running RAGDEFENDER on CONFLICTS, or running the conflict-reasoning prompt under the poisoning benchmark with ASR).
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems address fundamentally different problems: one helps a model behave sensibly when legitimate retrieved passages disagree (e.g., outdated facts vs. recent ones, or differing opinions), while the other defends a retrieval pipeline against deliberately injected malicious passages. Their reported numbers are computed on different datasets with different scoring schemes and different baselines, so placing them side by side on a single leaderboard would suggest a competition that does not exist and would push a practitioner toward the wrong tool for their actual problem.

paper_a_title: RoseRAG: Robust Retrieval-augmented Generation with Small-scale LLMs via Margin-aware Preference Optimization
paper_b_title: Faithfulness-Aware Uncertainty Quantification for Fact-Checking the Output of Retrieval Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Paper A (RoseRAG) targets noise-robust answer generation in small-scale LLMs via margin-aware preference optimization, reporting QA quality scores such as Exact Match and F1 on open-domain QA benchmarks. Paper B (FRANQ) targets hallucination detection in RAG outputs via uncertainty quantification, with an explicit distinction between faithfulness and factuality, evaluated as a detection task on a new long-form QA dataset. The two works differ on essentially every coordinate: what counts as the problem (noise-induced wrong answers vs. unfaithful/non-factual claims), what is done about it (training-time preference optimization vs. post-hoc per-statement scoring), the locus of the change (the generator itself vs. an external verifier), and what is reported (generation quality scores vs. error-detection performance). They therefore cannot be ranked on a shared leaderboard.

Paper A targets a training-time failure in multimodal LLMs (lack of unified generative+discriminative objectives) and intervenes by modifying the training procedure to improve multimodal understanding benchmarks. Paper B targets an inference-time efficiency failure in retrieval-augmented generation and intervenes by introducing sparse context selection to reduce latency/compute while preserving answer quality. They diverge on what is broken, what evidence is assumed sufficient, where in the pipeline the change is applied, which numbers are optimized (multimodal accuracy vs. throughput/latency), and what concrete recipe is prescribed. All five coordinates differ, so a direct comparison or ranking is not meaningful.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers would need to address the same underlying problem class (e.g., either both target inference efficiency of multimodal/RAG systems, or both target training-time quality improvements), share at least one common benchmark and primary scoring criterion, operate at the same stage of the pipeline, and propose alternative recipes whose outputs could be plotted on the same axes. None of these conditions plausibly hold here.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two works sit in different subfields and pursue different end goals: one improves how multimodal language models are trained to handle both generation and classification, while the other speeds up retrieval-augmented question answering at runtime by trimming context. A practitioner who saw their headline numbers side-by-side on one leaderboard would be seriously misled, because the systems, tasks, and scoring axes have essentially no overlap.

paper_a_title: CPA-RAG: Covert Poisoning Attacks on Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Large Language Models
paper_b_title: Divide-Then-Align: Honest Alignment based on the Knowledge Boundary of RAG
gold_rationale: All five coordinates diverge. Paper A targets a security failure mode (corpus poisoning) under an adversarial threat model where the evidence base is attacker-controlled, intervenes by crafting adversarial documents at the corpus/injection point, optimizes for attack success rate via black-box prompt-based generation with cross-LLM guidance. Paper B targets an honesty/calibration failure (hallucination when knowledge is absent) under a benign-but-noisy retrieval assumption, intervenes at the model post-training stage via DPO on quadrant-partitioned preference data, and optimizes for a balance of answer accuracy and appropriate abstention. The two systems share only the RAG label; their outcome variables (ASR vs. accuracy/abstention trade-off) are not commensurable.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both papers to address the same problem axis on shared benchmarks with a shared evaluation protocol. For example: (a) both reporting on poisoning robustness with DTA evaluated as a defense against CPA-RAG-style adversarial corpora, measured by post-attack ASR and abstention rate on the same datasets and retriever; or (b) both reporting on honesty/abstention metrics on the same QA benchmarks under matched retrieval conditions. Without such overlap in threat model, evaluation suite, and outcome metric, any head-to-head ranking is ill-defined.
independent_rubric_rationale: Placing these two headline numbers side by side on one leaderboard would seriously mislead a practitioner. One paper reports how often an adversary can force a chosen wrong answer into a RAG pipeline; the other reports how well a tuned model balances giving correct answers with saying 'I don't know.' The numbers measure different phenomena, are computed on different datasets and conditions, and reward opposing behaviors from opposing stakeholder viewpoints (attacker vs. defender of honesty). A reader could wrongly infer that a 90%+ score in one paper is comparable to or competitive with the trustworthiness scores in the other.

paper_a_title: Cutting Off the Head Ends the Conflict: A Mechanism for Interpreting and Mitigating Knowledge Conflicts in Language Models
paper_b_title: A Few Words Can Distort Graphs: Knowledge Poisoning Attacks on Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
gold_rationale: Paper A studies knowledge conflicts arising inside LMs when parametric memory disagrees with retrieved context, and proposes an internal mechanism (PH3 attention-head pruning) to steer the model toward memory or context. Paper B studies an adversarial security threat against graph-based RAG, where an attacker rewrites a tiny fraction of source text to corrupt the constructed knowledge graph and degrade QA accuracy. The failure modes (latent conflict resolution vs. corpus-side poisoning), the place where the work intervenes (attention heads inside the LM vs. raw text upstream of graph construction), the metrics (controllability of memory/context use and QA gains vs. attack success rate and QA collapse), the policy (defensive mitigation vs. offensive attack), and the underlying threat/evidence model are all different. There is no shared leaderboard or task on which these results could be meaningfully ranked.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both papers would need to share a common task and metric on the same RAG/GraphRAG setting—e.g., either (i) Paper A applied to GraphRAG under poisoned corpora measured by attack success / QA accuracy, or (ii) Paper B evaluated as a stress test against a defended pipeline that uses PH3-style head pruning—with matched models, retrievers, datasets, and identical evaluation protocols. Only then could their headline numbers be placed side by side.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two headline numbers describe entirely different phenomena on different pipelines: one quantifies how well an internal-mechanism technique can steer an LM between competing knowledge sources and improve QA, while the other quantifies how easily a tiny edit to source text can collapse GraphRAG accuracy. Putting them on the same leaderboard would suggest a comparison that does not exist and would likely lead a practitioner to draw unwarranted conclusions about robustness or effectiveness.

paper_a_title: FiD-Light: Efficient and Effective Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
paper_b_title: SURE-RAG: Sufficiency and Uncertainty-Aware Evidence Verification for Selective Retrieval-Augmented Generation
gold_rationale: Paper A (FiD-Light) targets efficiency/latency of retrieval-augmented generation via a decoder-side architectural change while still always producing an answer, and is evaluated on generation quality plus throughput/latency. Paper B (SURE-RAG) targets a different failure mode—unverified or insufficient evidence—via a post-retrieval set-level verifier that enables three-way abstention (SUPPORTED/REFUTED/INSUFFICIENT), and is evaluated with Macro-F1 on sufficiency labels plus risk@coverage on HotpotQA-RAG v3 and HaluBench. The two systems sit at different layers of the RAG pipeline, optimize different objectives, and use disjoint benchmarks and metrics; the answering policy itself differs (always-answer vs selective abstain). No common leaderboard exists.
what_valid_comparison_requires: Both systems would need to be evaluated on the same benchmark with a shared metric set covering both efficiency (latency/FLOPs/throughput) and answer reliability under a comparable answering policy (either both always-answer with quality scores, or both selective with risk@coverage). Minimally, FiD-Light would need to be wrapped with a sufficiency/abstention head, and SURE-RAG would need to be paired with a generator and timed end-to-end on a dataset like HotpotQA or a NaturalQuestions/KILT setting common to both.
independent_rubric_rationale: The two systems address fundamentally different problems within the broader RAG pipeline: one is about making generation faster while keeping answer quality, the other is about deciding when not to answer based on the quality of retrieved evidence. They report numbers on different datasets with different scoring schemes, so placing their headline scores side-by-side on a single ranked list would give a practitioner a false impression that one is 'better' than the other, when in fact they could be deployed together rather than as substitutes.

paper_a_title: The LiveRAG Challenge at SIGIR 2025
paper_b_title: Multi-Hop Paragraph Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
gold_rationale: Based on titles alone (no snippets available), Paper A is a 2025 challenge overview report summarizing a community competition on Retrieval-Augmented Generation, while Paper B is a 2019 methodological contribution proposing a specific multi-hop paragraph retrieval algorithm for open-domain QA. The failure_type differs (broad RAG system limitations addressed by many submissions vs. specifically multi-hop reasoning gaps in single-step retrievers). The evidence_assumption differs (LiveRAG's bespoke corpus and questions vs. likely HotpotQA-style benchmarks). The intervention_point differs (a meta-paper aggregating diverse participant approaches vs. one targeted retriever design). The metric_target differs (challenge-specific scoring vs. retrieval precision/recall on multi-hop benchmarks). The action_policy differs (report and synthesize findings across teams vs. recommend a particular retrieval architecture). the two artifacts operate at fundamentally different levels of analysis and on different data.
what_valid_comparison_requires: A valid comparison would require both papers to evaluate on a shared benchmark with overlapping metrics, address the same retrieval task formulation (e.g., both reporting multi-hop retrieval scores on the same dataset), and present numbers at compatible levels of granularity (system-level method comparison rather than challenge aggregate vs. single method). Additionally, controlling for the six-year gap in foundational models and corpora would be necessary, or restricting the comparison to a clearly delimited subtask where both report comparable numbers.
independent_rubric_rationale: One paper summarizes a 2025 community competition that aggregates results across many participating teams on a custom RAG task, while the other is a 2019 paper proposing a specific algorithm for multi-hop paragraph retrieval evaluated on standard QA benchmarks. Placing their headline numbers side by side on a single leaderboard would mislead a practitioner because the two works differ in scope (aggregate report vs. single proposed method), in the underlying datasets, in the era of base models available, and in what counts as a top-line score. A reader could easily draw unsupported conclusions about progress or relative quality.
